children.title: CSP Antecedents
children.top_down_role: Centralized constraint-satisfaction lineage relevant to distributed formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: CSP Antecedents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-domain constraint satisfaction underlying distributed feasibility models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite constraint satisfaction problem is a tuple \(P=(X,D,C)\), where \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) is a finite variable set, each variable \(x_i\) has a finite nonempty domain \(D_i\), and every constraint \(c\in C\) is a relation \(R_c\subseteq\prod_{x_i\in S_c}D_i\) on a scope \(S_c\subseteq X\). A solution is an assignment \(a\in\prod_{i=1}^nD_i\) satisfying \(a|_{S_c}\in R_c\) for every \(c\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite CSP seeks a complete variable assignment belonging to every constraint relation on its specified scope.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and every \(D_i\) are finite.
Each constraint has a specified scope and relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(P)=\{a\in\prod_iD_i: a|_{S_c}\in R_c\text{ for all }c\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: restriction of assignment a to the constraint scope

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-domain CSP definition is mathematically unambiguous
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain CSP definition is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: WCSP Antecedents
children.top_down_role: Centralized weighted-constraint lineage relevant to distributed objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: WCSP Antecedents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical additive, minimization-form weighted CSP antecedent of finite DCOPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite weighted constraint satisfaction problem is a tuple \(P=(X,D,F)\), where \(X\) and \(D=(D_i)_{i=1}^n\) form a finite-domain CSP and each cost function \(f\in F\) maps assignments on its scope \(S_f\) into \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Its objective is
\[a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\prod_iD_i}\sum_{f\in F}f(a|_{S_f}).\]
A value \(+\infty\) may encode a forbidden local tuple; otherwise costs express graded preference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted CSP minimizes the sum of local costs, with infinite cost optionally representing forbidden assignments.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains and the family \(F\) are finite.
Costs combine additively under a minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a}\sum_{f\in F}f(a|_{S_f})\).

notation.meaning: finite family of scoped cost functions

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive finite WCSP convention is standard and explicitly scoped
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive minimization formulation is coherent, but the particular WCSP convention, including extended-real costs, requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: COP Antecedents
children.top_down_role: Centralized constraint-optimization lineage relevant to DCOP models.

knowledge_statements.title: COP Antecedents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain constrained optimization antecedent, using minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-domain constraint optimization problem is a tuple \(P=(X,D,C,g)\), where \((X,D,C)\) is a finite CSP and \(g:\prod_iD_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is an objective function. Writing \(S=\operatorname{Sol}(X,D,C)\), the problem is feasible exactly when \(S\ne\varnothing\), and an optimal solution is any
\[a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in S}g(a).\]
If \(S=\varnothing\), the constrained optimization problem has no feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite COP optimizes an objective over assignments satisfying every hard constraint; an empty feasible set means infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The variable domains are finite and nonempty.
The objective is evaluated on complete assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in S}g(a)\); \(S=\varnothing\Rightarrow\) infeasibility.

notation.meaning: set of assignments satisfying all constraints

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite constrained-optimization formulation is standard
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite constrained-optimization definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but it has no inspectable COP-specific source.

children.title: Centralized-to-Distributed Lineage
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences between centralized antecedents and distributed problem classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Centralized-to-Distributed Lineage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic distribution of a finite centralized constraint model across agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a centralized model have variables \(X\), domains \(D\), and scoped relations or costs \(G\). A distributed representation adds a finite agent set \(A\), a variable-owner map \(o_X:X\to A\), and a constraint-holder map \(o_G:G\to 2^A\setminus\{\varnothing\}\), without changing domains or local functions. It is semantics-preserving when every complete assignment \(a\) has the same feasibility status and, in optimization models, the same aggregate value in both representations. Thus distribution changes ownership and information placement, not the centralized solution set or optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A centralized model becomes distributed by assigning variables and constraints to agents while preserving every assignment’s feasibility and objective value.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has exactly one designated owner.
Every relation or cost is held by at least one agent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}(P_{\mathrm{dist}})=\operatorname{Sol}(P_{\mathrm{cent}})\) and \(F_{\mathrm{dist}}(a)=F_{\mathrm{cent}}(a)\) for every complete assignment \(a\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: semantic preservation cleanly distinguishes distribution from model alteration
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic-preservation idea fits the lineage leaf, but the ownership/holder-map representation is not sourced, and the conclusion introduces F_dist and F_cent without formally defining them.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Feasibility Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite distributed constraint satisfaction with variable ownership and no optimization objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distributed feasibility problem is a tuple \(P=(A,X,D,C,o)\), where \((X,D,C)\) is a finite CSP, \(A\) is a finite agent set, and \(o:X\to A\) assigns each variable to one controlling agent. Constraint scopes may contain variables owned by different agents. A distributed solution is a jointly selected complete assignment \(a\in\prod_iD_i\) such that \(a|_{S_c}\in R_c\) for every \(c\in C\); the instance is infeasible when no such assignment exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents controlling distributed variables must jointly choose an assignment satisfying every local or cross-agent constraint.
assumptions_latex: Each variable has one controlling agent.
All domains, agents, and constraints are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is feasible if and only if \(\bigcap_{c\in C}\{a:a|_{S_c}\in R_c\}\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite DisCSP feasibility formulation is standard
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility formulation is plausible, but a DisCSP-specific source is needed to support the adopted ownership-based definition of distribution.

children.title: Max-DisCSP Models
children.top_down_role: Distributed satisfaction models organized around maximum attainable consistency.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-DisCSP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted violation-minimizing extension of a finite distributed CSP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite distributed CSP \(P=(A,X,D,C,o)\), define the violation indicator of constraint \(c\) by \(v_c(a)=0\) when \(a|_{S_c}\in R_c\) and \(v_c(a)=1\) otherwise. A Max-DisCSP solution is any complete assignment
\[a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\prod_iD_i}\sum_{c\in C}v_c(a).\]
Equivalently, it maximizes the number of satisfied constraints. The ownership structure remains distributed even though solution quality is defined by the global violation count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Max-DisCSP selects a distributed assignment violating as few constraints as possible, equivalently satisfying as many as possible.
assumptions_latex: The constraint set and all domains are finite.
Every constraint has unit violation weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a}\sum_{c\in C}v_c(a)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{a}\sum_{c\in C}(1-v_c(a))\).

notation.meaning: binary violation indicator for constraint c

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: unit-weight Max-DisCSP objective is standard and unambiguous
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-weight violation objective and its equivalence to maximizing satisfied constraints are mathematically correct, but no Max-DisCSP source is supplied.

children.title: Over-Constrained Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Distributed regimes where complete constraint satisfaction is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Over-Constrained Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact distributed feasibility and violation-tolerant optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite distributed CSP is over-constrained when its exact feasible set \(S=\{a:a|_{S_c}\in R_c\text{ for every }c\in C\}\) is empty. In that case no distributed protocol can return an assignment satisfying all constraints. Nevertheless, because the complete-assignment set \(\prod_iD_i\) is finite and nonempty, the violation objective \(V(a)=\sum_{c\in C}v_c(a)\) attains a minimum, and over-constrainedness implies \(\min_aV(a)\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When no assignment satisfies every constraint, exact feasibility fails, but a finite instance still has a minimum-violation assignment.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain is finite and nonempty.
Violations are counted by binary indicators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\varnothing\Rightarrow 1\le\min_{a\in\prod_iD_i}V(a)\le |C|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finiteness directly guarantees attainment of the violation minimum
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary and finite minimum-violation conclusion are coherent, but the record lacks an inspectable source for the over-constrained DisCSP interpretation.

children.title: Violation-Minimization Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for comparing unavoidable constraint violations.

knowledge_statements.title: Violation-Minimization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted, weighted, and lexicographic regimes for violation-tolerant distributed satisfaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For violation indicators \(v_c(a)\), three finite violation-minimization regimes are represented by
\[V_0(a)=\sum_{c\in C}v_c(a),\qquad V_w(a)=\sum_{c\in C}w_cv_c(a),\qquad V_{\mathrm{lex}}(a)=(V_1(a),\ldots,V_k(a)),\]
where \(w_c>0\), constraint classes \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) are priority ordered, and \(V_j(a)=\sum_{c\in C_j}v_c(a)\). The respective solutions minimize \(V_0\), minimize \(V_w\), or lexicographically minimize \(V_{\mathrm{lex}}\). These regimes coincide only under additional restrictions on weights or attainable violation vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Violations may be minimized by count, positive weights, or priority classes ordered lexicographically; these criteria need not select the same assignment.
assumptions_latex: All constraint sets and domains are finite.
Weighted-regime coefficients satisfy \(w_c>0\).
Priority classes form an ordered partition of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}V_0\), \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}V_w\), or \(a^*\in\operatorname*{lexargmin}V_{\mathrm{lex}}\), according to the selected regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: displayed objectives precisely define the three common regimes
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three objectives are clearly distinguished and fit the leaf, but the asserted taxonomy of violation-minimization regimes has no supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Discrete DCOPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite, additive, minimization-form distributed constraint optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite discrete DCOP is a tuple \(P=(A,X,D,F,o)\), where \(A\) is a finite agent set, \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), every \(D_i\) is finite and nonempty, \(o:X\to A\) assigns each variable to an agent, and each scoped cost \(f\in F\) maps \(\prod_{x_i\in S_f}D_i\) into \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Its global objective is
\[a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\prod_iD_i}F(a),\qquad F(a)=\sum_{f\in F}f(a|_{S_f}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite discrete DCOP distributes finite-domain variables among agents and minimizes the sum of scoped costs.
assumptions_latex: The agent, variable, domain, and cost-function families are finite.
Costs aggregate additively under minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\prod_iD_i}\sum_{f\in F}f(a|_{S_f})\).

notation.meaning: scope of local cost function f

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite additive DCOP definition is mathematically unambiguous
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical finite additive DCOP definition is precise and appropriate, but no authoritative DCOP citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Hard-Constraint DCOPs
children.top_down_role: DCOP variants dominated by mandatory feasibility conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Constraint DCOPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DCOPs in which designated local tuples are categorically forbidden.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hard-constraint DCOP is a finite discrete DCOP in which each designated hard cost \(h\) takes values in \(\{0,+\infty\}\). Its hard-feasible set is
\[S_H=\{a\in\textstyle\prod_iD_i:h(a|_{S_h})=0\text{ for every }h\in H\}.\]
An assignment outside \(S_H\) is inadmissible regardless of any finite soft cost. If all costs are hard, the optimization model reduces to distributed constraint satisfaction: every member of \(S_H\) is acceptable, and \(S_H=\varnothing\) means infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard constraints assign infinite cost to forbidden tuples; only assignments satisfying every hard constraint are admissible.
assumptions_latex: The underlying DCOP is finite and uses minimization.
Hard costs take only \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\text{ is admissible}\Longleftrightarrow a\in S_H\).

children.title: Soft-Constraint DCOPs
children.top_down_role: DCOP variants organized around graded preferences or costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Soft-Constraint DCOPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DCOPs whose local preferences are finite-valued and therefore violable at a cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A soft-constraint DCOP is a finite discrete DCOP whose local cost functions satisfy \(f(a|_{S_f})<+\infty\) for every complete assignment \(a\) and every \(f\in F\). Consequently every complete assignment is admissible, although assignments may have different aggregate costs. Since the assignment space is finite and nonempty, the global sum \(F(a)=\sum_{f\in F}f(a|_{S_f})\) attains a minimum. Soft constraints rank assignments rather than categorically excluding them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-valued soft constraints rank all complete assignments by aggregate cost without making any assignment categorically infeasible.
assumptions_latex: All domains and the cost-function family are finite.
Every local cost is real-valued on every local tuple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\prod_iD_i}F(a)\ne\varnothing\) and every \(a\in\prod_iD_i\) is admissible.

notation.meaning: sum of all finite local costs

children.title: Mixed Hard–Soft Feasibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Interactions between mandatory feasibility and preference optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Hard–Soft Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility and optimization boundary for finite DCOPs containing both hard and soft costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a finite DCOP contain hard costs \(H\), valued in \(\{0,+\infty\}\), and finite soft costs \(Q\). Define \(S_H=\{a:h(a|_{S_h})=0\text{ for all }h\in H\}\). The mixed model is feasible if and only if \(S_H\ne\varnothing\). When feasible, its solutions are
\[a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in S_H}\sum_{q\in Q}q(a|_{S_q}).\]
When \(S_H=\varnothing\), no improvement in soft cost restores feasibility; at least one hard constraint must instead be relaxed or changed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hard constraints determine feasibility; among hard-feasible assignments, soft costs determine optimality. Soft-cost improvement cannot repair an empty hard-feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP has finite nonempty domains.
Every hard cost is binary extended-valued and every soft cost is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is feasible}\Longleftrightarrow S_H\ne\varnothing\), with \(a^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in S_H}\sum_{q\in Q}q(a|_{S_q})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Variable Agent Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard one-agent–one-variable DCOP ownership model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite set of agents, \(X=\{x_i:i\in I\}\) a finite set of decision variables, and \(D_i\neq\varnothing\) the domain of \(x_i\). A single-variable agent model is a DCOP equipped with a bijection \(o:X\to A\). Agent \(o(x_i)\) exclusively selects the value of \(x_i\), while objective factors may involve variables owned by several agents. A joint assignment is \(x\in\prod_{i\in I}D_i\), and ownership affects control and communication but not the feasible assignment set or global objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent exclusively controls exactly one variable; objective factors may still couple variables controlled by different agents.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(X\) are finite.
\(D_i\neq\varnothing\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(o:X\to A\) is bijective, and \(o(x_i)\) uniquely controls \(x_i\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the bijective one-agent–one-variable convention and exclusivity claim require an authoritative DCOP source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Variable Agent Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitioned variable ownership allowing several variables per agent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite agent set and \(X\) a finite variable set with nonempty domains. A multi-variable agent model is a DCOP equipped with a total ownership map \(o:X\to A\). For each agent \(a\in A\), its controlled block is \(X_a=o^{-1}(\{a\})\); the nonempty blocks form a partition of \(X\), and an agent may control more than one variable. The agent chooses assignments in \(\prod_{x_i\in X_a}D_i\), while factors may couple variables belonging to different blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables are partitioned among agents, and each agent may jointly control a block containing several variables.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(X\) are finite.
Every variable has a nonempty domain.
\(o:X\to A\) is total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=\bigsqcup_{a\in o(X)}X_a\), where \(X_a=o^{-1}(\{a\})\).

notation.meaning: variable block controlled by agent a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind fits, but a total ownership map permits empty agent blocks and does not require any agent to own multiple variables. A source must establish the intended multi-variable-agent convention.

children.title: Shared Variable Models
children.top_down_role: Representations in which multiple agents participate in a common variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Variable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct joint control of one logical variable by multiple agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite agent set and \(X\) a finite set of logical variables. A shared-variable model assigns each variable \(x_i\in X\) a nonempty controller set \(O_i\subseteq A\). All agents in \(O_i\) refer to the same variable and the same value in \(D_i\), rather than maintaining distinct local copies. A joint assignment therefore contains one coordinate \(x_i\) for each logical variable, and any admissible update of \(x_i\) must satisfy the model's joint-authorization rule for \(O_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Several agents may control the same logical variable, whose assignment contains only one value rather than separate replicas.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(X\) are finite.
\(D_i\neq\varnothing\) and \(\varnothing\neq O_i\subseteq A\) for every \(x_i\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i\) contributes exactly one coordinate to \(\prod_i D_i\), even when \(|O_i|>1\).

notation.meaning: agents jointly controlling logical variable x_i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the leaf, but direct shared control and the unspecified joint-authorization rule are model-dependent and cannot be validated without a precise source.

children.title: Replicated Variable Models
children.top_down_role: Representations using agent-local copies of logically related variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Replicated Variable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-copy representation of shared logical variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let logical variable \(x_i\) have domain \(D_i\) and replica-holder set \(R_i\subseteq A\). Its replicated representation replaces \(x_i\) by local copies \(x_i^a\in D_i\) for \(a\in R_i\). Each holder updates or stores only its copy, and factors are expressed using designated local copies. The replicated model represents the original logical-variable model on the consistency set \(C_i=\{(x_i^a)_{a\in R_i}:x_i^a=x_i^b\text{ for all }a,b\in R_i\}\); projection of any point in \(C_i\) yields the unique logical value \(x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logical variable is replaced by agent-local copies; equal copies uniquely represent the original variable value.
assumptions_latex: \(R_i\) is finite and nonempty.
Every replica \(x_i^a\) has the common domain \(D_i\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_i\) is in bijection with \(D_i\) through the common replica value.

notation.meaning: replica-holder set for logical variable x_i
agent a's local replica of x_i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and equality-set construction are coherent, but the claims about holder updates, factor copies, and equivalence to the logical-variable model require a DCOP replication source.

children.title: Cross-Replica Consistency
children.top_down_role: Structural consistency requirements among replicated variable views.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Replica Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact consensus condition for replicas of each logical variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each logical variable \(x_i\), let \(R_i\) be its nonempty replica-holder set and let \(x_i^a\in D_i\) denote holder \(a\)'s copy. Exact cross-replica consistency holds precisely when every pair of copies of the same logical variable agrees: \[x_i^a=x_i^b\qquad\text{for every }i\text{ and every }a,b\in R_i.\] Equivalently, for each \(i\) there exists \(z_i\in D_i\) such that \(x_i^a=z_i\) for all \(a\in R_i\). No equality is required between replicas belonging to different logical variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicas are consistent exactly when all copies of each logical variable have one common value.
assumptions_latex: \(R_i\neq\varnothing\) for each logical variable.
All replicas indexed by \(R_i\) use the same domain \(D_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall i\;\exists z_i\in D_i\;\forall a\in R_i:\ x_i^a=z_i\).

notation.meaning: replica of logical variable x_i held by agent a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no source supports exact equality as the intended cross-replica consistency semantics in this taxonomy.

children.title: Factor Ownership
children.top_down_role: Allocation of graphical-model factors to participating agents.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment of objective-factor responsibility to agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite agent set and let a DCOP objective be \(F(x)=\sum_{k\in K}f_k(x_{S_k})\), where \(S_k\) is the scope of factor \(f_k\). A factor-ownership regime is a total map \(q:K\to A\). Agent \(q(k)\) is responsible for storing or evaluating \(f_k\) and issuing factor-dependent messages, but need not own every variable in \(S_k\). The ownership map changes the distributed representation, not the centralized function \(F\), provided every factor appears exactly once with unchanged scope and values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each objective factor is assigned to one responsible agent, independently of which agents own the factor's variables.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(K\) are finite.
\(F(x)=\sum_{k\in K}f_k(x_{S_k})\).
\(q:K\to A\) is total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is invariant under \(q\) when every \(f_k\) is retained exactly once and unchanged.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the factor-ownership leaf, but single ownership, storage/evaluation duties, and message responsibility are convention-dependent and unsourced.

children.title: Constraint Ownership
children.top_down_role: Allocation of constraints or their evaluation responsibility to agents.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment of feasibility-constraint responsibility to agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite agent set and let a distributed constraint model contain relations \(C_j\subseteq\prod_{i\in S_j}D_i\) indexed by \(j\in J\). A constraint-ownership regime is a total map \(r:J\to A\). Agent \(r(j)\) stores or checks membership in \(C_j\) and communicates information required to enforce it; ownership does not require control of every variable in \(S_j\). The represented feasible set remains \(\mathcal F=\{x:(x_i)_{i\in S_j}\in C_j\text{ for all }j\in J\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each feasibility constraint is assigned to a responsible agent, while its variables may be controlled by other agents.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(J\) are finite.
Each \(C_j\) is a relation over the domains indexed by \(S_j\).
\(r:J\to A\) is total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\bigcap_{j\in J}\{x:(x_i)_{i\in S_j}\in C_j\}\), independently of \(r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the asserted checking and enforcement responsibilities and their independence from variable control require an authoritative source.

children.title: Ownership Transfer Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where evaluation responsibility changes between agents.

knowledge_statements.title: Ownership Transfer Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantics-preserving reassignment of factor or constraint responsibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) denote the fixed set of factors or constraints and let \(o_t:E\to A\) be the ownership map at stage \(t\). A transfer from \(o_t\) to \(o_{t+1}\) is semantics-preserving when each element \(e\in E\) has exactly one owner after the transfer and its scope, table or defining function, and participation in the global model are unchanged. Under these conditions, reassignment changes only storage, evaluation, and communication responsibility; the centralized objective and feasible set before and after transfer are identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ownership may move between agents without changing the optimization problem if every model element remains unique and unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(A\) are finite.
\(o_t:E\to A\) and \(o_{t+1}:E\to A\) are total.
Every transferred element retains its mathematical definition and multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{t+1}=\mathcal F_t\) and \(F_{t+1}(x)=F_t(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal F_t\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the leaf, but it blends factor and constraint transfers while concluding preservation of both objective and feasibility. Transfer atomicity and preservation conditions need a model-specific source and separate treatment where appropriate.

children.title: Local Knowledge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Agent knowledge restricted to locally held model information.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Knowledge Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agent information restricted to its incident local subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a DCOP with agents \(A\), variables \(X\), and factors \(\{f_k\}_{k\in K}\). For each agent \(a\), let \(X_a\) be its owned variables and let \(K_a=\{k:S_k\cap X_a\neq\varnothing\}\) be its incident factors. A local-knowledge regime gives agent \(a\) the domains of \(X_a\), the definitions of factors assigned or visible to it, and the identities needed to contact incident agents, while withholding nonincident variables and factors unless revealed by messages. Thus its initial information is measurable with respect to its local subproblem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initially, an agent knows its controlled variables, visible incident factors, and relevant neighbors, but not the full global model.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP has finite agent, variable, and factor sets.
Each factor \(f_k\) has a specified scope \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I_a^0\subseteq\sigma(X_a,\{f_k:k\in K_a\},N(a))\).

notation.meaning: factors incident to agent a's variables
agents adjacent to a in the interaction graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Local-knowledge conventions are model-dependent and unsourced. Moreover, saying information is measurable with respect to local data is not correctly expressed by placing an information object inside a sigma-algebra generated from variables, factors, and neighbor identities without defining a probability or measurable-space model.

children.title: Partial Knowledge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Agent knowledge containing incomplete views of relevant DCOP information.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Knowledge Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit visibility subsets between purely local and global knowledge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the global model data be \(M=(X,D,K,\{S_k,f_k\}_{k\in K})\). A partial-knowledge regime specifies for every agent \(a\) a visibility set \(V_a\subseteq M\), interpreted as the model components available to that agent before communication. The regime is genuinely partial when some relevant component is hidden from some agent, so \(V_a\neq M\) for at least one \(a\), while each agent has sufficient data to interpret its owned variables and assigned factors. Message histories may enlarge knowledge over time, but do not retroactively alter \(V_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent initially sees a specified subset of the global model, with at least one relevant component hidden somewhere.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite encoded DCOP model.
Each \(V_a\) contains the domains and definitions needed for agent a's assigned operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_a\subseteq M\) for every \(a\in A\), and \(\exists a\in A:\ V_a\neq M\).

notation.meaning: components initially visible to agent a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but treating the structured tuple M as a set whose components admit ordinary subset relations requires a defined encoding. The sufficiency and relevance conditions are also model-specific and unsourced.

children.title: Knowledge-Visibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits on which model elements are visible across agents.

knowledge_statements.title: Knowledge-Visibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary incidence representation of initial model visibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the agent set and \(M\) a finite set of encoded model components. A knowledge-visibility boundary is represented by an incidence map \(B:A\times M\to\{0,1\}\), where \(B(a,m)=1\) exactly when component \(m\) is initially visible to agent \(a\). The visible information set is \(V_a=\{m\in M:B(a,m)=1\}\), and the boundary is its complement \(H_a=M\setminus V_a\). For a deterministic protocol, agent \(a\)'s action before receiving messages may depend on \(V_a\) and private state, but not on components in \(H_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A visibility matrix records which model components each agent initially sees; pre-message actions cannot depend on hidden components.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(M\) are finite.
The protocol is deterministic before receipt of messages.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The incidence representation fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but the pre-message nondependence claim requires a formal deterministic protocol model and an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Neighbor-Restricted Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication constrained by the DCOP interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(A,E)\) be an undirected agent-interaction graph, where \(\{a,b\}\in E\) when some factor or constraint couples variables controlled by both agents. A coordination protocol is neighbor-restricted if every direct message sent by agent \(a\) at every round has recipient in \(N_G(a)=\{b:\{a,b\}\in E\}\). Information may reach a nonneighbor only through a path of successive neighbor messages. Consequently, after \(t\) synchronous rounds, agent \(a\)'s state can depend only on initial data originating within graph distance at most \(t\) from \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents communicate only across interaction-graph edges; after t synchronous rounds, information can travel at most t hops.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(A,E)\) is the fixed interaction graph.
Communication proceeds in synchronous rounds.
Messages traverse at most one edge per round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Dep}(s_a^t)\subseteq\{b\in A:\operatorname{dist}_G(a,b)\le t\}\).

notation.meaning: neighbors of agent a in G
state of agent a after t rounds
agents whose initial data may influence the state

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the t-hop conclusion needs a distributed-computing source and a formal definition of Dep. It also depends on the stated synchronous, one-edge-per-round model and should not be generalized beyond it.

knowledge_statements.title: Cooperative Team-Objective Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the common-payoff semantics distinguishing cooperative DCOPs from strategic multi-agent optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cooperative distributed constraint optimization problem consists of agents \(A\), variables \(X=\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n\) with finite domains \(D_i\), ownership map \(o:X\to A\), and local cost functions \(f_k:\prod_{i\in S_k}D_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Every agent evaluates a joint assignment \(x\in\prod_iD_i\) through the same team objective \[F(x)=\sum_k f_k(x_{S_k}).\] The cooperative solution set is \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\prod_iD_i}F(x)\); ownership and restricted information affect computation and communication, but not the objective optimized by any agent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All agents optimize the same aggregate cost. Variable ownership and limited information govern coordination, not individual preferences or the definition of optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(X\) are finite.
Each domain \(D_i\) is finite and nonempty.
The extended-real sum \(F(x)\) is well defined for every joint assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) is team-optimal exactly when \(F(x^\star)=\min_{x\in\prod_iD_i}F(x)\).

notation.meaning: scope of local cost function k

review_flags: DCOP-specific authoritative source and exact locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the cooperative-semantics leaf, but the record supplies no citation. A DCOP source with a specific definition, section, or page locator is required to support the common team-objective interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Interested-Agent Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks where common-payoff DCOP semantics cease to model agents with distinct strategic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each agent \(a\in A\) have an individual cost \(J_a(x)\) over joint assignments. The model lies within cooperative team-objective semantics only if there exists a common function \(F\) such that every agent's preference ordering agrees with minimizing \(F\), for example \(J_a(x)=\alpha_aF(x)+\beta_a\) with \(\alpha_a>0\). If two agents rank some assignments oppositely, meaning \(J_a(x)<J_a(y)\) and \(J_b(x)>J_b(y)\), no single team minimizer represents both preferences. Equilibrium, incentive, or mechanism-design concepts are then required in addition to constraint optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing agent rankings cannot be represented by one shared team objective; the problem crosses into strategic optimization and requires equilibrium or incentive analysis.
assumptions_latex: All individual costs \(J_a\) are defined on the same joint-assignment set.
Lower values represent stronger preferences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Opposite rankings by two agents exclude an order-equivalent common team objective.
review_flags: boundary formulation needs a game-theoretic or DCOP source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf, and opposite strict rankings rule out a common objective reproducing both complete orderings. However, the broader assertion that equilibrium, incentive, or mechanism-design concepts are required is not universally implied because multiobjective or bargaining formulations may also apply. An authoritative source is needed to establish the intended DCOP-to-strategic-model boundary.

children.title: Structural Representation Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Graphical representations, reformulations, pseudo-trees, separators, and ordering structures used by distributed search and inference.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems and Applications: A Survey
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems and Applications: A Survey

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Scalable Method for Multiagent Constraint Optimization
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Scalable Method for Multiagent Constraint Optimization

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal graph representation of variable interactions in a finite DCOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) and cost-function scopes \(S_k\subseteq X\), the constraint graph is the undirected graph \(G_X=(X,E_X)\) satisfying \[\{x_i,x_j\}\in E_X\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i\ne j\text{ and }\exists k:\{x_i,x_j\}\subseteq S_k.\] Thus every scope induces a clique. Unary functions create no edge, and distinct functions may induce the same edge. The graph records which variable pairs interact structurally, but it does not retain function identities, values, or the arity of a scope beyond its induced clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables are vertices, and two distinct variables are adjacent exactly when some local cost function contains both; every higher-arity scope becomes a clique.
assumptions_latex: The variable and function collections are finite.
Each function has a specified variable scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_X\) is the primal interaction graph determined by the DCOP scopes.
review_flags: DCOP graph-representation source with exact locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly describes the primal constraint graph and fits the exact leaf, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Agent Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projects variable-level dependencies onto agents under a fixed ownership map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a constraint graph \(G_X=(X,E_X)\), agents \(A\), and ownership map \(o:X\to A\), the agent graph is the undirected graph \(G_A=(A,E_A)\) with \[\{a,b\}\in E_A\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\ne b\text{ and }\exists\{x_i,x_j\}\in E_X:\ o(x_i)=a,\ o(x_j)=b.\] Multiple variable edges between the same pair of agents collapse to one agent edge, while constraints involving only variables owned by one agent create no inter-agent edge. Hence \(G_A\) represents potential direct coordination or communication dependencies between owners.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents are adjacent when they own variables coupled by at least one constraint. Internal constraints create no inter-agent edge, and repeated couplings collapse.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has exactly one owner.
The constraint graph is undirected and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_A\) is the ownership quotient of \(G_X\) after deleting self-loops and merging parallel edges.
review_flags: authoritative DCOP source for the ownership projection is missing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ownership projection is mathematically coherent and the representation kind fits the agent-graph leaf. Because agent-graph conventions can differ, a DCOP source with an exact locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Hypergraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Retains complete constraint scopes as hyperedges rather than replacing them by pairwise edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(X\) and local functions \(\{f_k\}_{k\in K}\) with scopes \(S_k\subseteq X\), the constraint hypergraph is \(H=(X,\mathcal E)\), where \(\mathcal E\) contains one hyperedge \(e_k=S_k\) for each function occurrence. If function identity matters, use the indexed multiset \(\mathcal E=(S_k)_{k\in K}\), allowing equal scopes for distinct functions. Its two-section is the constraint graph having edge \(\{x_i,x_j\}\) whenever both variables occur in some \(S_k\). Unlike that graph, \(H\) preserves the arity and membership of every higher-order interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each function scope is a hyperedge on its variables. The representation preserves higher-order interaction membership that the pairwise constraint graph loses.
assumptions_latex: The collections of variables and functions are finite.
Every function has a nonempty finite scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two-section of \(H\) equals the constraint graph induced by the same scopes.
review_flags: hypergraph definition needs an authoritative constraint-optimization locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hypergraph representation and its two-section relation are precise and locally appropriate, including the distinction between a set and an indexed multiset of scopes. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite representation retaining variables, local functions, and their incidence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For variables \(X\) and indexed local functions \(F=\{f_k\}_{k\in K}\) with scopes \(S_k\subseteq X\), the factor graph is the bipartite graph \(G_F=(X\mathbin{\dot\cup}F,E_F)\) defined by \[\{x_i,f_k\}\in E_F\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_i\in S_k.\] Variable vertices and factor vertices form the two parts, so no variable-variable or factor-factor edge occurs. Together with the labels \(f_k\), the graph represents the separable objective \(F_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)=\sum_{k\in K}f_k(x_{S_k})\) without converting a higher-arity factor into a clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor graph has variable and function vertices; incidence edges connect each function to exactly the variables in its scope.
assumptions_latex: The variable and factor collections are finite.
Every factor is supplied with its scope and numerical table or rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The labeled graph determines the additive objective \(F_{\mathrm{tot}}\) and its factorization.
review_flags: factor-graph source with an exact definition locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bipartite incidence representation is mathematically standard and fits the factor-graph leaf, but the record has no citation. The claim that the labeled graph determines the objective also depends on labels retaining complete factor functions, which should be supported by the cited definition.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Multi-variable agents decomposition for DCOPs
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Multi-variable agents decomposition for DCOPs

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Variable Agent Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transforms multi-variable ownership into single-variable virtual agents while retaining the original team objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agent \(a\) own the block \(X_a=\{x_{a1},\ldots,x_{am_a}\}\). A single-variable decomposition replaces \(a\) by virtual agents \(a_1,\ldots,a_{m_a}\), where \(a_j\) owns \(x_{aj}\), and assigns every original factor \(f_k\) unchanged to its original variable scope. If an algorithm requires each factor to have a unique host, choose a host among the virtual agents incident to that factor without changing its value. The transformed objective satisfies \[\widetilde F(\widetilde x)=F(x)\] under the natural bijection \(\widetilde x_{a_j}=x_{aj}\), so feasible assignments and optima correspond exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split each multi-variable agent into one virtual agent per variable, retain every factor, and use the natural assignment bijection to preserve objective values and optima.
assumptions_latex: Each original variable has exactly one owning agent.
The reformulation changes computational ownership but not variable domains or factor values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The natural bijection preserves every assignment's cost and therefore preserves the optimal solution set.

notation.meaning: variables originally owned by agent a
virtual owner of one original variable

review_flags: DCOP-specific decomposition convention and source are needed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the decomposition leaf, and the stated assignment bijection preserves the objective under the given construction. A DCOP-specific source is still required, especially for the virtual-agent and factor-host conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes exact reformulations obtained by introducing variables and minimizing over their extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be an original objective and let \(Y\) be a product of auxiliary-variable domains. An extended objective \(\widetilde F:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is an exact auxiliary-variable reformulation when \[F(x)=\min_{y\in Y}\widetilde F(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Consequently, \(\min_xF(x)=\min_{x,y}\widetilde F(x,y)\). Every transformed minimizer projects to an original minimizer, and each original minimizer has at least one optimal auxiliary extension whenever the displayed minima are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary reformulation is exact when minimizing its extended objective over auxiliary variables recovers every original assignment cost, ensuring corresponding optimal solutions.
assumptions_latex: The auxiliary minimum exists for every original assignment.
Both objectives use the same minimization convention, including infeasibility encoded by \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection from optimal extended assignments to original variables preserves optimality and the optimal value.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

review_flags: locator is provisional and may not state the pointwise exactness criterion in this form

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise minimization criterion is a coherent exact-reformulation definition, but the cited provisional locator concerns smooth and disjunctive reformulations and is not shown to state this criterion or its projection consequences. The source uncertainty affects the defining formula, so a directly supporting section, theorem, or definition is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Arity Constraint Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact replacement of a high-arity factor by lower-arity factors using auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\prod_{i\in S}D_i\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) have arity \(|S|>r\). An exact arity-\(r\) decomposition introduces auxiliary variables \(y\in Y\) and factors \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\), each depending on at most \(r\) original or auxiliary variables, such that \[f(x_S)=\min_{y\in Y}\sum_{j=1}^m g_j((x_S,y)_{T_j})\qquad\text{for every }x_S.\] Substituting this expression into any additive DCOP objective preserves the minimum value; projected transformed minimizers are original minimizers, provided the auxiliary minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a high-arity factor by lower-arity factors whose minimized sum equals it pointwise; then optimal values and projected optimal assignments are preserved.
assumptions_latex: All original and auxiliary domains are nonempty.
Each replacement scope satisfies \(|T_j|\le r\).
The auxiliary minimum is attained for every original local assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise equality makes the lower-arity model an exact extended formulation of the original factor.
review_flags: exact lower-arity decomposition source and DCOP convention required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, and the pointwise minimized-sum identity is sufficient for the stated optimization preservation under attainment. No authoritative source with a specific locator supports this exact higher-arity decomposition convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Ownership-Preserving Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies when an exact reformulation retains decentralized control of every original variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(o:X\to A\) be the original ownership map and let an exact reformulation use variables \(X\cup Y\) with ownership map \(\widetilde o:X\cup Y\to A\). The reformulation is ownership-preserving when \[\widetilde o(x)=o(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X,\] and each auxiliary variable \(y\in Y\) is assigned to a designated agent without duplicating control of any original variable. Exactness additionally requires \(F(x)=\min_y\widetilde F(x,y)\). Thus projection removes only auxiliary coordinates and returns an assignment controlled by precisely the original owners.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reformulation preserves ownership when every original variable retains its owner, auxiliaries receive designated owners, and projecting auxiliaries recovers the exact original problem.
assumptions_latex: Every variable has one owner before and after reformulation.
The auxiliary-variable reformulation is exact and its relevant minima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection preserves both original ownership assignments and optimal solutions.
review_flags: ownership-preservation terminology needs a DCOP-specific authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind fits the leaf and the original-variable ownership equality is precise. The treatment of auxiliary ownership and the term ownership-preserving require a DCOP-specific authoritative source and locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Depth-First Pseudo-Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the rooted pseudo-tree structure used to organize DCOP dependencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected constraint graph \(G=(V,E)\), a rooted spanning tree \(T=(V,E_T)\) is a depth-first pseudo-tree when every non-tree edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\setminus E_T\) joins comparable vertices in the ancestor order of \(T\): either \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\), or \(v\) is an ancestor of \(u\). Tree edges are parent-child edges; remaining graph edges are pseudo-edges. A spanning tree produced by depth-first search has this property. For a disconnected graph, a pseudo-forest applies the definition separately to each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A depth-first pseudo-tree is a rooted spanning tree in which every original non-tree edge connects a vertex to one of its ancestors.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, undirected, and connected.
\(T\) is a rooted spanning tree of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every edge of \(G\) connects two vertices comparable in the ancestor order of \(T\).
review_flags: authoritative DCOP pseudo-tree definition and locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the depth-first pseudo-tree leaf and correctly states the ancestor-comparability property for non-tree edges in an undirected DFS tree. No DCOP or graph-theoretic source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Ancestor Separators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the ancestor context separating a pseudo-tree subtree from the remaining constraint graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a rooted pseudo-tree of \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(V_i\) be the vertices in the subtree rooted at \(i\). The ancestor separator of \(i\) is \[\operatorname{Sep}(i)=\{a\in V\setminus V_i: a\text{ is an ancestor of }i\text{ in }T\text{ and }\exists v\in V_i\text{ with }\{a,v\}\in E\}.\] Removing \(\operatorname{Sep}(i)\) eliminates every graph edge from \(V_i\) to \(V\setminus(V_i\cup\operatorname{Sep}(i))\). Hence, after fixing separator assignments, the subtree's cost contribution is conditionally independent of all other outside variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ancestor separator contains outside ancestors adjacent to a subtree. Fixing their assignments isolates that subtree from every other outside variable.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected constraint graph.
\(T\) is a rooted depth-first pseudo-tree of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sep}(i)\) separates \(V_i\) from all remaining vertices outside the subtree.

notation.meaning: vertices in the subtree rooted at i

review_flags: separator terminology varies across DCOP algorithms; authoritative locator required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separator definition is coherent for a depth-first pseudo-tree and the content kind fits the leaf. Because separator/context terminology varies across DCOP algorithms and the conditional-independence interpretation depends on the objective factorization, an authoritative source with an exact locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Induced-Width Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the filled primal graph under a fixed elimination ordering and states a worst-case tabular storage bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) in order. Immediately before eliminating \(v_i\), connect every pair of its remaining neighbors, and let \(N_i^+\) denote those neighbors. The induced width of \(\pi\) is \[w_\pi=\max_{1\le i\le n}|N_i^+|.\] Equivalently, \(w_\pi+1\) is the maximum clique size formed by an eliminated vertex together with its remaining neighbors. If every variable domain has size at most \(q\), a tabular function produced by eliminating \(v_i\) has at most \(q^{|N_i^+|}\) entries; hence the worst-case maximum table size is at most \(q^{w_\pi}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Induced width is the maximum number of remaining neighbors encountered after fill edges are added. With domains of size at most q, an intermediate table has at most q raised to the induced width entries.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP primal graph is a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\).
A total elimination ordering \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) is fixed.
Every variable domain has size at most \(q\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced width is \(w_\pi=\max_i|N_i^+|\), and the largest generated tabular scope has at most \(q^{w_\pi}\) entries.

notation.meaning: remaining neighbors of vertex \(v_i\) after fill edges are added

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard induced-width definition and tabular scope bound

children.title: Pseudo-Tree Depth
children.top_down_role: Depth characteristics of pseudo-tree organizations.

assumptions_latex: The pseudo-tree \(T=(V,E_T)\) is finite and rooted at \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its depth is \(d(T)=\max_{v\in V}\operatorname{dist}_T(r,v)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard rooted-tree depth applied to a DCOP pseudo-tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth is measured in tree edges; a one-vertex pseudo-tree has depth zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each vertex \(v\in V\), its level is the number of tree edges on the unique path from the root \(r\) to \(v\). The pseudo-tree depth is \[d(T)=\max_{v\in V}\operatorname{dist}_T(r,v).\] Any protocol whose causal dependency follows every root-to-leaf tree edge sequentially has a critical path of at least \(d(T)\) communication steps. A complete downward-and-upward traversal has critical-path length at least \(2d(T)\), apart from local computation and communication latency conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-tree depth is the maximum root-to-vertex tree distance and determines the critical-path length of protocols that propagate information along tree edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Tree Depth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted-tree depth definition is precise and fits the leaf, but the DCOP communication critical-path claims have no inspectable source or specified protocol model.

children.title: Branch-Level Parallelism
children.top_down_role: Concurrency exposed by structurally independent pseudo-tree branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Level Parallelism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallelism is conditional on a fixed assignment to all ancestor variables appearing in the child separators and on independent communication resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) have children \(c\in\operatorname{ch}_T(v)\), and let \(S_c\) be the ancestor separator of the subtree rooted at \(c\). If every primal-graph edge from that subtree to a vertex outside it ends in \(S_c\), then fixing a compatible assignment \(s\) to \(\bigcup_{c\in\operatorname{ch}_T(v)}S_c\) separates the optimization problems in the distinct child subtrees. Their optimal conditional costs \(U_c(s|_{S_c})\) may therefore be computed concurrently, and their combined contribution at \(v\) is \[\sum_{c\in\operatorname{ch}_T(v)}U_c(s|_{S_c}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once compatible assignments to the child separators are fixed, distinct child subtrees are independent. Their conditional optimal costs can be computed concurrently and summed at the parent.
assumptions_latex: The rooted pseudo-tree \(T\) separates each child subtree from the rest of the primal graph through its ancestor separator.
The separator assignments are mutually compatible.
Messages on distinct communication links may proceed concurrently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conditioned on the relevant separator assignment, child-subtree computations can execute concurrently and their conditional optimal costs combine additively.

notation.meaning: ancestor separator of the subtree rooted at child \(c\)
optimal cost of child subtree \(c\) conditioned on the restriction of assignment \(s\) to \(S_c\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional separability of pseudo-tree branches

children.title: Depth–Concurrency Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural relationships between pseudo-tree depth and available concurrency.

assumptions_latex: A pseudo-tree-based exact DCOP method performs sequential propagation along tree paths and concurrent work across conditionally independent branches.
Per-edge latency and local workload are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reducing \(d(T)\) shortens the propagation critical path, while increasing independent branch counts enlarges available concurrency; neither criterion alone controls induced width.

notation.meaning: number of simultaneously ready independent branches at level \(\ell\)
induced width associated with the pseudo-tree ordering

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: critical-path versus branch-parallelism tradeoff in pseudo-tree algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A structural principle, not a universal runtime formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted pseudo-tree \(T\), sequential root-to-leaf dependencies contribute a critical path proportional to \(d(T)\), whereas up to \(b_\ell(T)\) conditionally independent branches at level \(\ell\) may be processed concurrently. Thus, under uniform step latency, the structural parallel time is bounded below by a depth term, while attainable speedup is bounded by the available branch count. Replacing \(T\) by a shallower tree can increase separator sizes and \(w(T)\), so minimizing depth need not minimize memory, message size, or total computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shallow pseudo-trees shorten sequential propagation and broad levels offer concurrency, but these gains may enlarge separators and induced width, increasing memory and total inference work.
knowledge_statements.title: Depth–Concurrency Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local scope are appropriate, but the asserted relationship between shallower pseudo-trees, separators, and induced width requires an inspectable DCOP source.

assumptions_latex: Each agent controls one variable in a finite connected DCOP primal graph \(G=(V,E)\).
Agents communicate reliably with graph neighbors and use unique identifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The protocol outputs a total order \(\pi\) known consistently to all agents, without changing the DCOP objective.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distributed greedy ordering with deterministic tie breaking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a generic synchronous distributed greedy ordering protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U=V\) and \(\pi=()\). In round \(k\), every agent in \(U\) computes a deterministic priority \(p_k(v)\) from currently available structural data, such as remaining degree or estimated fill. Agents perform neighbor communication and a distributed reduction to select the lexicographically minimum pair \((p_k(v),\operatorname{id}(v))\). Append the selected variable \(v_k\) to \(\pi\), broadcast its selection, update local structural data, and set \(U\leftarrow U\setminus\{v_k\}\). Stop when \(U=\varnothing\); output \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents repeatedly elect one unnumbered variable using a shared structural priority and identifier tie-break, broadcast the choice, update local scores, and thereby construct a consistent total order.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Variable Ordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a plausible distributed ordering template, but the reduction, dissemination, structural-data update, synchronization, and complexity model are unspecified. No source identifies or validates the protocol.

assumptions_latex: The finite primal graph \(G=(V,E)\) is connected.
Agents communicate reliably with graph neighbors and have distinct identifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The protocol returns a rooted spanning tree \(T\) in which every non-tree edge of \(G\) joins a vertex to one of its ancestors.

notation.meaning: parent of vertex \(v\) in the tree

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distributed depth-first traversal constructs a DFS pseudo-tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a token-based distributed depth-first traversal of a connected primal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose the minimum-identifier agent as root and give it a traversal token. When an unvisited agent \(v\) first receives the token from \(u\), set \(p(v)=u\), mark \(v\) visited, and forward the token to its least ordered unvisited neighbor. When none remains, return the token to \(p(v)\); already visited neighbors are recorded as pseudo-edges. Terminate when the root has exhausted its neighbors. The parent edges form a rooted spanning tree \(T\), and the depth-first traversal ensures that every edge in \(E\setminus E_T\) connects ancestor-related vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed depth-first token traversal assigns first-contact parents and records edges to visited agents as pseudo-edges, producing a rooted DFS pseudo-tree of the primal graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Pseudo-Tree Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A serial distributed DFS can construct the stated pseudo-tree, but root election, visited-state coordination, token handling, and termination detection need a cited protocol. No supporting source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Consistency Preprocessing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain feasibility preprocessing by distributed generalized arc consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each constraint \(C_a\subseteq\prod_{j\in S_a}D_j\) and each \(i\in S_a\), compute the currently supported values \[P_{a,i}=\left\{d\in D_i:\exists x_{S_a\setminus\{i\}}\in\prod_{j\in S_a\setminus\{i\}}D_j\text{ such that }(d,x_{S_a\setminus\{i\}})\in C_a\right\}.\] Replace \(D_i\) by \(D_i\cap P_{a,i}\), notify affected constraint agents after every deletion, and recompute affected supports. Under fair processing and eventual message delivery, stop at distributed quiescence or when some \(D_i=\varnothing\). The resulting domains form a fixed point of generalized arc consistency, and every value occurring in a globally feasible assignment is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents repeatedly delete values that lack support among the current domains of the other variables in a constraint. With fair processing and reliable eventual delivery, the process reaches generalized arc-consistency or detects an empty domain without deleting any globally feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: Every variable \(x_i\) has a finite current domain \(D_i\).
Each constraint is a relation \(C_a\subseteq\prod_{j\in S_a}D_j\) available to the agents responsible for its scope.
Every affected support check is eventually processed and every notification is eventually delivered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure reaches a generalized arc-consistency fixed point or an empty domain and preserves every globally feasible assignment.

notation.meaning: values of \(x_i\) currently supported by constraint \(C_a\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distributed generalized arc-consistency fixed-point procedure

children.title: DCOP Extension Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical extensions distinguished by valuation structure, objectives, time variation, uncertainty, controllability, resources, openness, and variable domains.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems and Applications: A Survey
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Distributed Constraint Optimization Problems and Applications: A Survey

assumptions_latex: Agents are indexed by a finite set \(A\), and variables have finite domains.
Each local cost function is assigned to exactly one evaluating agent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment \(x\) has social cost \(F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}F_a(x)\), while distinct agents may assign different costs to the same joint decision.

notation.meaning: cost function owned by agent \(a\) on scope \(S_{a,k}\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: agent-indexed decomposition of asymmetric DCOP costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents asymmetry by retaining the identity of the agent evaluating each local cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each agent \(a\in A\), let \(\mathcal{K}_a\) index its owned cost functions and define \[F_a(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_a}f_{a,k}(x_{S_{a,k}}),\qquad F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}F_a(x).\] Agent-specific representation permits functions owned by different agents to have the same scope but unequal values: for some \(a\ne b\), scope \(S\), and assignment \(x_S\), one may have \(f_{a}(x_S)\ne f_b(x_S)\). An asymmetric DCOP minimizes \(F(x)\) subject to all variable-domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric DCOP keeps separate cost functions for each evaluating agent; the global objective sums these local objectives even when agents value the same joint assignment differently.
knowledge_statements.title: Agent-Specific Cost Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The agent-indexed cost representation is coherent and fits the leaf, but no cited source establishes that this is the intended asymmetric-DCOP formalism or aggregation convention.

assumptions_latex: Variables have finite domains and are placed in a fixed total order \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\).
All incremental agent-specific costs can be evaluated when their scopes become assigned, and costs are bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon termination, the incumbent assignment minimizes the summed agent-specific cost over all complete assignments.

notation.meaning: valid lower bound extending partial assignment \(P_k\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: synchronous distributed branch-and-bound template for asymmetric costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic complete synchronous branch-and-bound family, not one named SyncABB variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the incumbent bound \(B=+\infty\) and an empty partial assignment. Following the fixed variable order, the responsible agent extends \(P_k\) by each value of \(x_{k+1}\), obtains all newly determined agent-specific costs, and computes a valid lower bound \(L(P_{k+1})\). Prune an extension when \(L(P_{k+1})\ge B\); otherwise continue synchronously. For a complete assignment \(P_n\), replace \(B\) and the incumbent whenever its total cost is smaller. Backtrack after exhausting a domain, and terminate after the root exhausts all values. Output the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SyncABB methods synchronously extend an ordered partial assignment, aggregate asymmetric incremental costs, prune branches whose lower bound reaches the incumbent, and return the best complete assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: SyncABB Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic finite branch-and-bound template is mathematically plausible, but it is not tied to a documented SyncABB family or variant, and synchronization, cost disclosure, lower-bound construction, and termination are underspecified.

assumptions_latex: The asymmetric DCOP has finite domains and agent-indexed local costs.
A rooted pseudo-tree is fixed, and every generated utility table retains all cost components needed for exact aggregation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact elimination and aggregation return \(\min_x\sum_{a\in A}F_a(x)\), provided no component is discarded or approximated.

notation.meaning: agent-indexed utility table sent by node \(i\)
local agent-specific costs assigned to node \(i\)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pseudo-tree elimination extended with agent-indexed asymmetric cost components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exact inference template preserving agent-indexed cost information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At each pseudo-tree node \(i\), collect child tables and form \[Q_i(x_i,x_{S_i})=F_i^{\mathrm{loc}}(x_i,x_{S_i})+\sum_{c\in\operatorname{ch}(i)}U_c(x_{S_c}).\] Retain agent-indexed entries until every asymmetric contribution determined at \(i\) has been incorporated, then eliminate \(x_i\) by \[U_i(x_{S_i})=\min_{x_i\in D_i}Q_i(x_i,x_{S_i}).\] Send \(U_i\) to the parent. The root minimizes its aggregate table, after which a downward pass selects compatible minimizing values. Stop after every variable has selected a value; output the resulting assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymmetric inference propagates separator tables while preserving each agent’s cost contributions, eliminates variables by minimization, and reconstructs an optimal assignment in a downward pass.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Inference Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a generic elimination template rather than a sourced asymmetric inference family. Exactness depends on cost ownership and scope-allocation conditions that are not fully specified or cited.

assumptions_latex: Every complete assignment \(x\in X\) has an objective vector \(F(x)=(F_1(x),\ldots,F_m(x))\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
Weights satisfy \(\lambda_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scalarized DCOP minimizes \(S_\lambda(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_jF_j(x)\); every minimizer is weakly Pareto efficient, and it is Pareto efficient when all weights are positive.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted-sum scalarization and its Pareto-efficiency implications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted-sum scalarization for finite multiobjective DCOP assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F(x)=(F_1(x),\ldots,F_m(x))\), choose \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) with \(\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j=1\) and define \[S_\lambda(x)=\lambda^\top F(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_jF_j(x).\] The scalarized model is \(\min_{x\in X}S_\lambda(x)\), which is an ordinary scalar DCOP whenever each \(F_j\) decomposes into local costs. Any minimizer is weakly Pareto efficient. If \(\lambda_j>0\) for every \(j\), every minimizer is Pareto efficient, although varying weights need not recover unsupported Pareto points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted-sum model combines all objectives using nonnegative normalized weights. Its optima are weakly Pareto efficient, and positive weights yield Pareto-efficient solutions, but unsupported points may be missed.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalarized Multiobjective Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-sum representation and Pareto-efficiency statements are standard and internally consistent, but no authoritative source supports their multiobjective-DCOP specialization or the unsupported-point claim.

assumptions_latex: The feasible assignment set \(X\) is nonempty.
Each assignment has a minimization objective vector \(F(x)\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pareto set is \(P=\{x\in X:\nexists y\in X\text{ with }F(y)\preceq F(x)\text{ and }F(y)\ne F(x)\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Pareto dominance and efficiency definitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise minimization with equality allowed in some objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in X\), assignment \(y\) dominates \(x\) when \(F_j(y)\le F_j(x)\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(F_k(y)<F_k(x)\) for at least one \(k\). An assignment is Pareto efficient if no feasible assignment dominates it. Hence \[P=\{x\in X:\nexists y\in X\text{ such that }F(y)\preceq F(x)\text{ and }F(y)\ne F(x)\},\qquad Y_P=\{F(x):x\in P\}.\] A Pareto-oriented DCOP seeks \(P\), \(Y_P\), or a specified approximation thereof rather than one prespecified scalar optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible assignment is Pareto efficient when no other assignment is no worse in every objective and strictly better in at least one; Pareto-oriented models seek all such outcomes.
knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Oriented Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance and Pareto-set definitions are precise, mutually consistent, and appropriate for the leaf, but the record contains no citation for the multiobjective-DCOP formalism.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Multiobjective DCOP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain exact methods returning the full Pareto frontier and associated assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite multiobjective DCOP with feasible assignments \(X\) and cost map \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}^m\) to be minimized, initialize a distributed search or elimination structure containing all locally feasible partial assignments. Combine compatible partial assignments, add their objective vectors, and discard a partial assignment only when another compatible partial assignment weakly dominates it. Continue until all finite search states or elimination messages have been processed. Output \(P=\{(F(x),x):x\in X,\nexists z\in X\text{ with }F(z)\leq F(x)\text{ and }F(z)\neq F(x)\}\). The method is complete when it terminates finitely and returns exactly \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete method finitely explores or eliminates the finite DCOP and returns exactly every globally nondominated objective vector with a witnessing assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and nonempty.
