children.top_down_role: Structural limits separating partial overlays from broader mediation regimes.

assumptions_latex: The DCOP interaction graph is \(G=(V,E)\), and a mediation step optimizes variables in \(S\subseteq V\).
Costs crossing from \(S\) to \(V\setminus S\) are evaluated using a possibly stale boundary assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Overlay mediation is globally centralized exactly when \(S=V\); for \(S\subsetneq V\), omitted boundary interactions can invalidate any claim of global optimality.

notation.meaning: Variables included in the current mediation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates partial mediation from full centralization and identifies the external-coupling failure mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an overlay \(S\), define \(\delta(S)=\{\{i,j\}\in E:i\in S,\ j
otin S\}\). If \(S=V\), exact solution of the mediated subproblem is exact centralized solution of the finite DCOP. If \(S\subsetneq V\) and \(\delta(S)
e\varnothing\), a minimizer conditional on the observed boundary assignment need not minimize the global objective after outside variables change. Concretely, with binary variables \(u\in S\) and \(v
otin S\), the crossing cost \(f(u,v)=\mathbf 1\{u=v\}\) makes the preferred value of \(u\) depend on \(v\). Thus overlay-local optimality alone is not a global-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-overlay mediation is centralized optimization. A proper overlay with crossing constraints can lose local optimality when outside assignments change, so its solution is not globally certified.
knowledge_statements.title: Overlay-Mediation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, and the counterexample supports the limited claim that conditional overlay optimality is not a global certificate. However, the asserted equivalence between full overlay and global centralization depends on the mediator possessing all costs, current information, and authority; no source establishes that protocol interpretation.

assumptions_latex: A finite DCOP supplies each agent with its local variable domain and incident cost functions.
Messages are eventually delivered, and each accepted update is evaluated against a locally consistent neighborhood view.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the latest assignment generated by asynchronous improving subproblem updates; global optimality is not implied without stronger coordination assumptions.

notation.meaning: Variable subset selected for one local optimization
Current assignment at logical update t
Objective terms incident to the selected subset

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic asynchronous local-optimization template; the exact named DALO protocol requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize an assignment \(x^0\in\prod_iD_i\). At logical update \(t\), an activated agent selects a local subset \(S_t\) and obtains a consistent view of variables incident to \(\mathcal F(S_t)=\{f\in\mathcal F:\operatorname{scp}(f)\cap S_t\ne\varnothing\}\). It computes \[y_{S_t}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z_{S_t}}\sum_{f\in\mathcal F(S_t)}f\bigl(z_{S_t},x^t_{V\setminus S_t}\bigr).\] The update is committed only if its protocol-defined improvement and concurrency conditions hold; then \(x^{t+1}_{S_t}=y_{S_t}\), while other components remain unchanged. Stop at quiescence, a budget, or a deadline, and return the latest assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents asynchronously optimize selected local subproblems against consistent neighborhood views and commit admissible improvements until quiescence or a resource limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Asynchronous Local Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is plausible, but the record supplies a generic asynchronous block-coordinate template rather than a sourced definition of Distributed Asynchronous Local Optimization. Selection, consistency, improvement, concurrency, and termination rules can materially change the named method, so a protocol source with a specific locator is required.

assumptions_latex: A finite DCOP is organized by a pseudo-tree or an acyclic cluster tree.
Every original cost is assigned to a cluster containing its scope, and running intersection holds for variables shared by clusters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact cluster messages recover a globally optimal assignment; the largest cluster or separator determines the exponential dimension.

notation.meaning: Separator between cluster a and its parent
Utility message from cluster a to its parent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clustered DPOP abstraction covering partial centralization through multi-variable supernodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let clusters \(C_a\subseteq V\) form a rooted tree and let \(S_a=C_a\cap C_{p(a)}\). Assign each cost function to one cluster containing its scope. In the upward phase, cluster \(a\) computes \[U_{a\to p(a)}(x_{S_a})=\min_{x_{C_a\setminus S_a}}\left(\sum_{f\in\mathcal F_a}f(x_{\operatorname{scp}(f)})+\sum_{b\in\operatorname{ch}(a)}U_{b\to a}(x_{S_b})\right).\] The root minimizes its aggregate expression; a downward value phase chooses stored minimizers consistently. Singleton clusters give ordinary variable-level decomposition, whereas larger clusters partially centralize computation. Exact tables require space exponential in the largest separator and time exponential in the largest eliminated cluster scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DPOP can centralize groups of variables into clusters, exchange exact separator tables upward, and reconstruct an optimum downward; larger clusters trade communication structure for exponential local work.
knowledge_statements.title: Partially Centralized DPOP Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clustered representation is mathematically plausible, but no DCOP/DPOP source supports the claimed family interpretation, message convention, exactness conditions, or complexity statement. It is also unclear whether this terminal container calls for a family representation or an algorithmic characterization. A source identifying the relevant partially centralized DPOP family is required.

assumptions_latex: A finite DCOP has variable set \(V\).
Each mediation episode selects a participant set \(S_t\subseteq V\) and solves its induced conditional subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A run crosses the full-centralization boundary when some episode has \(S_t=V\); bounded proper subsets remain partially centralized.

notation.meaning: Variables controlled by the mediator at episode t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural boundary based on the variables jointly controlled during a mediation episode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the mediation width of a run by \[w_{\mathrm{med}}=\max_t |S_t|.\] The run is partially centralized when every episode satisfies \(S_t\subsetneq V\), equivalently \(w_{\mathrm{med}}<|V|\). It reaches full algorithmic centralization when some mediator simultaneously obtains the information and authority needed to optimize every variable, so that \(S_t=V\) and \(w_{\mathrm{med}}=|V|\). Overlap among proper mediation sets, even when \(\bigcup_tS_t=V\), does not by itself cross this boundary because no single conditional optimization controls the complete assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mediation becomes fully centralized only when one episode jointly controls and optimizes every variable; overlapping proper subsets remain partially centralized even if they eventually cover the network.
knowledge_statements.title: Mediation Centralization Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is an appropriate role for a boundary leaf, but the proposed mediation width and the identification of full centralization solely with one episode satisfying S_t=V are unsourced. Centralization may also depend on information aggregation, decision authority, and implementation architecture, so the stated equivalence cannot be accepted without a DCOP-specific source.

assumptions_latex: Each agent controls one variable in a finite-domain DCOP and knows its incident costs.
Rounds provide each agent with the current values of all constraint-neighbors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DSA returns the incumbent assignment at termination but generally supplies neither monotonic descent nor a global-optimality certificate.

notation.meaning: Best local response to the current neighbor values

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous stochastic local-search template shared by common DSA variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize each \(x_i^0\in D_i\). In round \(t\), agents exchange current values and independently compute \[b_i^t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in D_i}\sum_{f:\,i\in\operatorname{scp}(f)}f\bigl(v,x^t_{\operatorname{scp}(f)\setminus\{i\}}\bigr).\] According to the selected DSA variant, agent \(i\) declares \(b_i^t\) admissible using its strict-improvement, non-worsening, and tie rules. An admissible agent sets \(x_i^{t+1}=b_i^t\) with independent probability \(p\); otherwise it retains \(x_i^t\). After a prescribed round limit or stabilization test, output the best observed or latest assignment, as specified by the implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DSA repeatedly computes local best responses and adopts admissible changes with a fixed probability, reducing simultaneous-update conflicts but offering no general optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: DSA Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the DSA family, but the record deliberately blends strict-improvement, non-worsening, tie-handling, stabilization, and incumbent-output variants. Those choices define materially different DSA variants, and no authoritative source or locator is supplied to justify this family-level template.

children.title: Distributed Breakout Methods
children.top_down_role: Distributed local-search families based on breakout-style conflict adaptation.

assumptions_latex: The DCOP is represented by nonnegative weighted local violation costs.
Rounds provide current neighbor values and proposed local gains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When no improving move exists, violated constraints gain weight, changing the landscape from which later distributed moves are selected.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core distributed breakout scheme with weighted violations and coordinated unilateral changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x^0\) and positive weights \(w_f^0\), and define \(F_t(x)=\sum_fw_f^t f(x_{\operatorname{scp}(f)})\). Each agent computes its maximal unilateral decrease \[g_i^t=F_t(x^t)-\min_{v\in D_i}F_t(v,x^t_{-i}).\] Agents exchange gains; a protocol-defined nonconflicting set of locally maximal positive-gain agents adopts corresponding minimizing values. If no admissible positive-gain move exists, perform breakout by increasing weights of currently violated constraints according to the selected update rule; otherwise retain the weights. Continue until a feasible zero-violation assignment is found or a resource limit is reached, and return the best assignment observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed breakout alternates coordinated improving moves on a weighted violation objective with weight increases on persistent violations whenever search reaches a local minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Breakout Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the terminal container, but the gain comparison, compatible-move selection, stagnation predicate, weight update, and stopping rule are all protocol-specific. No primary DBA source is cited, so the exact algorithm and its scope cannot be verified.

children.title: DBA Variants
children.top_down_role: Variant families derived from distributed breakout algorithm designs.

assumptions_latex: All variants maintain an assignment and positive constraint weights.
Each round can identify local gains and whether the current state triggers breakout.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Changing the move, coordination, or weight-update operators yields distinct DBA variants while preserving the breakout template.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-level classification; names and exact rules of historical DBA variants require primary-source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent a distributed breakout variant by a triple \((M,C,B)\). Given state \((x^t,w^t)\), \(M\) maps each local view to candidate value changes and weighted gains; \(C\) selects a mutually compatible subset of candidates using priorities, gain comparisons, or stochastic activation. If \(C(M(x^t,w^t))\ne\varnothing\), apply the selected moves to obtain \(x^{t+1}\). Otherwise apply \[w^{t+1}=B(w^t,x^t)\] and retain \(x^{t+1}=x^t\). Variants may additionally replace single-variable moves by coordinated moves or alter tie handling, but they remain breakout methods only when stagnation invokes a persistent modification of constraint weights or penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DBA variants differ in candidate moves, conflict resolution, and penalty updates, while sharing the defining response to stagnation: persistent reweighting of violated constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: DBA Variants

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A representation can fit a variants leaf, but the (M,C,B) classification and the proposed defining criterion for membership in the DBA family appear to be an unsourced abstraction. A primary or authoritative survey source must map actual DBA variants to these operators before this record is reliable.

children.title: Breakout-Weight Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes for conflict weighting within distributed breakout families.

assumptions_latex: Each constraint has a positive weight and a nonnegative violation value.
A breakout event occurs only under the algorithm's stagnation predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Additive updates preserve linear growth per breakout, multiplicative updates produce geometric growth, and bounded updates cannot permanently amplify a constraint beyond their cap.

notation.meaning: Weight of constraint f after k relevant breakouts

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares additive, multiplicative, and capped breakout-weight dynamics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose constraint \(f\) is selected at each of \(k\) breakout events. Under an additive regime, \(w_f^{(k+1)}=w_f^{(k)}+\eta_f\), hence \(w_f^{(k)}=w_f^{(0)}+k\eta_f\). Under a multiplicative regime, \(w_f^{(k+1)}=\rho_fw_f^{(k)}\), hence \(w_f^{(k)}=\rho_f^kw_f^{(0)}\). Under a capped additive regime, \(w_f^{(k+1)}=\min\{W_f,w_f^{(k)}+\eta_f\}\), so \(w_f^{(k)}\le W_f\). Consequently, only uncapped regimes guarantee unbounded amplification under indefinitely repeated selection; multiplicative amplification dominates additive amplification asymptotically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated breakout makes additive weights grow linearly and multiplicative weights geometrically, whereas capped regimes limit amplification and may preserve persistent local minima.
knowledge_statements.title: Breakout-Weight Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence calculations are internally correct and the property kind fits the leaf, but no source establishes that additive, multiplicative, and capped updates are the intended DBA weight regimes. The plain statement additionally claims capped regimes may preserve persistent local minima, which is not stated or established by the LaTeX claim. Source support is needed before choosing the appropriate corrected formulation.

assumptions_latex: Each agent controls one finite-domain variable and communicates synchronously with constraint-neighbors.
Agents can exchange their proposed unilateral gains before changing values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each committed MGM round is non-increasing for the global cost, provided simultaneously selected agents share no cost function.

notation.meaning: Agent i's maximal unilateral cost decrease
A best-response value for agent i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard maximum-gain messaging template with deterministic tie breaking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x^0\). In round \(t\), agent \(i\) computes a best response \(b_i^t\) and gain \[g_i^t=\sum_{f:\,i\in\operatorname{scp}(f)}f(x^t_{\operatorname{scp}(f)})-\sum_{f:\,i\in\operatorname{scp}(f)}f\bigl(b_i^t,x^t_{\operatorname{scp}(f)\setminus\{i\}}\bigr).\] Agents exchange gains. Agent \(i\) changes to \(b_i^t\) exactly when \(g_i^t>0\) and its pair \((g_i^t,\pi_i)\) is lexicographically maximal among \(\{(g_j^t,\pi_j):j\in N(i)\cup\{i\}\}\), where \(\pi_i\) is a unique priority. Stop at a round budget or when all gains are nonpositive; return the current assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MGM lets only locally maximum-gain agents move in each round. Unique priorities prevent adjacent simultaneous changes, making accepted rounds monotonically non-worsening.
knowledge_statements.title: MGM Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the MGM family, and monotonicity is plausible when simultaneous movers share no factor. However, the exact priority and tie-breaking rule is variant-dependent, and N(i) must be explicitly defined to include every agent sharing any cost function, especially for nonbinary scopes. No MGM source with a specific locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: A finite DCOP assigns each variable to one agent and each cost scope to communicating agents.
A temporary ordering or priority relation determines which agent aggregates each local cooperative proposal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: CoCoA produces a feasible incumbent by cooperative local cost approximation, but the resulting assignment is not generally globally optimal.

notation.meaning: Neighbor j's approximate contribution for candidate v
Aggregated approximate cost at agent i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative cooperative-cost-approximation template; exact CoCoA protocol details require a primary source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a partial or complete assignment and a protocol priority order. When agent \(i\) is selected, it requests from each relevant neighbor \(j\) a vector \(q_{j\to i}:D_i\to\mathbb R\) approximating the minimum incident cost compatible with \(j\)'s current commitments. Agent \(i\) forms \[Q_i(v)=q_i(v)+\sum_{j\in N(i)}q_{j\to i}(v)\] and commits a value in \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{v\in D_i}Q_i(v)\), using the protocol's tie and backtracking rules. The commitment and updated local view are propagated, and selection continues until all variables are assigned or the stopping rule fires. Output the best complete assignment encountered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CoCoA builds assignments by exchanging neighbor-specific cost approximations, aggregating them for each candidate value, and committing locally preferred values according to a distributed priority protocol.
knowledge_statements.title: CoCoA Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the CoCoA leaf, but the message vectors, approximation semantics, priority order, commitment, backtracking, and output rules are not defined precisely and may not match the named CoCoA protocol. A primary source is necessary to determine the correct mathematical statement.

assumptions_latex: A finite DCOP has a current complete assignment and a distributed method for selecting neighborhoods.
Each selected neighborhood can be solved exactly or approximately conditional on its boundary assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted exact neighborhood replacement is non-increasing in global cost; global optimality is not guaranteed unless the neighborhood schedule and acceptance mechanism provide it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic distributed large-neighborhood-search scheme with boundary-conditioned repair and incumbent acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x^0\in\prod_iD_i\). At iteration \(t\), distributed coordination selects a possibly connected neighborhood \(S_t\) and fixes \(x^t_{V\setminus S_t}\). A designated distributed or partially centralized subsolver computes \[y_{S_t}\approx\operatorname*{argmin}_{z_{S_t}\in\prod_{i\in S_t}D_i}F(z_{S_t},x^t_{V\setminus S_t}).\] Form \(y=(y_{S_t},x^t_{V\setminus S_t})\). Under descent acceptance, set \(x^{t+1}=y\) only if \(F(y)<F(x^t)\); otherwise retain \(x^t\). Update neighborhood-selection statistics, repeat until a time or iteration budget is exhausted, and output the best assignment observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed LNS repeatedly relaxes a coordinated variable neighborhood, repairs it against the fixed boundary, and accepts an improving complete assignment until its resource budget expires.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Large-Neighborhood Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits distributed large-neighborhood search, and strict descent acceptance makes accepted updates improving regardless of subsolver quality. Nevertheless, the notation y approximately in argmin has no formal approximation criterion, while neighborhood selection, distributed solving, and acceptance vary across DLNS methods. An authoritative DCOP-specific source is required to fix the intended variant and formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Population-Based DCOP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic population-based incomplete search for finite DCOPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite DCOP objective \(F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}f_a(x_{N(a)})\), maintain a population \(P_t\subseteq\prod_{i\in V}D_i\). At iteration \(t\), agents select parent assignments using communicated fitness values \(F(x)\), generate candidates by distributed recombination and local mutation, evaluate every affected factor, and form \(P_{t+1}\) by a specified replacement rule. Preserve an incumbent \(x_t^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\cup_{s\le t}P_s}F(x)\). Stop after a prescribed budget or stopping test and output \(x_t^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents evolve a population of complete assignments through selection, recombination, mutation, and replacement, while retaining the best evaluated assignment as the anytime output.
assumptions_latex: \(V\), every domain \(D_i\), and the factor set \(A\) are finite.
Every candidate's affected factor values can be evaluated consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x_{t+1}^\star)\ge F(x_t^\star)\) whenever the incumbent is preserved.

notation.meaning: population of complete assignments at iteration t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the method-family leaf, and incumbent preservation implies the stated monotonicity. However, no cited source establishes that this generic evolutionary template is the intended DCOP population-based family or supports its distributed evaluation and recombination protocol.

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Factor-Graph Max-Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact max-sum inference on a finite tree factor graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V\cup A,E)\) be a finite tree and \(F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}f_a(x_{N(a)})\). Define messages, up to additive normalization constants, by \(q_{i\to a}(x_i)=\sum_{b\in N(i)\setminus\{a\}}r_{b\to i}(x_i)\) and \(r_{a\to i}(x_i)=\max_{x_{N(a)\setminus\{i\}}}\bigl[f_a(x_{N(a)})+\sum_{j\in N(a)\setminus\{i\}}q_{j\to a}(x_j)\bigr]\). After one inward and one outward pass, \(b_i(x_i)=\sum_{a\in N(i)}r_{a\to i}(x_i)\) is the exact max-marginal up to a constant; root maximization followed by consistent traceback produces a global maximizer of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a finite tree factor graph, two-pass max-sum computes exact max-marginals, and a consistent traceback recovers a globally optimal assignment.
assumptions_latex: Each variable domain \(D_i\) is finite.
All factor values are finite real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\prod_iD_i}F(x)\).

notation.meaning: neighbors of node u in the factor graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the exactness claim for acyclic factor graphs, and the finite-domain hypotheses and two-pass equations are mathematically plausible. No inspectable citation is supplied for exact max-marginals and globally consistent traceback, so the theorem cannot be accepted at candidate review.

knowledge_statements.title: Loopy Max-Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative max-sum updates on factor graphs containing cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite factor graph, initialize every directed message \(q_{i\to a}^{0}\) and \(r_{a\to i}^{0}\). Iteratively apply \(q_{i\to a}^{t+1}(x_i)=\sum_{b\in N(i)\setminus\{a\}}r_{b\to i}^{t}(x_i)\) and \(r_{a\to i}^{t+1}(x_i)=\max_{x_{N(a)\setminus\{i\}}}\bigl[f_a(x_{N(a)})+\sum_{j\in N(a)\setminus\{i\}}q_{j\to a}^{t}(x_j)\bigr]\), with optional additive normalization. At termination, choose values from beliefs \(b_i^t(x_i)=\sum_{a\in N(i)}r_{a\to i}^t(x_i)\), resolving conflicts by a specified coordination rule. Cycles generally remove guarantees of convergence and global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Loopy max-sum repeatedly exchanges variable and factor messages on cyclic graphs, then decodes local beliefs; convergence and optimality are not guaranteed in general.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain is finite.
A message schedule and termination rule are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i^t\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x_i\in D_i}b_i^t(x_i)\) defines the uncoordinated local decoding.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits this leaf, and the record appropriately avoids asserting general convergence or optimality. An authoritative source is still required for the synchronous update convention, normalization, decoding procedure, and stated failure boundary.

children.title: Damped Max-Sum
children.top_down_role: Max-Sum variants using message damping for loopy inference behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Damped Max-Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-weight damping of iterative max-sum messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) denote one normalized, undamped max-sum message update on the complete message vector \(m^t\). Choose \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and update synchronously by \(m^{t+1}=(1-\alpha)m^t+\alpha T(m^t)\). Equivalently, apply this convex combination componentwise after computing each raw variable-to-factor and factor-to-variable message. Stop when a prescribed residual test or iteration budget is met, and decode the resulting beliefs. Any converged message vector satisfies the same normalized fixed-point equation \(m=T(m)\) as undamped max-sum when \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Damped max-sum mixes each old message with its raw update using a fixed weight, reducing oscillation while preserving normalized fixed points.
assumptions_latex: Messages are represented under a fixed additive normalization.
The damping weight satisfies \(0<\alpha\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m^{t+1}=m^t\) implies \(m^t=T(m^t)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the stabilization-method leaf. The fixed-point implication is correct for the displayed normalized operator and positive update weight, but no source establishes that this precise synchronous convex-combination convention is the intended Damped Max-Sum variant.

children.title: Decaying-Factor Max-Sum
children.top_down_role: Max-Sum variants using decaying factor influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Decaying-Factor Max-Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Max-sum damping with a time-varying update weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be the normalized raw max-sum update and choose a sequence \((\alpha_t)_{t\ge0}\) with \(0<\alpha_t\le1\). Starting from \(m^0\), set \(m^{t+1}=(1-\alpha_t)m^t+\alpha_tT(m^t)\), then decode beliefs after a residual test or finite budget. A decaying-factor regime additionally requires \(\alpha_t\to0\). To prevent the total capacity for correction from being finite, a standard admissibility condition is \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\alpha_t=\infty\); without it, messages may freeze before reaching a fixed point even when every individual update is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method progressively reduces the weight of raw max-sum updates; nonsummable weights avoid allocating only a finite total amount of correction.
assumptions_latex: Messages use a fixed additive normalization.
The schedule satisfies \(0<\alpha_t\le1\) and \(\alpha_t\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m^{t+1}=(1-\alpha_t)m^t+\alpha_tT(m^t)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role is plausible, but 'decaying-factor Max-Sum' is not identified by a source, and the record may be importing a generic diminishing-relaxation schedule into a differently defined DCOP variant. A primary source is needed to determine the intended update and whether the nonsummability condition belongs in this container.

children.title: Stabilization-Regime Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Applicability and behavior boundaries among Max-Sum stabilization regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stabilization-Regime Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence comparison under a contractive normalized update operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the normalized max-sum operator \(T\) is a contraction with modulus \(\rho<1\) in a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\), with fixed point \(m^\star\). For \(m^{t+1}=(1-\alpha_t)m^t+\alpha_tT(m^t)\), \[\lVert m^{t+1}-m^\star\rVert\le\bigl(1-\alpha_t(1-\rho)\bigr)\lVert m^t-m^\star\rVert.\] Thus fixed damping \(\alpha_t=\alpha>0\) gives geometric convergence, while decaying damping converges under \(\sum_t\alpha_t=\infty\), generally without a uniform geometric rate. This comparison does not assert that ordinary loopy max-sum is contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under contraction, fixed damping converges geometrically, whereas nonsummable decaying damping converges more slowly; the comparison gives no general loopy max-sum guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a contraction with modulus \(\rho<1\).
\(0<\alpha_t\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert m^t-m^\star\rVert\le\prod_{s<t}(1-\alpha_s(1-\rho))\lVert m^0-m^\star\rVert\).

notation.meaning: contraction modulus of the normalized update

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits a comparison leaf, and the contraction inequality and its fixed-versus-decaying consequences are mathematically coherent. No source ties this generic relaxed-fixed-point comparison to the named Max-Sum stabilization regimes, so its local relevance and terminology remain unsupported.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Max-Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive optimality certificate obtained by tree-structured edge removal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite pairwise maximization DCOP, remove an edge set \(R\) so that the remaining objective \(F_T\) has a tree factor graph, and compute \(x_T\in\operatorname*{argmax}_xF_T(x)\) exactly by max-sum. With removed-edge factors \(f_e\), define \(L=F(x_T)\) and \(U=F_T(x_T)+\sum_{e\in R}\max_{x_e}f_e(x_e)\). Then \(L\le F(x^\star)\le U\) for every global maximizer \(x^\star\). Moreover, \(U-L\le\sum_{e\in R}(\max f_e-\min f_e)\), yielding a directly checkable additive suboptimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After removing edges to obtain a tree, exact tree optimization plus extrema of removed factors gives computable lower and upper bounds on the original optimum.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP is finite and pairwise.
Removing \(R\) leaves a tree-structured factor graph.
Every removed factor has finite maximum and minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le F(x^\star)-F(x_T)\le U-L\le\sum_{e\in R}(\max f_e-\min f_e)\).

notation.meaning: certified interval containing the optimum value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the claimed computable optimality interval. The displayed bounds are plausible when R indexes entire removed factors, but the statement alternates between removing factor-graph edges and removing pairwise factors; those operations are not interchangeable. A primary Bounded Max-Sum source is required to resolve the intended construction and certify the formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Max-Sum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent-preserving wrapper for iterative max-sum decoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run a specified max-sum message process and, at checkpoints \(t=0,1,\ldots\), construct a globally consistent complete assignment \(x^t\) by a coordination or spanning-tree decoding procedure. Evaluate \(F(x^t)\) exactly through distributed aggregation. Initialize \(\hat x^0=x^0\), and set \(\hat x^{t+1}=x^{t+1}\) if \(F(x^{t+1})>F(\hat x^t)\), otherwise set \(\hat x^{t+1}=\hat x^t\). On interruption after any completed checkpoint, output \(\hat x^t\). The incumbent values are monotone even if the underlying loopy messages oscillate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each checkpoint, the method evaluates a consistent decoded assignment and retains it only when it improves the incumbent, providing a valid anytime output.
assumptions_latex: Every checkpoint produces a feasible complete assignment.
The global objective of each candidate can be aggregated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\hat x^{t+1})\ge F(\hat x^t)\) for every completed checkpoint \(t\).

notation.meaning: candidate assignment decoded at checkpoint t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits this leaf, and the monotone incumbent conclusion follows from the stated wrapper. No source shows that this wrapper, its spanning-tree or coordinated decoding, and exact distributed objective aggregation constitute the intended Anytime Max-Sum method rather than a generic incumbent mechanism.

knowledge_statements.title: DUCT Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed UCT-style sampling over a rooted DCOP decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Arrange finite-domain variables in a rooted pseudo-tree. At each sampled traversal, an agent choosing value \(d\) uses an upper-confidence score \(Q_i(d)+c\sqrt{\log N_i/N_i(d)}\), assigning infinite priority to unvisited values. Descendants condition their choices on the sampled ancestor context; a complete traversal supplies a realized objective value from local factors. Aggregate that value upward and increment the corresponding visit counts and empirical means. After a prescribed sampling budget, output the best complete sampled assignment, or the assignment induced by the designated final-selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DUCT distributes upper-confidence tree search over a pseudo-tree, sampling assignments and propagating realized utilities upward to update visit counts and empirical values.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP and all variable domains are finite.
A rooted pseudo-tree and complete traversal protocol are fixed.
The exploration constant satisfies \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_i(d)\leftarrow Q_i(d)+\bigl(R-Q_i(d)\bigr)/N_i(d)\) after observing return \(R\).

notation.meaning: number of sampled choices of value d at agent i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the DUCT-family leaf, but the compact UCT statistics suppress ancestor-context dependence that can materially change the distributed method. A primary DUCT source is needed to confirm the acronym, pseudo-tree traversal, reward attribution, contextual statistics, and final-selection rule.

knowledge_statements.title: D-Gibbs Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed Gibbs updates for finite DCOP assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For inverse temperature \(\beta>0\), define \(\pi_\beta(x)\propto\exp(\beta F(x))\). When agent \(i\) is activated, it samples \(x_i'\) from \[\Pr(x_i'=d\mid x_{-i})=\frac{\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{a:i\in N(a)}f_a(d,x_{N(a)\setminus\{i\}})\right)}{\sum_{e\in D_i}\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{a:i\in N(a)}f_a(e,x_{N(a)\setminus\{i\}})\right)}.\] Nonadjacent agents may update simultaneously under a proper interaction-graph coloring. With a fair schedule, these local updates preserve \(\pi_\beta\); irreducibility and aperiodicity give convergence to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents repeatedly resample their values from local Gibbs conditionals; properly scheduled updates target a distribution increasingly concentrated on high-utility assignments.
assumptions_latex: The state space is finite and all factor values are finite.
The update schedule is fair and simultaneous agents share no factor.
The induced chain is irreducible and aperiodic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(X^t)\to\pi_\beta\) as \(t\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: assignment of all variables except i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the family leaf, and the displayed single-site Gibbs conditional is mathematically standard. A source is required to establish that D-Gibbs uses this target, coloring-based simultaneous schedule, and convergence regime; the supplied local inventory contains no relevant DCOP or Gibbs reference.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed MCMC Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity criterion for distributed local Markov updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi_\beta(x)=Z_\beta^{-1}\exp(\beta F(x))\) on a finite DCOP state space. Suppose each distributed update kernel \(K_s\) changes only an independent or coordinated block of variables and satisfies detailed balance \(\pi_\beta(x)K_s(x,y)=\pi_\beta(y)K_s(y,x)\). Then every \(K_s\), and every state-independent mixture of them, preserves \(\pi_\beta\). If the resulting chain is irreducible and aperiodic, its distribution converges to \(\pi_\beta\); optimization is obtained approximately by retaining the best sampled assignment or increasing \(\beta\) under a separate annealing schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed MCMC kernels that obey detailed balance preserve the Gibbs distribution; irreducibility and aperiodicity then ensure convergence to that target.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP state space is finite.
Every scheduled kernel satisfies detailed balance with the common target.
The combined chain is irreducible and aperiodic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu K^t\to\pi_\beta\) for every initial distribution \(\mu\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role is suitable for a family-level stationarity criterion. Detailed balance supports invariance for each kernel and state-independent mixtures, but the conclusion written as K^t presumes a fixed homogeneous combined kernel and does not cover arbitrary scheduling. A relevant source is needed to fix the distributed scheduling scope and support the family characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: K-Optimal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regional optimality against changes involving at most K variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite DCOP with feasible set \(X\subseteq\prod_{i\in V}D_i\) and integer \(K\ge1\), a feasible assignment \(x\in X\) is \(K\)-optimal if, for every subset \(S\subseteq V\) with \(|S|\le K\) and every \(y\in X\) satisfying \(y_{V\setminus S}=x_{V\setminus S}\), one has \(F(x)\ge F(y)\). A regional method certifies this condition by solving each permitted regional subproblem with boundary variables fixed. Every global optimum is \(K\)-optimal, and \(K\)-optimality implies \(J\)-optimality for every \(1\le J\le K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment is K-optimal when no feasible reassignment of at most K variables improves its objective; larger K gives a stronger regional optimality condition.
assumptions_latex: The feasible DCOP state space \(X\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is }K\text{-optimal}\Rightarrow x\text{ is }J\text{-optimal}\) for \(1\le J\le K\).

notation.meaning: region of variables permitted to change

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits a regional-optimality leaf, and the stated cardinality-based condition has the claimed monotonicity in K. However, no authoritative DCOP source establishes that this is the intended K-optimal notion; the literature-specific definition may restrict deviations to connected regions or use a different neighborhood parameterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Optimal Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conditional optimization over a prescribed family of tree-structured regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite DCOP have objective \(F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}f_a(x_a)\) on \(X=\prod_{i\in V}D_i\), and let \(\mathcal T\) be a finite family of variable sets whose induced interaction subgraphs are trees. Initialize any \(x^0\in X\). At iteration \(t\), choose \(S\in\mathcal T\), compute \(y_S\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z_S\in\prod_{i\in S}D_i}F(z_S,x^t_{V\setminus S})\) by exact tree inference, and set \(x^{t+1}=(y_S,x^t_{V\setminus S})\) when this strictly improves the objective. Stop after every region has been tested without improvement. The output \(\bar x\) satisfies \(F(\bar x)\leq F(z_S,\bar x_{V\setminus S})\) for every \(S\in\mathcal T\) and every admissible \(z_S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly optimize each designated tree region while fixing all other variables. When no region improves the objective, the assignment is optimal against every permitted tree-region deviation.
assumptions_latex: \(V\), every \(D_i\), and \(\mathcal T\) are finite.
Each selected tree subproblem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall S\in\mathcal T,\ \forall z_S,\ F(\bar x)\leq F(z_S,\bar x_{V\setminus S})\).

notation.meaning: Global DCOP objective to be minimized.
Permitted family of tree-structured variable regions.

review_flags: DCOP-specific authoritative source and terminology locator required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-descent algorithm and regional-optimality conclusion are coherent, and the algorithm kind fits the method-family leaf. However, no cited source establishes that this construction is a recognized DCOP tree-optimal method or supports the stated terminology.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Bounded Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mini-bucket-style elimination with a fixed scope-size bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite minimization DCOP, fix an elimination order and an integer bound \(i\geq1\). When eliminating \(x_j\), partition its bucket of functions into mini-buckets \(B_{j1},\ldots,B_{jr}\) so that the union of scopes in each mini-bucket contains at most \(i+1\) variables. Replace each \(B_{jk}\) by the table \(g_{jk}(s)=\min_{x_j}\sum_{h\in B_{jk}}h(x_j,s)\), whose remaining scope has size at most \(i\). Continue until no variables remain, obtaining a lower bound \(L_i\); separately retain any reconstructed feasible assignment as an incumbent. The computation stores only tables over at most \(i\) remaining variables, while splitting may make \(L_i\) strictly smaller than the true optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split elimination buckets so every generated table respects a scope bound. This limits memory and yields a valid lower bound, although splitting can destroy exactness.
assumptions_latex: All variable domains are finite.
Every mini-bucket partition obeys the stated scope bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_i\leq\min_x F(x)\), and every generated message has scope cardinality at most \(i\).

notation.meaning: Maximum number of variables in a generated table scope.
A mini-bucket used while eliminating variable j.
Resulting lower bound for the minimization problem.

review_flags: Authoritative DCOP or mini-bucket inference source with an exact locator required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mini-bucket construction and minimization lower-bound direction are plausible, and algorithm is the appropriate kind. A precise authoritative locator is required for the i-bound convention, generated-scope claim, and lower-bound guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Solution-Improvement Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent-preserving distributed methods interruptible after any completed update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a finite DCOP objective to minimize. Initialize with a feasible incumbent \(x^0\) and value \(U_0=F(x^0)\). At completed update \(t\), distributed agents may propose any feasible \(y^t\); set \(x^{t+1}=y^t\) and \(U_{t+1}=F(y^t)\) if \(F(y^t)<U_t\), and otherwise retain \((x^t,U_t)\). If a valid lower bound \(L_t\leq F^*=\min_xF(x)\) is also maintained, replace it only by a valid nondecreasing bound. Upon interruption after a completed update, output \(x^t\). Then \(U_{t+1}\leq U_t\), every output is feasible, and \(0\leq U_t-F^*\leq U_t-L_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Keep the best feasible assignment found so far and accept only improvements. Interruption always returns a feasible incumbent whose objective never worsens; a maintained lower bound quantifies its gap.
assumptions_latex: At least one feasible initial assignment is available.
Each reported lower bound is globally valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_{t+1}\leq U_t\) and \(0\leq U_t-F^*\leq U_t-L_t\).

notation.meaning: Objective value of the incumbent after update t.
Certified global lower bound after update t.

review_flags: Authoritative source for the DCOP anytime-method formulation required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Incumbent monotonicity and the stated bound-gap inequality are mathematically sound, and algorithm fits this method-family container. No source supports this as the defining DCOP anytime-family characterization or its distributed interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Search Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness of exhaustive finite search with sound pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{i\in V}D_i\) be the finite assignment space of a DCOP with objective \(F:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). A complete search partitions or enumerates \(X\), evaluates every unpruned complete assignment, and prunes a subset \(Q\subseteq X\) only when a valid bound proves \(F(x)\geq U\) for every \(x\in Q\), where \(U\) is the value of a known feasible incumbent. If the search terminates after every assignment has been evaluated or soundly pruned, its returned incumbent \(\bar x\) satisfies \(F(\bar x)=\min_{x\in X}F(x)\). Thus completeness plus sound bounding is sufficient for exactness, independently of the distributed exploration order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminating search is exact when every finite assignment is either evaluated or removed by a valid bound that cannot discard a better solution.
assumptions_latex: The joint assignment space \(X\) is finite.
Every pruning bound is valid and all unpruned assignments are eventually explored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x)=\min_{x\in X}F(x)\).

notation.meaning: Set of assignments removed by one pruning decision.

review_flags: DCOP complete-search exactness source with a precise theorem or section locator required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exactness statement is precise under finite exhaustive coverage and sound pruning, and property fits the exactness-regime leaf. It lacks a DCOP complete-search theorem or section citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Tree Inference Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variable elimination on a pseudo-tree without message approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite DCOP and a rooted pseudo-tree of its primal constraint graph. Assign each cost function to a deepest variable in its scope. For every variable \(i\), let \(S_i\) be the separator consisting of ancestors adjacent to \(i\) or to a descendant of \(i\). Suppose the upward message from the subtree rooted at \(i\) tabulates, for every assignment \(s_i\) of \(S_i\), the exact minimum total cost contributed by that subtree conditional on \(s_i\), with no projection, splitting, or truncation. Then the root minimum equals the global optimum. A downward value-selection pass choosing stored minimizing assignments produces a globally optimal feasible joint assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full separator tables on a valid pseudo-tree summarize each subtree exactly. Root minimization gives the optimum, and downward reconstruction yields an optimal assignment.
assumptions_latex: All domains and function values required by the messages are finite or extended-real minima are attained.
Every separator message is represented and minimized exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\bar x)=\min_xF(x)\), where \(\bar x\) is reconstructed from the exact messages.

notation.meaning: Pseudo-tree separator of the subtree rooted at variable i.
Assignment reconstructed by the downward pass.

review_flags: Authoritative source for pseudo-tree or DPOP exactness and separator conventions required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem matches pseudo-tree inference exactness and states the essential exact-message assumptions. A source is needed to verify the function-assignment and separator conventions and the reconstruction guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclic Max-Sum Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Max-sum exactness on a finite tree factor graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite DCOP maximize \(U(x)=\sum_{a\in A}u_a(x_a)\), and suppose its bipartite factor graph is a tree. Run exact max-sum messages \(m_{i\to a}(x_i)=\sum_{b\in N(i)\setminus\{a\}}m_{b\to i}(x_i)\) and \(m_{a\to i}(x_i)=\max_{x_{a\setminus i}}\bigl(u_a(x_a)+\sum_{j\in N(a)\setminus\{i\}}m_{j\to a}(x_j)\bigr)\), up to arbitrary additive normalizations. After messages have propagated from every leaf across every edge, maximizing a root belief and backtracking through stored maximizing arguments yields \(\bar x\) with \(U(\bar x)=\max_xU(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a tree factor graph, exact max-sum messages pass complete subtree summaries. Root maximization followed by consistent backtracking returns a globally optimal assignment.
assumptions_latex: The factor graph is connected and acyclic.
All variable domains are finite and all message maximizations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U(\bar x)=\max_xU(x)\).

notation.meaning: Local utility factor indexed by a.
Neighbors of node v in the factor graph.
Max-sum message from node p to adjacent node q.

review_flags: Authoritative max-sum exactness theorem and scheduling locator required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The max-sum equations and tree exactness claim are standard in form, and theorem is the correct kind. An authoritative theorem or section must support the scheduling condition, additive normalization allowance, and backtracking conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Loopy-Inference Exactness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A cycle removes the general exactness guarantee for ordinary max-sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Acyclicity cannot be omitted from the general max-sum exactness statement. Consider three binary variables \(x_1,x_2,x_3\in\{0,1\}\) on a triangle, with utility \(u_{ij}(x_i,x_j)=1\) when \(x_i\neq x_j\) and \(0\) otherwise. The optimum utility is \(2\). Under synchronous max-sum initialized with zero messages, every factor-to-variable update assigns the same value to both states and hence remains zero after normalization. All variable beliefs therefore tie forever. A deterministic decoder selecting state \(0\) at every tie returns \((0,0,0)\), whose utility is \(0\). Consequently, ordinary loopy max-sum has no unconditional exactness guarantee, even if its messages reach a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an antiferromagnetic binary triangle, zero-initialized max-sum can remain at an uninformative fixed point and decode an assignment of value zero although the optimum is two.
assumptions_latex: Messages are updated synchronously from zero and normalized by subtracting a state-independent constant.
The decoder resolves every tied binary belief in favor of \(0\).

notation.meaning: Sum of the three edge utilities.

review_flags: A published locator for the loopy max-sum failure boundary is required; the displayed counterexample should be independently checked.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed triangle example is internally plausible and failure_boundary exactly fits the leaf. Because no published locator is supplied, the claimed loopy max-sum fixed-point failure remains unsupported candidate knowledge.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching feasible objective and valid global bound for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization DCOP with optimum \(F^*=\min_{x\in X}F(x)\), a global optimality certificate consists of a feasible assignment \(\bar x\in X\), its value \(U=F(\bar x)\), and a verifiable global lower bound \(L\) satisfying \(L\leq F(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). If the certificate also establishes \(L=U\), then \(L\leq F^*\leq U=L\), so \(\bar x\) is globally optimal. In a distributed implementation, the bound may be assembled from locally checkable messages or subproblem bounds, provided their aggregation is proved to be a lower bound for the same global objective and no cost term is omitted or counted inconsistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible solution and a valid global lower bound certify optimality when their values match, provided distributed bound components cover the objective consistently.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is globally feasible.
\(L\) is a valid lower bound for the complete objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=F(\bar x)\Longrightarrow F(\bar x)=F^*\).

notation.meaning: Objective value of the certified feasible assignment.

review_flags: Authoritative source for distributed global-bound aggregation and certification required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Matching a feasible incumbent with a valid global lower bound is a correct optimality-certificate pattern, and certificate fits the container. The distributed aggregation conditions are nontrivial and have no supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Suboptimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive or multiplicative guarantees from incumbent-bound gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization DCOP, let \(\bar x\) be feasible with \(U=F(\bar x)\), and let \(L\leq F^*=\min_xF(x)\) be a verifiable global lower bound. For a requested additive tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the inequality \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(F(\bar x)-F^*\leq\varepsilon\). If costs are nonnegative, \(L>0\), and a multiplicative factor \(\rho\geq1\) is requested, the inequality \(U\leq\rho L\) certifies \(F(\bar x)\leq\rho F^*\). Distributed components form a valid certificate only when their aggregation preserves the claimed global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent and global lower bound certify additive error through their gap, or multiplicative error through their ratio when the optimum is positive.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is feasible and \(L\leq F^*\).
For the multiplicative form, \(F\geq0\) and \(L>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow U-F^*\leq\varepsilon\); \(U\leq\rho L\Rightarrow U\leq\rho F^*\).

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound and feasible incumbent value.

review_flags: Authoritative approximation-certificate source with DCOP context required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive and multiplicative implications have the correct direction under the stated assumptions, and certificate is the correct kind. A precise authoritative source is required for this certificate formulation in the DCOP setting.

knowledge_statements.title: Regional Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact no-improvement certificates for prescribed variable regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar x\) be feasible for a finite minimization DCOP and let \(\mathcal R\) be a prescribed family of variable regions. For each \(S\in\mathcal R\), compute and certify the exact conditional value \(m_S=\min_{z_S}F(z_S,\bar x_{V\setminus S})\), including every factor affected by variables in \(S\). Since \(z_S=\bar x_S\) is admissible, \(m_S\leq F(\bar x)\). The collection \(\{m_S:S\in\mathcal R\}\), together with equalities \(m_S=F(\bar x)\), certifies that no simultaneous reassignment confined to any certified region strictly improves \(\bar x\). It does not certify global optimality unless the regional family or an additional theorem makes regional optimality sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact conditional optimization shows that no permitted region can improve the incumbent while outside variables stay fixed. This is not generally a global certificate.
assumptions_latex: Every regional conditional problem is solved exactly.
All factors affected by each region are included consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall S\in\mathcal R,\ \forall z_S,\ F(\bar x)\leq F(z_S,\bar x_{V\setminus S})\).

notation.meaning: Family of regions covered by the certificate.
Exact conditional optimum for region S.

review_flags: DCOP-specific source defining regional optimality certificates required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-minimum equalities correctly certify absence of improving deviations in the prescribed regions, and certificate fits the leaf. No source establishes the DCOP-specific regional-certificate terminology or formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Termination Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent-cut certification of global quiescence in asynchronous computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an asynchronous distributed algorithm with reliable channels and a finite set of processes. A termination certificate is a consistent global cut \(C\) such that every process is passive at its local state in \(C\), every channel contains no application message crossing into the future of \(C\), and the algorithm creates new work only while processing an application message or performing already recorded local work. These conditions are locally checkable from the recorded process states and channel accounting. Their conjunction certifies global quiescence at \(C\): no process is active, no message capable of reactivating a process is in transit, and no further algorithmic state transition can occur without external input. The certificate establishes termination, not solution quality, unless paired with an optimality or approximation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent snapshot certifies termination when all processes are passive and no work-carrying message is in transit. It does not by itself certify solution quality.
assumptions_latex: The process set is finite and communication is reliable.
New internal work can arise only from recorded work or receipt of an application message.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\forall p,\ p\text{ is passive at }C\bigr)\land\bigl(\forall e,\ e\text{ is empty at }C\bigr)\Rightarrow C\text{ is globally quiescent}\).

notation.meaning: Consistent global cut or distributed snapshot.

review_flags: Authoritative distributed termination-detection source and exact channel model required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The passive-process and empty-channel criterion is appropriate in spirit, and certificate fits the termination-certificate leaf. A precise termination-detection or snapshot source is required to validate the channel-state wording, consistency requirements, and work-generation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Induced-Width Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination cost parameterized by induced width and domain size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a DCOP have \(n\) variables, maximum domain size \(d\), and a fixed elimination order. During elimination, connect all uneliminated neighbors of each eliminated variable; let \(w\) be the maximum number of such neighbors at any step, namely the induced width of the order. Exact tabular elimination forms an intermediate function over at most \(w\) remaining variables and minimizes a table involving at most \(w+1\) variables. Under unit-cost table arithmetic, its worst-case time is \(O(n d^{w+1})\) and the total size of all stored intermediate tables is \(O(n d^w)\). Thus exact pseudo-tree inference is exponential in induced width but polynomial in \(n\) for fixed \(w\) and \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed elimination order, exact inference uses time exponential in induced width plus one and stores tables exponential in induced width.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain has cardinality at most \(d\).
Intermediate functions are represented as explicit tables with unit-cost arithmetic.

notation.meaning: Induced width of the chosen elimination order.

review_flags: Authoritative variable-elimination complexity source with matching width convention required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated tabular-elimination bounds are plausible for the given induced-width convention, and complexity_bound is the correct kind. An authoritative locator must confirm the width indexing, time bound, and total stored-table memory model.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudo-Tree Depth Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the depth parameter governing sequential dependencies in pseudo-tree-based DCOP algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the primal constraint graph be \(G=(V,E)\). A rooted spanning tree \(T\) of \(G\) is a pseudo-tree when the endpoints of every edge in \(E\setminus E(T)\) are related as ancestor and descendant in \(T\). Its depth is \[h(T)=\max_{v\in V}\operatorname{dist}_{T}(r,v),\] where \(r\) is the root and distance counts tree edges. The minimum pseudo-tree depth of \(G\) is \[h^*(G)=\min\{h(T):T\text{ is a pseudo-tree of }G\}.\] For a fixed pseudo-tree algorithm, pseudo-tree depth complexity is the dependence of its sequential rounds or longest dependency chain on \(h(T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-tree depth is the longest root-to-agent tree path; minimizing it over valid pseudo-trees gives the graph’s minimum pseudo-tree depth.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite connected primal constraint graph}
T\text{ is a rooted spanning pseudo-tree of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h^*(G)=\min_T\max_{v\in V}\operatorname{dist}_T(r,v)
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but no source supports the DCOP pseudo-tree convention, depth convention, or claimed relationship to sequential rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Size Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the domain-cardinality parameter used in finite-domain DCOP resource bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-domain DCOP with variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) and domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\), define the maximum domain size by \[q=\max_{1\le i\le n}|D_i|.\] A uniform domain-size complexity bound expresses a resource \(R\), such as time, memory, or communicated table entries, as a function of \(q\) while the remaining structural parameters are displayed separately. In particular, explicitly enumerating assignments to any set \(S\) of variables requires \(\prod_{X_i\in S}|D_i|\) entries, which is at most \(q^{|S|}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum domain size is the largest variable-domain cardinality; a table over a variable set has at most the corresponding power of this parameter entries.
assumptions_latex: X_i\text{ has a finite nonempty domain }D_i\text{ for }1\le i\le n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q=\max_i|D_i|\quad\text{and}\quad\prod_{X_i\in S}|D_i|\le q^{|S|}

notation.meaning: Set of variables indexed by a table

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-domain parameterization and table-size inequality are precise and fit the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Arity Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines maximum constraint scope size and its direct tabular representation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the finite collection of cost functions in a DCOP, and let \(\operatorname{scope}(f)\) be the variables on which \(f\) depends. The maximum constraint arity is \[a=\max_{f\in F}|\operatorname{scope}(f)|.\] If every variable domain has cardinality at most \(q\), an extensional table for any original constraint contains \[\prod_{X_i\in\operatorname{scope}(f)}|D_i|\le q^a\] cost entries. This bound concerns original constraint representation; intermediate inference factors may have scopes larger than \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint arity is the largest original cost-function scope. With maximum domain size q, each original extensional constraint has at most q to that arity entries.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is finite}
|D_i|\le q\text{ for every variable }X_i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a=\max_{f\in F}|\operatorname{scope}(f)|\quad\text{and}\quad|\operatorname{table}(f)|\le q^a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes original constraint arity from intermediate factor scope and fits the leaf, but no citation supports it.

knowledge_statements.title: Search Message-Volume Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents communication volume for a completed execution of a distributed search algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution \(e\) of a distributed search algorithm, let \(M(e)\) be the multiset of transmitted messages. If \(b(m)\) is the encoded length of message \(m\), define the search message-volume profile by \[\mathcal V(e)=\bigl(N(e),B(e),N_1(e),\ldots,N_k(e)\bigr),\] where \[N(e)=|M(e)|,\qquad B(e)=\sum_{m\in M(e)}b(m),\qquad N_j(e)=|\{m\in M(e):\operatorname{type}(m)=j\}|.\] Worst-case, expected, or empirical profiles must specify the instance class, execution policy, and randomness over which these quantities are aggregated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search message-volume profile records total messages, transmitted bits, and counts by message type under a specified instance and execution model.
assumptions_latex: e\text{ is a finite completed execution}
b(m)\text{ uses one fixed message encoding}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(e)=\sum_{m\in M(e)}b(m)\quad\text{and}\quad N(e)=\sum_{j=1}^{k}N_j(e)

notation.meaning: Multiset of messages transmitted during execution e

knowledge_statements.title: Inference Message-Size Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds tabular inference messages by separator scope and variable-domain sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In pseudo-tree dynamic programming, suppose an agent sends a tabular message whose key variables form a separator \(S\). With one scalar value stored for every assignment to \(S\), the message has exactly \[E(S)=\prod_{X_i\in S}|D_i|\] value entries. If \(|D_i|\le q\) and \(|S|\le w\), then \[E(S)\le q^w.\] Thus the entry-count profile of all inference messages is determined by their separator scopes; encoded bit size additionally depends on the scalar representation and metadata encoding.

|D_i|\le q\text{ for every }X_i\in S
|S|\le w

knowledge_statements.title: Local Memory Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines per-agent and aggregate peak memory profiles for distributed optimization executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an execution \(e\) with agents \(A\), let \(L_i(t)\) be the number of storage units held by agent \(i\) at time \(t\), under a fixed accounting convention. Define \[L_i^{\max}(e)=\max_t L_i(t),\qquad L_{\max}(e)=\max_{i\in A}L_i^{\max}(e),\qquad L_{\Sigma}(e)=\max_t\sum_{i\in A}L_i(t).\] The local memory profile is the vector \(\bigl((L_i^{\max})_{i\in A},L_{\max},L_{\Sigma}\bigr)\). A valid asymptotic profile must state whether storage units are bits, assignments, table entries, or queued messages.

children.title: Parallelism Profiles
children.top_down_role: Available concurrency across distributed computation structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallelism Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents available concurrency in the dependency graph of a distributed computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent one algorithm execution by a finite acyclic task graph \(H=(U,F)\), where an edge \((u,v)\) requires task \(u\) to finish before \(v\) begins. For unit-duration tasks, define level sets recursively by \[\ell(u)=1+\max_{(v,u)\in F}\ell(v),\] taking the maximum over an empty set as zero. The level-parallelism profile is \[p_j=|\{u\in U:\ell(u)=j\}|.\] Its total work is \(W=\sum_jp_j=|U|\), its span is \(S=\max_u\ell(u)\), and its maximum instantaneous structural parallelism is \(p_{\max}=\max_jp_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parallelism profile counts dependency-ready tasks at each graph level and yields total work, span, and maximum structural concurrency.
assumptions_latex: H=(U,F)\text{ is a finite directed acyclic task graph}
\text{tasks have unit duration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W=\sum_{j=1}^{S}p_j=|U|\quad\text{and}\quad p_{\max}=\max_jp_j

notation.meaning: Number of tasks at dependency level j

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-task DAG representation is coherent, but the level profile measures ASAP structural concurrency rather than generally available runtime concurrency; a source must establish this intended convention.

children.title: Latency Profiles
children.top_down_role: Delay characteristics across distributed solver execution regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Latency Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines end-to-end and per-stage latency for a causally ordered distributed execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=(U,F)\) be an acyclic execution graph. Assign each task \(u\) a processing duration \(c(u)\ge0\) and each dependency edge \((u,v)\) a communication delay \(d(u,v)\ge0\). Under unlimited processors, define earliest completion times by \[C(u)=c(u)+\max_{(v,u)\in F}\bigl(C(v)+d(v,u)\bigr),\] with an empty maximum equal to zero. The latency profile is the collection \((C(u))_{u\in U}\), and the end-to-end latency is \[L=\max_{u\in U}C(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Latency propagates processing and communication delays through the execution DAG; end-to-end latency is the latest earliest-completion time.
assumptions_latex: H=(U,F)\text{ is a finite directed acyclic graph}
c(u)\ge0\text{ and }d(u,v)\ge0
\text{processors are unlimited and tasks are nonpreemptive}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L=\max_{u\in U}\left[c(u)+\max_{(v,u)\in F}(C(v)+d(v,u))\right]

notation.meaning: Communication delay on a dependency edge
