children.title: Cryptographic DCOP Methods
children.top_down_role: DCOP protection families built on cryptographic computation or communication mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: A DCOP functionality \(F\) maps private local inputs to prescribed outputs.
The protocol uses cryptographic primitives under stated computational assumptions and targets coalitions of size at most \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cryptographic DCOP method securely realizes the DCOP functionality when correctness and coalition-view simulation both hold.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: secure-realization definition specialized to DCOP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Secure-computation characterization of cryptographic methods for solving DCOPs under bounded collusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(I_1,\ldots,I_n)=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)\) be the ideal DCOP functionality and let \(\Pi\) be a cryptographic protocol. The protocol is a cryptographic DCOP method secure against semi-honest coalitions of size at most \(t\) when it computes \(F\) with the declared correctness probability and, for every \(C\subseteq N\) with \(|C|\le t\), there exists a probabilistic polynomial-time simulator satisfying \[S_C(I_C,Y_C)\mathrel{\approx_c}\operatorname{View}_C^{\Pi}(I_1,\ldots,I_n).\] The security claim must identify the primitive assumptions, leakage function, collusion threshold, and whether communication metadata belongs to the protected view.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cryptographic DCOP protocol correctly realizes the desired optimization functionality while hiding inputs from every coalition within its declared threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Cryptographic DCOP Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The secure-realization statement is coherent for semi-honest bounded coalitions, but no cryptographic DCOP source supports the selected ideal functionality, threshold, leakage, or metadata requirements. Because this leaf denotes a family of methods rather than a single security notion, the choice of definition rather than principle or representation also requires source confirmation.

children.title: Collusion-Secure DCOP Methods
children.top_down_role: Privacy-preserving DCOP families designed for cooperating adversarial participants.

knowledge_statements.title: Collusion-Secure DCOP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulation-based security against semi-honest coalitions of bounded size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite DCOP instance, let \(P\) be a distributed protocol computing solution output \(y=P(I)\), and let \(C\) be any coalition with \(|C|\leq t\). The protocol is \(t\)-collusion-secure for leakage function \(L_C\) if there exists a probabilistic polynomial-time simulator \(S_C\) such that \[\mathsf{View}_C(P,I)\mathrel{\approx_c}S_C\bigl(I_C,y_C,L_C(I,y)\bigr).\] Thus coalition members learn, up to computational indistinguishability, no information beyond their inputs, outputs, and declared leakage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DCOP protocol resists coalitions of at most t agents when their joint transcript can be simulated from only their permitted inputs, outputs, and leakage.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite, explicitly encoded DCOP instance.
Coalitions are semi-honest and contain at most \(t\) agents.
Cryptographic primitives and simulators use probabilistic polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{View}_C(P,I)\mathrel{\approx_c}S_C(I_C,y_C,L_C(I,y))\) for every admissible coalition \(C\).

notation.meaning: joint random view of coalition C during protocol execution
explicitly permitted leakage to coalition C

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simulation-based multiparty security gives the conventional formal meaning of collusion resistance
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simulation-based definition is plausible and the content kind fits, but no inspectable citation supports its application to collusion-secure DCOP protocols or the stated leakage interface.

children.title: Collusion-Threat Regimes
children.top_down_role: Adversary structures distinguished by the size or capability of colluding groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Collusion-Threat Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coalition classes parameterized by size, behavior, and corruption timing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an agent set \(A\), a collusion-threat regime is a triple \(\mathcal T=(\Gamma,\beta,\tau)\), where \(\Gamma\subseteq 2^A\) is the family of admissible corrupt coalitions, \(\beta\in\{\mathrm{semi\text{-}honest},\mathrm{malicious}\}\) specifies behavior, and \(\tau\in\{\mathrm{static},\mathrm{adaptive}\}\) specifies corruption timing. The threshold regime with bound \(t\) has \(\Gamma_t=\{C\subseteq A:|C|\leq t\}\). A security claim is meaningful only relative to a stated \(\mathcal T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A collusion regime specifies which coalitions may form, whether corrupted agents follow the protocol, and whether corruption choices are static or adaptive.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite set of DCOP agents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T=(\Gamma,\beta,\tau)\) completely identifies the modeled coalition class, behavior, and corruption timing.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: coalition structure, adversarial behavior, and corruption timing are standard multiparty threat-model dimensions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tuple captures several standard adversary dimensions, but the claim that it completely identifies the threat regime omits possible channel, leakage, computational-power, and security-goal assumptions. A supporting threat-model source is required.

children.title: Obfuscation DCOP Methods
children.top_down_role: DCOP protection families that obscure sensitive model or message content.

knowledge_statements.title: Obfuscation DCOP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized message transformation preserving the underlying DCOP protocol output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a DCOP protocol \(P\), agents sample private randomness \(r_i\). Whenever \(P\) would send message \(m_{ij}^k\), agent \(i\) instead sends \(z_{ij}^k=E_{ij}^k(m_{ij}^k;r_i)\); the authorized recipient computes \(D_{ij}^k(z_{ij}^k)=m_{ij}^k\) and performs the prescribed update of \(P\). Execution stops when \(P\)'s stopping rule holds and returns the same assignment as \(P\). Correctness requires \(D_{ij}^k(E_{ij}^k(m;r))=m\) for every admissible message and randomness value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents randomize protocol messages, authorized recipients recover them, and the wrapped execution returns the same DCOP assignment as the original protocol.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has specified message, update, and stopping rules.
Every authorized recipient possesses the information required by its decoder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformed execution preserves \(P\)'s output whenever all encoder-decoder pairs satisfy exact correctness.

notation.meaning: randomized encoder for the round-k message from i to j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: randomized encode-decode wrapping is a generic formalization of message obfuscation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits a method container, but exact encode-decode correctness describes a generic wrapper and does not by itself establish obfuscation or privacy. A DCOP-specific source and threat-dependent concealment criterion are required.

children.title: Steganographic DCOP Methods
children.top_down_role: DCOP protection families that conceal sensitive communication within cover channels.

knowledge_statements.title: Steganographic DCOP Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding protocol messages within an innocent-looking cover channel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) generate message \(m_{ij}^k\) in round \(k\), and let \(Q_{ij}^k\) be a cover-object distribution. Agent \(i\) samples or constructs \(c_{ij}^k\leftarrow\operatorname{Embed}(m_{ij}^k,Q_{ij}^k;r_i)\), sends \(c_{ij}^k\), and agent \(j\) recovers \(\widehat m_{ij}^k=\operatorname{Extract}(c_{ij}^k)\) before applying \(P\)'s update. The method is reliable with error \(\delta\) when \(\Pr[\widehat m_{ij}^k\neq m_{ij}^k]\leq\delta\); it outputs \(P\)'s assignment after the original stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A steganographic wrapper embeds DCOP messages in cover objects, extracts them at authorized recipients, and follows the original protocol with bounded decoding error.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has specified message, update, and stopping rules.
Sender and recipient share a compatible embedding and extraction scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each hidden message is recovered with error at most \(\delta\), enabling execution of the wrapped protocol.

notation.meaning: cover-object distribution for a communication channel
transmitted cover object containing a protocol message

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: embed-extract reliability is the conventional abstract steganographic construction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Embed-extract reliability alone does not characterize steganographic security. Moreover, a per-message error bound does not guarantee that the complete execution returns the original protocol's assignment. The mathematical version requires authoritative support and an explicit undetectability and execution-level error model.

children.title: Concealment-Channel Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Applicability limits separating content obfuscation from covert-channel protection.

knowledge_statements.title: Concealment-Channel Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detectability and semantic-leakage limits of concealment-only channels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_m\) denote the transmitted-object distribution when hidden message \(m\) is sent. If there exist \(m_0,m_1\) and an event \(B\) with \(\Pr[Z_{m_0}\in B]=1\) and \(\Pr[Z_{m_1}\in B]=0\), an observer distinguishes the messages with probability \(1\); hence the channel provides no message indistinguishability. Moreover, if a public deterministic encoding is injective, observing its output uniquely determines the encoded message. Concealment alone therefore does not imply cryptographic confidentiality or coalition security.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint message-dependent cover distributions are perfectly distinguishable, and public injective obfuscation is reversible; concealment alone does not ensure confidentiality.
assumptions_latex: The observer knows the relevant transmitted-object distributions or public encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Perfectly separable cover distributions or public injective encodings fail to hide the underlying message.

notation.meaning: random transmitted object conditional on hidden message m

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: disjoint-support distinguishability and inversion of public injective maps are elementary information-security boundaries
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinguishability and injective-encoding boundaries are mathematically sound and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the record has no inspectable source connecting these limits to concealment-channel DCOP methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Privacy-Loss Metrics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case transcript privacy loss between neighboring DCOP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a randomized DCOP mechanism \(M\), an observable transcript space \(\mathcal Y\), and a neighboring-instance relation \(\sim\). For neighboring instances \(I\sim I'\), define the pointwise privacy loss at transcript \(y\) by \(L_{I,I'}(y)=\log\!\left(\Pr[M(I)=y]/\Pr[M(I')=y]\right)\), with the usual extended-real conventions. The worst-case privacy loss is \(\varepsilon(M)=\sup_{I\sim I'}\sup_{S\subseteq\mathcal Y}\log\!\left(\Pr[M(I)\in S]/\Pr[M(I')\in S]\right)\). Finite \(\varepsilon(M)\) yields pure differential privacy for the chosen adjacency relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Privacy loss is the worst log-likelihood ratio between observable transcripts produced by neighboring DCOP instances; smaller values indicate stronger indistinguishability.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a randomized mechanism with measurable observable transcripts.
The relation \(\sim\) specifies which private DCOP changes must be hidden.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(I\sim I'\) and measurable \(S\), \(\Pr[M(I)\in S]\leq e^{\varepsilon(M)}\Pr[M(I')\in S]\).

notation.meaning: randomized DCOP mechanism including its observable communication

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: worst-case log-likelihood ratio is the standard pure differential-privacy metric
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended pure differential-privacy metric is standard, but the pointwise probability-mass formula is not valid for an arbitrary measurable transcript space, and the event-ratio definition needs explicit zero-denominator conventions. An authoritative source and a discrete or measure-theoretic formulation are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Privacy–Communication Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of privacy loss versus communication consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a protocol class \(\Pi\), let \(p(P)\) be privacy loss and \(c(P)\) its communication cost under fixed instance, adversary, and accuracy conventions. The achievable set is \(\mathcal A_{pc}=\{(p(P),c(P)):P\in\Pi\}\). A protocol \(P\) lies on the privacy-communication frontier exactly when no \(Q\in\Pi\) satisfies \(p(Q)\leq p(P)\) and \(c(Q)\leq c(P)\) with at least one strict inequality. Equivalently, the frontier consists of the nondominated points of \(\mathcal A_{pc}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The privacy–communication tradeoff is the nondominated frontier of achievable privacy-loss and communication-cost pairs under fixed evaluation conventions.
assumptions_latex: Every \(P\in\Pi\) is evaluated on the same instance class and adversary model.
Privacy loss and communication cost are ordered so that smaller values are preferable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The privacy-communication frontier equals the set of nondominated points of \(\mathcal A_{pc}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nondominance is the standard mathematical representation of a two-objective resource tradeoff
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto representation and content kind fit the tradeoff container, but no citation supports this DCOP formulation, and the communication-cost, instance, adversary, and accuracy conventions remain uninstantiated.

knowledge_statements.title: Privacy–Solution-Quality Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of privacy loss versus DCOP suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a protocol class \(\Pi\), let \(p(P)\) be privacy loss and let \(g(P)=\mathbb E[F(\widehat x_P)-F(x^*)]\) be expected suboptimality for a minimization DCOP. Define \(\mathcal A_{pg}=\{(p(P),g(P)):P\in\Pi\}\). A protocol \(P\) is privacy-quality efficient exactly when no \(Q\in\Pi\) satisfies \(p(Q)\leq p(P)\) and \(g(Q)\leq g(P)\) with at least one strict inequality. The tradeoff frontier is the nondominated subset of \(\mathcal A_{pg}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The privacy–quality tradeoff is the nondominated set of achievable privacy-loss and expected-suboptimality pairs for a fixed DCOP evaluation model.
assumptions_latex: All protocols use the same minimization objective \(F\) and instance distribution.
An optimal assignment \(x^*\) exists and the displayed expectations are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The privacy-quality frontier equals the nondominated subset of \(\mathcal A_{pg}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expected optimality gap and Pareto nondominance give a standard optimization-quality tradeoff
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto representation fits the container, but the randomness underlying the expectation and the common instance distribution are not defined in the statement, and no authoritative source supports the DCOP-specific formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Privacy–Computation Tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of privacy loss versus computational resource use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a protocol class \(\Pi\), let \(p(P)\) be privacy loss and \(w(P)\) its computational cost under a fixed machine or oracle model. The achievable set is \(\mathcal A_{pw}=\{(p(P),w(P)):P\in\Pi\}\). A protocol \(P\) lies on the privacy-computation frontier exactly when no \(Q\in\Pi\) satisfies \(p(Q)\leq p(P)\) and \(w(Q)\leq w(P)\) with at least one strict inequality. Thus the frontier is the nondominated subset of \(\mathcal A_{pw}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The privacy–computation tradeoff is the nondominated frontier of achievable privacy-loss and computational-cost pairs under one fixed cost model.
assumptions_latex: All protocols are evaluated under the same adversary, accuracy, and computational models.
Privacy loss and computational cost are ordered so that smaller values are preferable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The privacy-computation frontier equals the nondominated subset of \(\mathcal A_{pw}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nondominance is the standard mathematical representation of a privacy-resource tradeoff
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nondominated-set representation fits the tradeoff container, but the computational cost model and evaluation conventions are placeholders and no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Trust Models
children.top_down_role: Trust assumptions governing agent participation, information exchange, or delegated computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal trust assumptions governing agents, coalitions, and delegated actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A DCOP trust model is a tuple \(\mathcal M=(A,\Gamma,B,R)\), where \(A\) is the agent set, \(\Gamma\subseteq2^A\) is the family of coalitions whose coordinated behavior is considered, \(B_i\) is the admissible behavior set of agent \(i\), and \(R\subseteq A\times A\times\mathcal K\) is a context-indexed trust relation. The predicate \((i,j,k)\in R\) means that agent \(i\) accepts agent \(j\)'s action or report in context \(k\) without additional verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust model specifies agents, possible coalitions, admissible behaviors, and which agents accept one another's actions in each coordination context.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and the context set \(\mathcal K\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M\) determines the trust assumptions under which a DCOP coordination protocol is interpreted.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: participants, coalitions, admissible behaviors, and reliance relations are standard trust-model components
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed tuple is an unsupported custom formalization rather than an established DCOP trust-model definition. It also cannot determine all protocol trust assumptions without semantics for behaviors, verification, delegation, and failures.

children.title: Trust-Aware Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination structures shaped by heterogeneous or limited trust.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Aware Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination restricted by trust thresholds and verifiable fallback actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a DCOP, trust scores \(s_{ij}^k\), thresholds \(\theta_i^k\), and a base coordination protocol \(P\), agent \(i\) initializes its local state as in \(P\). On receiving report \(m\) from \(j\) in context \(k\), it accepts and applies \(P\)'s update only if \(s_{ij}^k\geq\theta_i^k\); otherwise it requests verification or invokes a specified safe fallback. Trust scores are updated by a declared rule after verifiable outcomes. The algorithm stops under \(P\)'s stopping rule and returns the resulting assignment and unresolved-verification flags.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents apply protocol updates only when contextual trust meets a threshold; otherwise they verify or use a safe fallback and report unresolved checks.
assumptions_latex: The base protocol \(P\), score-update rule, thresholds, and fallback actions are specified.
Every accepted or rejected report has a well-defined coordination context.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every unverified report with \(s_{ij}^k<\theta_i^k\) is excluded from the ordinary update path.

notation.meaning: agent i's trust score for agent j in context k
acceptance threshold of agent i in context k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: threshold gating with verification or fallback is a generic trust-aware coordination rule
