children.title: XCSP Encodings
children.top_down_role: XCSP representations used for centralized constraint models within DCOP interchange workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: XCSP Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite DCOP representation as variables, domains, cost functions, and ownership metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite DCOP \(D=(A,X,(D_x)_{x\in X},F,\alpha)\), an XCSP-style encoding introduces one finite-domain variable for each \(x\in X\), one intensional or extensional constraint for each cost function \(f\in F\), and a minimization objective equal to \(\sum_{f\in F}f(x_{\operatorname{scp}(f)})\). Agent ownership \(\alpha:X\to A\) must be preserved by supported metadata or an external correspondence table. The encoding is semantics-preserving when every complete assignment has the same feasibility and total cost in both representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An XCSP-style encoding preserves DCOP variables, domains, constraints, total objective value, and—through metadata or an external table—agent ownership.
assumptions_latex: The DCOP has finite variables, finite domains, and explicitly representable cost functions.
The selected XCSP version supports the required constraint and objective forms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every complete assignment \(a\), the encoded instance is feasible exactly when \(a\) is DCOP-feasible, and its objective value equals \(\sum_{f\in F}f(a_{\operatorname{scp}(f)})\).

notation.meaning: finite family of DCOP cost functions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but XCSP syntax and semantics are version-dependent, and the ownership-metadata claim is not supported. A specific XCSP standard version and inspectable schema or specification locator are required.

children.title: XDisCSP Encodings
children.top_down_role: XDisCSP representations carrying distributed model structure.

knowledge_statements.title: XDisCSP Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract XDisCSP representation; exact schema elements require a format specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An XDisCSP encoding of a distributed constraint problem is a tuple \(E=(A,X,D,C,\alpha,\omega)\), where \(A\) is a finite agent set, \(X\) is a finite variable set, \(D=(D_x)_{x\in X}\) gives finite domains, \(C\) is a finite collection of scoped relations or cost functions, \(\alpha:X\to A\) assigns every variable to one agent, and \(\omega:C\to 2^A\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) records constraint ownership. The encoding denotes the feasible assignments, or assignment costs, obtained by evaluating every member of \(C\) on its declared scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An XDisCSP instance records agents, variables, domains, constraints, variable owners, and nonempty constraint-owner sets, while preserving the represented feasible assignments or costs.
assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(X\), and \(C\) are finite.
Each \(D_x\) is finite and nonempty.
Every constraint references declared variables and domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) determines a distributed constraint problem together with ownership metadata.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No XDisCSP specification or version is cited. The tuple fields, single variable ownership, nonempty set-valued constraint ownership, and denotational semantics may be a proposed abstraction rather than the actual format schema.

children.title: Cross-Format Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Representational correspondence, conversion limits, plus interoperability across the two formats.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Format Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic compatibility between centralized XCSP-style and distributed XDisCSP-style instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) encode problems over corresponding variables and domains, and let \(\pi\) be a bijection between their complete assignments. They are cross-format compatible when there exists a constant \(k\in\mathbb R\), with \(k=0\) for exact compatibility, such that every assignment \(s\) satisfies \(F_{E_2}(\pi(s))=F_{E_1}(s)+k\), using \(+\infty\) for infeasibility, and when ownership metadata erased from the distributed encoding does not alter this equality. Hence corresponding optimal assignments and feasibility statuses agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two encodings are compatible when an assignment bijection preserves feasibility and objective values up to an assignment-independent constant, irrespective of erased distribution metadata.
assumptions_latex: The formats admit the same objective convention, including \(+\infty\) for infeasibility.
\(\pi\) preserves variable-domain membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_{E_2}=\pi(\operatorname*{argmin}F_{E_1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No XCSP–XDisCSP correspondence source supports this compatibility criterion. Preservation up to an additive constant is plausible but may not be the formats' defined compatibility relation; moreover, the displayed argmin equality suppresses the different assignment spaces and should apply the bijection explicitly to the first argmin set.

knowledge_statements.title: Extensional Constraint Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain table representation of hard or weighted constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scope \(S=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) with finite domains, an extensional hard constraint is represented by a table \(T\subseteq D_{x_1}\times\cdots\times D_{x_k}\) and a flag declaring whether \(T\) lists allowed or forbidden tuples. A weighted constraint is represented by finitely many pairs \((t,w_t)\), where \(t\) is a scope tuple and \(w_t\in\overline{\mathbb R}\), together with a default cost \(w_0\). Its value is \(w_t\) for a listed tuple and \(w_0\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extensional constraint explicitly lists allowed, forbidden, or weighted scope tuples and uses a declared default for unlisted tuples.
assumptions_latex: Every scoped domain is finite.
Each listed tuple has the scope arity and respects its component domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The table determines a total predicate or cost function on \(\prod_{i=1}^k D_{x_i}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard, but no authoritative constraint-format source with a specific locator is supplied for allowed, forbidden, weighted, and default-cost table semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Intensional Constraint Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expression-based representation evaluated over a declared constraint scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered scope \(S=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), an intensional constraint is represented by a typed expression \(eindnasrepma S\) whose free variables are contained in \(S\). Under an environment \(s\in\prod_{i=1}^kD_{x_i}\), deterministic evaluation yields either a Boolean value \(\llbracket e\rrbracket_s\in\{\mathsf{false},\mathsf{true}\}\) for a hard constraint or a cost \(\llbracket e\rrbracket_s\in\overline{\mathbb R}\). All operators, exceptional values, and evaluation order must have format-defined semantics, making the represented predicate or cost independent of the solver implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intensional constraint is a typed expression whose evaluation on each scope assignment deterministically returns a truth value or cost under defined operator semantics.
assumptions_latex: The free variables of \(e\) lie in \(S\).
Every operator in \(e\) has declared types and deterministic semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\mapsto\llbracket e\rrbracket_s\) defines the encoded constraint.

notation.meaning: value of e under assignment s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No expression-language specification is cited, and the phrase "eindnasrepma S" is corrupted and makes the formal statement syntactically unreliable. A sourced replacement must identify the expression grammar, types, exceptional values, and evaluation semantics.

children.title: Variable Ownership Metadata
children.top_down_role: Agent responsibility annotations for variables, decisions, or local state.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Ownership Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-owner metadata for variables in a distributed constraint instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite agent set \(A\) and variable set \(X\), variable ownership metadata is a total map \(\alpha:X\to A\). The assertion \(\alpha(x)=a\) declares agent \(a\) responsible for maintaining the current value of \(x\) and issuing authorized value changes. An encoding is ownership-complete precisely when \(\alpha\) is defined for every \(x\in X\), and ownership-consistent precisely when each variable has exactly one image under \(\alpha\). Replicas or observers, if recorded, are separate from this owner map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable ownership is a total single-valued map assigning each variable to the agent responsible for its authoritative value and changes.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(X\) are finite.
\(A\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall x\in X\;\exists!a\in A:\alpha(x)=a\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No DCOP metadata schema supports the asserted total, single-owner map or the stronger operational meaning of authority to maintain and change values. DCOP formalisms differ in whether ownership is explicit and what responsibility entails.

children.title: Constraint Ownership Metadata
children.top_down_role: Responsibility annotations for constraints, costs, or utility components.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Ownership Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metadata assigning responsibility for constraint evaluation or enforcement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given agents \(A\) and constraints \(C\), constraint ownership metadata is a map \(\omega:C\to2^A\setminus\{\varnothing\}\). For each \(c\in C\), every member of \(\omega(c)\) is designated to evaluate, store, or enforce \(c\), according to the declared responsibility mode. Single ownership requires \(|\omega(c)|=1\); replicated ownership permits larger sets. If the schema requires a constraint owner to control a scoped variable, consistency additionally requires \(\omega(c)\cap\{\alpha(x):x\in\operatorname{scope}(c)\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint ownership assigns each constraint a nonempty responsible agent set, with optional consistency requiring an owner to control a scoped variable.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(C\) are finite.
Variable ownership \(\alpha\) is available when scope-based consistency is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall c\in C:\omega(c)\neq\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonempty set-valued owner map and the alternatives "evaluate, store, or enforce" are schema-dependent and unsupported. The optional scope-owner consistency condition also requires a cited specification identifying when it applies.

children.title: Distribution Topology Metadata
children.top_down_role: Placement, locality, visibility, plus communication-relevant model annotations.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution Topology Metadata
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph metadata describing permitted direct communication among deployed agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For agents \(A\), distribution topology metadata is a graph \(G=(A,E,\tau)\), where \(E\subseteq A\times A\) contains the permitted direct communication links and \(\tau:E\to L\) assigns optional link attributes such as transport or direction. An undirected topology requires \((a,b)\in E\) exactly when \((b,a)\in E\). For every constraint whose evaluation requires agents in \(B_c\subseteq A\), communication feasibility requires that the vertices of \(B_c\) lie in one connected component of the underlying graph, unless an external relay is declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distribution topology is an attributed agent graph; agents jointly needed for a constraint must be mutually reachable unless an external relay is specified.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is finite.
Every endpoint appearing in \(E\) belongs to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall c\in C\), the required agent set \(B_c\) is connected or externally relayed.

notation.meaning: agents required to evaluate constraint c

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No topology schema supports this attributed-graph representation or the asserted connectivity condition. The conclusion introduces C without defining it, link-attribute codomain L is not explained, and external-relay semantics are unspecified.

children.title: Agent Lifecycle Management
children.top_down_role: Agent creation, activation, suspension, shutdown, plus lifecycle state observability.

knowledge_statements.title: Agent Lifecycle Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state lifecycle protocol for distributed solver agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each agent \(a\), initialize \(q_a:=\mathsf{created}\). Accept only transitions in \(\mathsf{created}\to\mathsf{configured}\to\mathsf{running}\to\mathsf{stopping}\to\mathsf{terminated}\), with optional \(\mathsf{running}\leftrightarrow\mathsf{suspended}\) and failure transitions from any nonterminal state to \(\mathsf{failed}\). Configuration validates the local model and communication endpoints before entering \(\mathsf{running}\). On stopping, reject new computation messages, drain or cancel queued work according to policy, release resources, and enter \(\mathsf{terminated}\). The runtime completes when every agent is terminal and reports either a result or failure status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent follows validated creation, configuration, execution, shutdown, and terminal states, with explicit suspension, failure, queue-draining, and completion rules.
assumptions_latex: The agent set is finite.
Lifecycle events for each agent are processed sequentially.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall a\), the final state satisfies \(q_a\in\{\mathsf{terminated},\mathsf{failed}\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-state protocol is implementation-specific and uncited. The assumptions do not guarantee that every agent eventually reaches a terminal state, so the conclusion is not established merely by the stated transition rules.

children.title: Agent Deployment Topologies
children.top_down_role: Process, host, container, plus site placement patterns for distributed solver agents.

knowledge_statements.title: Agent Deployment Topologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mapping logical DCOP agents onto physical runtime processes and hosts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be logical agents, \(P\) runtime processes, and \(H\) hosts. A deployment topology is a pair of total maps \(\delta:A\to P\) and \(\eta:P\to H\), together with an interprocess link graph \(G_P=(P,E_P)\). Agents \(a,b\) are colocated exactly when \(\delta(a)=\delta(b)\); their host locations are \(\eta(\delta(a))\) and \(\eta(\delta(b))\). A deployment realizes a required logical communication edge \((a,b)\) when the corresponding processes coincide or are connected by an allowed path in \(G_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deployment maps every logical agent to a process and every process to a host, while ensuring required logical communications are realizable.
assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(P\), and \(H\) are finite and nonempty.
Every edge of \(E_P\) has endpoints in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall(a,b)\in E_A\), either \(\delta(a)=\delta(b)\) or \(\delta(a)\leadsto_{G_P}\delta(b)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No runtime deployment specification supports these maps or path-realization semantics. The conclusion uses the required logical-edge set E_A without introducing it in the statement, assumptions, or notation.

children.title: Lifecycle-Deployment Coupling
children.top_down_role: Operational dependencies between agent state transitions plus deployment placement.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifecycle-Deployment Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safety condition linking agent lifecycle transitions to deployment availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_a\) be agent \(a\)'s lifecycle state and \(\delta_t(a)\) its process placement at time \(t\). Lifecycle and deployment are safely coupled when \(q_a(t)=\mathsf{running}\) implies that \(\delta_t(a)\) is defined, its process is live, and every required communication endpoint is bound; placement changes occur only while \(q_a(t)\in\{\mathsf{configured},\mathsf{suspended}\}\); and process loss forces \(q_a\) to \(\mathsf{failed}\) or \(\mathsf{suspended}\) before further solver actions. Termination must release the placement and its exclusive resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A running agent must have a live, connected placement; migration requires a safe state, process loss halts computation, and termination releases resources.
assumptions_latex: Lifecycle state and process liveness are observable atomically at transition boundaries.
Required endpoints are known before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_a(t)=\mathsf{running}\Rightarrow\operatorname{live}(\delta_t(a))\land\operatorname{ready}(a,t)\).

notation.meaning: agent lifecycle state at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The running-state invariant is plausible, but the allowed migration states, process-loss response, endpoint readiness, and exclusive-resource release rules are uncited implementation policies rather than established general DCOP conditions.

children.title: Message Queue Management
children.top_down_role: Buffering, prioritization, backpressure, plus queue capacity concerns.

knowledge_statements.title: Message Queue Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-agent queue discipline for asynchronous distributed-solver messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each receiving agent \(a\), initialize an empty queue \(Q_a\) and a monotonically increasing arrival counter. On receipt of a valid message \(m\), attach its priority \(p(m)\) and arrival index \(r(m)\), then insert it into \(Q_a\). When \(a\) is runnable, remove a message minimizing \((-p(m),r(m))\), dispatch it once, and record its disposition. Reject malformed, expired, or duplicate messages according to declared identifiers. On shutdown, either drain \(Q_a\) completely or cancel every remaining entry, as fixed by the lifecycle policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent validates and queues messages, dispatches them by priority then arrival order, handles duplicates and expiry, and drains or cancels on shutdown.
assumptions_latex: Each accepted message has a receiver and unique identifier.
Arrival indices are unique within each receiver queue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every removed message is dispatched once or receives an explicit cancellation disposition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The priority/FIFO discipline and duplicate, expiry, and shutdown policies are implementation-specific and unsupported. The conclusion also omits messages that remain queued indefinitely, so it does not express a completeness or liveness guarantee without an additional progress assumption.

children.title: Communication Transports
children.top_down_role: Local, networked, brokered, plus direct communication substrates.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Transports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract transport interface independent of concrete network technology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A communication transport over endpoints \(U\) is a tuple \(T=(M,\mathsf{send},\mathsf{recv},\sigma)\), where \(M\) is the message space, \(\mathsf{send}:U\times U\times M\to R\) submits a message, \(\mathsf{recv}:U\to M^*\) exposes delivered messages, and \(\sigma\) declares ordering, reliability, duplication, and failure behavior. A transport realizes a logical channel \((a,b)\) when the agents' bound endpoints belong to \(U\) and each accepted send is handled exactly according to \(\sigma\). Serialization and deserialization must preserve the message's type and semantic payload.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transport supplies send and receive operations plus declared ordering, reliability, duplication, failure, and serialization semantics for bound agent endpoints.
assumptions_latex: Endpoint bindings are established before communication.
Messages admitted by \(\mathsf{send}\) are serializable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{decode}(\operatorname{encode}(m))=m\) semantically, and delivery conforms to \(\sigma\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No transport-interface specification supports this tuple and its guarantees. The receive signature U to M* does not model time, blocking, or state, R is undefined, and semantic serialization equality and conformance to sigma require explicit sourced definitions.

children.title: Message Delivery Semantics
children.top_down_role: Ordering, duplication, persistence, acknowledgement, plus delivery guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Message Delivery Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-based semantics for reliable point-to-point runtime messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each sent message have a unique identifier, and let \(S_{ij}\) and \(D_{ij}\) be the send and delivery traces from agent \(i\) to agent \(j\). Delivery is at-most-once when every identifier occurs at most once in \(D_{ij}\); at-least-once when every message sent to a nonfaulty recipient eventually occurs in \(D_{ij}\); and exactly-once when both properties hold. Delivery is FIFO when, for messages \(m_1,m_2\), the order \(m_1<_{S_{ij}}m_2\) implies \(m_1<_{D_{ij}}m_2\) whenever both are delivered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delivery guarantees specify message multiplicity, eventual delivery to nonfaulty recipients, and whether each sender–recipient channel preserves send order.
assumptions_latex: \(S_{ij}\) and \(D_{ij}\) are traces indexed by one directed channel.
Every logical message has a unique identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{exactly-once}=\text{at-most-once}\wedge\text{at-least-once}\), independently of the FIFO property.

notation.meaning: send trace from agent i to agent j
delivery trace from agent i to agent j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the selected delivery model. At-least-once delivery to a nonfaulty recipient requires explicit channel, retry, fairness, and failure assumptions; exactly-once also depends on the meaning of logical-message identity and duplicate suppression.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Preprocessing Services
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-preserving preprocessing for a finite DCOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite DCOP \(P=(X,D,F)\), agents repeatedly exchange locally derived domain and cost summaries and apply transformations that delete infeasible values, aggregate constants, or tighten cost bounds. Each transformation must produce a reduced instance \(P'\), an offset \(c\), and a reconstruction map \(R\) satisfying \(\operatorname{OPT}(P)=c+\operatorname{OPT}(P')\) and mapping every optimizer of \(P'\) to an optimizer of \(P\). Processing stops when a distributed fixed point is reached; the service outputs \((P',c,R)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents cooperatively reduce a DCOP while retaining an exact objective offset and a map that reconstructs an optimizer of the original instance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and all domains in \(D\) are finite.
Every accepted preprocessing rule supplies a valid reconstruction map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(P)=c+\operatorname{OPT}(P')\) and \(R(\arg\min P')\subseteq\arg\min P\).

notation.meaning: original finite distributed constraint optimization problem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the preprocessing-services container, but no source establishes this distributed fixed-point procedure or its exact offset and reconstruction guarantees. The permitted transformations and termination conditions are insufficiently specified.

knowledge_statements.title: Termination Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global termination condition for asynchronous message-driven DCOP computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a consistent global cut \(C\), termination is detected precisely when every nonfaulty agent is passive and every channel between nonfaulty agents contains no message whose receipt can reactivate computation. Formally, with activity indicator \(a_i(C)\) and in-transit multiset \(M_{ij}(C)\), the predicate is \[T(C)\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\bigl(\forall i\in A_{\mathrm{nf}},\ a_i(C)=0\bigr)\ \wedge\ \bigl(\forall i,j\in A_{\mathrm{nf}},\ M_{ij}(C)=\varnothing\bigr).\] A correct detector announces termination only when \(T(C)\) holds and eventually announces it once the predicate remains true.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Termination requires a consistent global state in which every nonfaulty agent is passive and no in-transit message can restart computation.
assumptions_latex: Communication events defining \(C\) form a consistent cut.
Only receipt of an in-transit computational message can reactivate a passive agent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A sound and live detector announces termination exactly when the stable predicate \(T(C)\) holds.

notation.meaning: messages in transit from i to j at cut C
activity indicator of agent i at cut C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative termination-detection source and precise failure model are required. The prose allows in-transit messages that cannot reactivate computation, whereas the displayed predicate requires every relevant channel to be empty; the final 'exactly when' wording also conflates detection safety and eventual detection.

children.title: Fault Detection
children.top_down_role: Monitoring signals, failure suspicion, timeout interpretation, plus fault localization.

knowledge_statements.title: Fault Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eventually accurate crash-failure detector for solver agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fault detector outputs at each agent \(i\) and time \(t\) a suspicion set \(S_i(t)\subseteq A\). For crash failures, it is eventually strongly complete if every crashed agent is eventually permanently suspected by every nonfaulty agent, and eventually weakly accurate if some nonfaulty agent is eventually never suspected by any nonfaulty agent. A detector satisfying both properties may issue false suspicions before stabilization, so suspicion is evidence for recovery coordination rather than a proof of failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each agent maintains suspects; crashed agents eventually remain suspected, while at least one correct agent eventually remains unsuspected after transient mistakes cease.
assumptions_latex: Agents fail only by crashing.
Time is used semantically and need not be globally synchronized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Diamond\mathcal{S}\) combines eventual strong completeness with eventual weak accuracy.

notation.meaning: agents suspected by agent i at time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The properties resemble the eventually-strong failure-detector class, but no source is cited. The label 'eventually strongly complete' should be checked against standard terminology, which ordinarily combines strong completeness with eventual weak accuracy for the stated class.

children.title: Runtime Recovery
children.top_down_role: Restart, rollback, state restoration, replication, plus degraded continuation regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkpoint-and-replay recovery after crash detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each epoch \(e\), agents persist a checkpoint representing a consistent cut \(C_e\) and durably identify messages committed before that cut. After a crash, the replacement process restores the latest agreed checkpoint, discards uncommitted state, and replays each post-checkpoint logical message exactly once in causal order. Recovery completes only after all participating agents enter a common epoch \(e+1\). The recovered execution must be equivalent, for solver state and objective output, to some failure-free execution extending \(C_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents restore a consistent checkpoint, replay post-checkpoint messages once, and resume in a shared epoch with failure-free-equivalent solver state.
assumptions_latex: A durable consistent checkpoint \(C_e\) exists.
Logical message identifiers survive crashes.
The DCOP instance does not change during recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recovered execution is observationally equivalent to a failure-free execution extending \(C_e\).

notation.meaning: consistent checkpoint cut for epoch e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this checkpoint-and-replay algorithm or its observational-equivalence guarantee. Exactly-once causal replay requires durable logging, duplicate suppression, output-commit, and protocol assumptions not stated here.

children.title: Detection-Recovery Coordination
children.top_down_role: Dependencies between failure evidence, recovery initiation, plus consistency restoration.

knowledge_statements.title: Detection-Recovery Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epoch fencing between failure suspicion and recovery actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each recovery attempt carry a monotonically increasing epoch \(e\). An agent may install recovered state for epoch \(e\) only after receiving a recovery certificate naming the failed or suspected members and the selected checkpoint. Once epoch \(e\) is installed, the agent rejects solver and recovery messages tagged with any \(e'<e\). Recovery is committed only when a quorum or all nonfaulty participants, as prescribed by the failure model, acknowledge the same epoch and checkpoint; thus concurrent detections cannot install incomparable recovered states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monotone epochs fence stale messages, and recovery commits only when the required participants agree on one failure view and checkpoint.
assumptions_latex: Epoch identifiers are totally ordered and never reused.
The acknowledgement rule is adequate for the assumed failure model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No agent accepting epoch \(e\) subsequently installs or processes solver state from an epoch \(e'<e\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epoch-fencing principle fits the container, but 'a quorum or all nonfaulty participants' does not define a protocol or sufficient safety condition. A cited failure model, membership model, certificate semantics, and commit rule are required.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: FRODO DisCSP and DCOP Benchmarks in XCSP Format
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: FRODO DisCSP and DCOP Benchmarks in XCSP Format

children.title: Random Max-DisCSP Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Randomized distributed satisfaction instances with controllable density, tightness, plus size.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Max-DisCSP Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary random Max-DisCSP generator with explicit density and tightness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\) variables with common domain \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Independently include each unordered variable pair as a constraint with probability \(p\). For every included pair, independently mark each value pair forbidden with probability \(q\), defining binary cost \(f_{ij}(a,b)=1\) for a forbidden pair and \(0\) otherwise. The benchmark objective is \[\min_{x\in[d]^n}\ \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} f_{ij}(x_i,x_j).\] Instances should report \((n,d,p,q)\) and the random seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark samples a random constraint graph and random forbidden value pairs, then minimizes the number of violated binary constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated instance is a finite binary Max-DisCSP with objective values in \(\{0,1,\ldots,|E|\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is mathematically coherent and fits the benchmark container, but no benchmark source confirms that independent edge sampling and independent forbidden-tuple sampling are the intended Random Max-DisCSP variant.

children.title: Random Graph Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Graph-generated DCOP instances parameterized by topology or structural statistics.

knowledge_statements.title: Random Graph Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Erdős–Rényi constraint-graph generator for DCOP evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\) agents, sample an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) by including each pair \(\{i,j\}\) independently with probability \(p\). Associate one decision variable with each vertex and one binary cost function with each sampled edge; costs may then be drawn from a separately declared distribution \(\mathcal{D}\). The benchmark record consists of \((n,p,\mathcal{D},s)\), where \(s\) is the seed, and has expected edge count \(p\binom{n}{2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Erdős–Rényi graph determines which agent variables interact; a declared distribution supplies edge costs, and a seed makes sampling reproducible.
assumptions_latex: All edge-inclusion trials are independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[|E|]=p\binom{n}{2}\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\deg(i)]=p(n-1)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Erdős–Rényi calculations are standard, but no DCOP benchmark citation is supplied. The domain specification and edge-cost distribution are also necessary to define complete benchmark instances.

children.title: Generator Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter regions supporting comparable difficulty, sparsity, connectivity, plus scaling studies.

knowledge_statements.title: Generator Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling regimes for random binary constraint-graph generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a random binary benchmark with \(n\) variables, domain size \(d\), edge probability \(p_n\), and forbidden-tuple probability \(q_n\), the sparse bounded-degree regime satisfies \(p_n(n-1)\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)\); the growing-degree sparse regime satisfies \(p_n\to0\) and \(p_n(n-1)\to\infty\); and the dense regime satisfies \(p_n\to p\in(0,1]\). Tightness is held fixed when \(q_n\to q\in(0,1)\), or scaled separately when studying feasibility transitions. Comparative experiments must report the complete parameter sequence and seeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Benchmark regimes distinguish bounded expected degree, growing sparse degree, and dense graphs while separately controlling constraint tightness and reproducibility.
assumptions_latex: \(n\to\infty\), \(d\ge2\), and \(p_n,q_n\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected degree \((n-1)p_n\) determines the stated graph-density regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymptotic regimes are coherent definitions, but no source establishes these conventions for the target benchmark family. The role of domain-size scaling is also unclear because the statement introduces d without specifying whether it is fixed or size-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Graph-Coloring Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted graph coloring represented as a finite DCOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\ge2\) colors, assign variable \(x_i\in[k]\) to the agent controlling vertex \(i\). For each edge \(\{i,j\}\), define \(f_{ij}(a,b)=w_{ij}\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}\), where \(w_{ij}>0\). The distributed benchmark is \[\min_{x\in[k]^{|V|}}\ \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E} w_{ij}\mathbf{1}\{x_i=x_j\}.\] An objective value of zero certifies a proper \(k\)-coloring; positive values measure weighted conflicts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each vertex agent chooses a color, and the objective minimizes the total weight of edges whose endpoints choose the same color.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected.
\(k\ge2\) and \(w_{ij}>0\) for every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum equals \(0\) if and only if \(G\) admits a proper \(k\)-coloring.

notation.meaning: conflict weight of edge between vertices i and j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-conflict DCOP representation is mathematically correct for positive edge weights and fits the container, but no source identifies it as the intended distributed graph-coloring benchmark variant.

children.title: Meeting Scheduling Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Participant availability, preference, location, plus time-slot coordination instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Meeting Scheduling Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed finite-slot meeting scheduling with attendance and resource costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be meetings, \(T\) time slots, and \(P_m\) the participants of meeting \(m\). Each meeting has variable \(x_m\in A_m\subseteq T\) and unary preference cost \(c_m(x_m)\). For meetings \(m\ne r\), define \(h_{mr}(x_m,x_r)=+\infty\) when they overlap and either share a participant or require the same exclusive resource, and \(0\) otherwise. The benchmark minimizes \[\sum_{m\in M}c_m(x_m)+\sum_{\{m,r\}}h_{mr}(x_m,x_r)\] over all meeting assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Meetings choose feasible slots, incur preference costs, and may not overlap when they share a participant or exclusive resource.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) and \(T\) are finite.
Every availability set \(A_m\) is a subset of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite-valued optimizer is conflict-free and minimizes total declared preference cost among conflict-free schedules.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular meeting-scheduling benchmark. Meeting duration, overlap semantics, exclusive-resource data, and the index set for the pairwise sum are not defined, so the mathematical instance cannot yet be reproduced reliably.

children.title: Event Scheduling Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Multi-resource event placement instances with venue, capacity, timing, plus conflict structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Event Scheduling Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed event placement with capacities, resources, and cross-event costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each event \(e\in E\) choose a start time and venue \(x_e=(t_e,r_e)\) from a finite feasible set \(A_e\). Unary cost \(c_e(x_e)\) represents preferences. For each coupled pair \(\{e,f\}\), let \(g_{ef}(x_e,x_f)\) be \(+\infty\) for forbidden combinations, including overlapping use of an exclusive venue or resource, and finite otherwise. The benchmark minimizes \[\sum_{e\in E}c_e(x_e)+\sum_{\{e,f\}\in H}g_{ef}(x_e,x_f),\] with venue-capacity restrictions included in \(A_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each event selects a feasible time and venue; hard resource conflicts are forbidden, while preferences and permitted cross-event interactions contribute costs.
assumptions_latex: The event set and every feasible assignment set \(A_e\) are finite.
All hard resource conflicts are encoded by feasible sets or infinite pairwise costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite-valued optimizer satisfies venue capacities and exclusive-resource restrictions while minimizing total coordination cost.

notation.meaning: feasible time–venue assignments for event e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source establishes this event-scheduling benchmark variant. Event duration, venue capacity demand, resource ownership, and the construction of interaction graph H require specification; capacity restrictions can be placed in unary feasible sets only when they depend solely on one event assignment.

children.title: Cross-Event Coordination Regimes
children.top_down_role: Benchmark settings involving coupled events, shared resources, or distributed calendars.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Event Coordination Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coordinated-scheduling instances whose constraints or utility factors couple decisions belonging to distinct events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite event set, let \(x_e\in D_e\) encode the decision for event \(e\), and let \(F\) be a collection of utility factors. A cross-event coordination regime is the DCOP \[\max_{x\in\prod_{e\in E}D_e}\ \sum_{f\in F}f(x_{S_f})\] subject to the hard factors, where at least one scope \(S_f\subseteq E\) contains two distinct events. Its interaction graph has vertex set \(E\) and edge \(\{e,e'\}\) whenever some factor scope contains both events.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduling benchmark is cross-event when at least one constraint or utility term jointly depends on decisions for two different events.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and every \(D_e\) are finite.
Hard-factor violations are represented as infeasible assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists f\in F:\lvert S_f\rvert\ge 2\), so event decisions are not mutually separable.

notation.meaning: Events whose decisions enter factor f.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cross-event coupling is represented by multi-event factor scopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable citation supports this benchmark-specific definition. A factor scope containing two events creates a primal-graph edge but does not by itself imply functional nonseparability; the factor may be constant or additively separable.

children.title: Resource Allocation Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Distributed assignment instances involving scarce, divisible, reusable, or heterogeneous resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Allocation Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite capacitated allocation benchmarks represented as maximization DCOPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be agents and \(R\) resources. For each admissible pair, let \(x_{ar}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) be the quantity of resource \(r\) assigned to agent \(a\), with value \(v_a(x_a)\). A resource-allocation benchmark is \[\max_x\ \sum_{a\in A}v_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{a\in A}d_{ar}x_{ar}\le c_r\ \text{ for every }r\in R,\] together with stated local bounds on \(x_a\). Distribution assigns each \(x_a\) and \(v_a\) to agent \(a\), while capacity constraints induce inter-agent factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents choose resource quantities to maximize total value while shared resource capacities and local assignment bounds remain satisfied.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(R\) are finite.
\(c_r\ge0\) and \(d_{ar}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible benchmark solutions satisfy \(\sum_a d_{ar}x_{ar}\le c_r\) for every \(r\).

notation.meaning: Quantity of resource r allocated to agent a.
Local allocation value of agent a.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited resource-allocation section may support the capacitated model, but the DCOP ownership and inter-agent factor interpretation is not supported by the supplied locator and requires a DCOP-specific source.

children.title: Auction Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Bid-based coordination instances with private valuations, bundles, plus market constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Auction Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial-auction winner-determination instances used as distributed optimization benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be indivisible goods and \(B_i\subseteq2^G\) the bundles bid on by bidder \(i\). With bid values \(w_{iS}\) and binary acceptance variables \(y_{iS}\), an auction benchmark solves \[\max_y\ \sum_i\sum_{S\in B_i}w_{iS}y_{iS}\] subject to \(\sum_{S\in B_i}y_{iS}\le1\) for every bidder and \(\sum_i\sum_{S\in B_i:g\in S}y_{iS}\le1\) for every good \(g\). Bidder variables and valuations are local; item-conflict constraints coordinate bidders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The benchmark selects nonconflicting bundle bids of maximum total value, accepting at most one bid per bidder and allocation per good.
assumptions_latex: \(G\), the bidder set, and every \(B_i\) are finite.
Goods are indivisible and each accepted bid receives its entire bundle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted bids form a bidder-feasible, pairwise item-disjoint family maximizing reported value.

notation.meaning: Indicator that bidder i's bid for bundle S is accepted.
Reported value of the bundle bid.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: winner determination uses bidder and item packing constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The winner-determination formulation is standard and fits the benchmark leaf, but no inspectable source is cited for either the auction formulation or its distributed-benchmark interpretation.

children.title: Allocation-Auction Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Comparable instance structures, representation choices, plus limits of cross-family evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Allocation-Auction Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between indivisible allocation and combinatorial-auction winner determination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For indivisible goods \(G\) and agents with bundle values \(v_i(S)\), introduce one bid \((i,S,v_i(S))\) and binary variable \(y_{iS}\) for each represented bundle. The allocation \((S_i)_i\) corresponds to \(y_{iS_i}=1\), with all other variables zero. The auction constraints \(\sum_S y_{iS}\le1\) and \(\sum_{i,S:g\in S}y_{iS}\le1\) are respectively single-bundle and disjoint-allocation constraints, and \[\sum_i v_i(S_i)=\sum_i\sum_S v_i(S)y_{iS}.\] Thus feasible solutions and objective values are preserved in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bundle allocation and winner determination are equivalent when bids encode agents' bundle values: feasibility and total value are preserved.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and the represented bundle families are finite.
Each agent receives at most one represented bundle.
Unallocated goods are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an objective-preserving bijection between feasible represented allocations and feasible bid selections.

notation.meaning: Indicator selecting agent i's bundle S.
Agent i's value for bundle S.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: both formulations share the same set-packing variables and objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact correspondence lacks a source, and the stated bijection is not well-defined as written: auction feasibility permits a bidder to select no bundle, whereas the allocation tuple assigns each agent an S_i unless an explicit empty-bundle convention is imposed.

children.title: Sensor Coordination Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Sensing assignment, coverage, tracking, activation, plus observation coordination instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Sensor Coordination Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage-oriented sensor coordination benchmarks with local capacity and shared target factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be sensors and \(T\) targets, with visibility relation \(E\subseteq S\times T\). A sensor-coordination benchmark uses \(x_{st}\in\{0,1\}\) for \((s,t)\in E\), sensor capacities \(b_s\), and target rewards \(q_t\). It maximizes \[\sum_{t\in T}q_t\min\!\left\{1,\sum_{s:(s,t)\in E}x_{st}\right\}-\sum_{(s,t)\in E}c_{st}x_{st}\] subject to \(\sum_{t:(s,t)\in E}x_{st}\le b_s\) for every sensor. Each sensor controls its assignments; target-coverage factors couple sensors observing the same target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sensors select observable targets under capacity limits, maximizing covered-target rewards minus sensing costs while coordinating overlapping observations.
assumptions_latex: \(S\), \(T\), and \(E\) are finite.
\(b_s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), \(q_t\ge0\), and \(c_{st}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible assignment respects sensor capacities, and each target reward is counted at most once.

notation.meaning: Indicator that sensor s is assigned to target t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sensor coordination is modeled by capacitated maximum coverage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a specific capacitated maximum-coverage model rather than a source-supported definition of the full sensor-coordination benchmark family. A citation is needed to establish the intended local benchmark regime.

children.title: Network Configuration Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Channel, topology, capacity, interference, plus service-configuration instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Configuration Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Costed network-design instances whose distributed decisions select links or capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a candidate network, let \(x_e\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether edge \(e\) is installed, and let \(c_e\ge0\) be its cost. A network-configuration benchmark minimizes \[\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\] over configurations satisfying a declared service predicate \(P(x)\), such as terminal connectivity, capacity, reliability, or degree requirements. Edge or node owners control designated variables, and every component of \(P\) involving several owners becomes a coordination constraint. An instance must state \(P\) explicitly so that feasibility is independently checkable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed owners configure candidate network components at minimum cost while satisfying an explicit connectivity, capacity, reliability, or degree requirement.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite.
Installation costs satisfy \(c_e\ge0\).
The service predicate \(P\) is decidable on every binary configuration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal configuration belongs to \(\arg\min\{\sum_e c_ex_e:P(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: Installation indicator for candidate edge e.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The locator concerns network design, but the arbitrary service predicate and distributed ownership interpretation materially extend that model. A source supporting this DCOP benchmark definition is required.

children.title: Routing Benchmarks
children.top_down_role: Path selection, traffic distribution, vehicle movement, plus delivery coordination instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Routing Benchmarks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated multicommodity routing represented as a distributed constraint optimization benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be directed, and let each commodity \(k\in K\) have source \(s_k\), sink \(t_k\), and demand \(d_k\ge0\). A routing benchmark chooses flows \(f_e^k\ge0\) minimizing \[\sum_{e\in E}c_e\!\left(\sum_{k\in K}f_e^k\right)\] subject to flow conservation for every commodity and \(\sum_k f_e^k\le u_e\) for every edge. Distribution assigns variables to commodity, node, or link agents; conservation and shared-capacity constraints define their coordination factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity flows minimize routing cost while satisfying source-to-sink conservation and shared link capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(K\) are finite.
Capacities satisfy \(u_e\ge0\).
Each edge-cost function \(c_e\) is specified on \([0,u_e]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible flows conserve each demand and satisfy \(\sum_k f_e^k\le u_e\) on every edge.

notation.meaning: Flow of commodity k on edge e.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited minimum-cost-flow section does not, from the supplied evidence, establish the multicommodity formulation, nonlinear aggregate edge costs, or the DCOP ownership layer. Those extensions need specific support.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Quality Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-quality metrics for feasible solutions of finite maximization DCOPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization DCOP with optimum \(z^*\) and a feasible solution of value \(z\), define absolute suboptimality \(\Delta=z^*-z\ge0\) and relative suboptimality \[\rho=\frac{z^*-z}{\max\{1,|z^*|\}}.\] If only a valid upper bound \(U\ge z^*\) is known, report the certified upper-gap \(U-z\), or its normalized form \((U-z)/\max\{1,|U|\}\), explicitly distinguishing it from exact suboptimality. Comparisons must use identical instances, objective conventions, feasibility rules, and termination conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quality evaluation reports feasible objective value and exact or bound-based suboptimality under identical instance and termination conventions.
assumptions_latex: The reported solution is feasible.
The problem uses a maximization convention.
Any reported \(U\) is a valid upper bound on \(z^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le z^*-z\le U-z\) whenever \(U\ge z^*\).

notation.meaning: Objective value of the evaluated feasible solution.
Certified upper bound on the optimum.

children.title: Runtime Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Wall-clock time, processing time, latency distribution, plus scaling behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime measures separating elapsed time, computation, and distributed synchronization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed DCOP instance, implementation, platform, and stopping rule, elapsed runtime is \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=t_{\mathrm{stop}}-t_{\mathrm{start}}\). In a synchronous execution, round complexity is the number \(R\) of completed communication-computation rounds before stopping; local computational work may additionally be reported as \(W=\sum_a W_a\). A runtime evaluation records \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}\), \(R\), or \(W\) separately and specifies whether initialization, preprocessing, communication delay, and solution verification are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime evaluation separately reports elapsed time, synchronous rounds, or local computational work under a fully specified platform and timing boundary.
assumptions_latex: Start and stop events are defined before measurement.
All compared runs use the same stopping criterion.
Included execution phases are stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each reported runtime quantity has a fixed measurement boundary and resource interpretation.

notation.meaning: Local computational work performed by agent a.

source_refs.locator: 3.4.3 Ease of computing the solution p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.3 Ease of computing the solution p. 37

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited generic computing-ease section does not establish the distributed distinctions among wall time, rounds, and aggregate local work. A distributed-algorithm evaluation source and a defined unit for W_a are needed.

children.title: Memory Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Peak, cumulative, local, plus aggregate storage consumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak and aggregate memory metrics for distributed optimization executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m_a(t)\) be the bytes of live algorithmic state held by agent \(a\) at time \(t\), under a stated accounting rule. Define per-agent peak memory \(M_a=\max_t m_a(t)\), system peak memory \[M_{\mathrm{sys}}=\max_t\sum_a m_a(t),\] and worst-agent peak \(M_{\max}=\max_a M_a\). An evaluation reports at least one of these metrics and states whether code, input storage, message buffers, runtime overhead, and replicated data are counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory evaluation measures peak live state per agent or system-wide under an explicit rule for buffers, inputs, overhead, and replication.
assumptions_latex: The set of participating agents is fixed for the measured run.
Memory accounting uses the same inclusion rule throughout the run.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{\mathrm{sys}}\le\sum_a M_a\) and \(M_{\max}=\max_a M_a\).

notation.meaning: Counted live bytes at agent a and time t.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distributed memory requires per-agent and simultaneous aggregate peaks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports these distributed-memory accounting conventions. The time domain should also be specified or maxima replaced by suprema unless the execution is explicitly modeled by finitely many measurement states.

children.title: Runtime-Memory Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparative regimes where computation time shifts against local or distributed memory demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Runtime-Memory Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of runtime and memory at a fixed solution-quality requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance set, platform, stopping convention, and required solution quality \(q_0\). For each method \(A\) attaining \(q(A)\ge q_0\), let \(T(A)\) and \(M(A)\) be identically defined runtime and memory metrics. Method \(A\) dominates method \(B\) when \[T(A)\le T(B),\qquad M(A)\le M(B),\] with at least one strict inequality. The runtime-memory tradeoff frontier is the set of qualifying methods not dominated by another qualifying method. Any scalar ranking must declare normalized, commensurable metrics \(\widehat T\) and \(\widehat M\) and a weight \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), for example \(\alpha\widehat T+(1-\alpha)\widehat M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed quality requirement, a method lies on the runtime-memory Pareto frontier when no qualifying competitor uses no more runtime and no more memory with a strict improvement in at least one metric.
assumptions_latex: All compared methods satisfy the same quality threshold \(q_0\).
Runtime and memory use identical accounting conventions across methods.
\(T(A)\ge0\) and \(M(A)\ge0\) for every qualifying method \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A qualifying method \(A\) is frontier-efficient if and only if no qualifying method \(B\) dominates \(A\).

notation.meaning: Declared scalarization weight in the interval [0,1].

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: two-resource comparisons use Pareto dominance at fixed quality

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Message, byte, round, and bottleneck metrics for distributed DCOP executions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a terminating execution with transmitted-message multiset \(\mathcal M\), define message count \(N=|\mathcal M|\), communicated bytes \(B=\sum_{m\in\mathcal M}\operatorname{size}(m)\), and per-agent traffic \(B_a\) as bytes sent or received by agent \(a\), according to a declared convention. Report the bottleneck \(B_{\max}=\max_a B_a\); for synchronous protocols also report the number \(R\) of communication rounds. The accounting rule must state whether headers, retransmissions, broadcasts, initialization, and termination detection are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication evaluation reports messages, bytes, bottleneck agent traffic, and rounds using an explicit accounting rule for protocol overhead.
assumptions_latex: The measured execution terminates.
Every counted transmission has a defined sender, recipient convention, and encoded size.
The accounting boundary is fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\), \(B\), \(B_{\max}\), and, when applicable, \(R\) are reproducible under the declared convention.

notation.meaning: Maximum counted traffic of any agent.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: distributed communication is measured by counts, volume, rounds, and bottleneck load

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metrics are coherent and fit communication evaluation, but no inspectable citation supports the selected accounting conventions or their DCOP-specific use.

children.title: Anytime Performance Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Solution-quality trajectories, interruption points, incumbent stability, plus early-result usefulness.

assumptions_latex: The DCOP is a minimization problem with feasible set \(X\) and objective \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\).
A run reports feasible incumbents at ordered resource budgets \(0\le b_1<\cdots<b_m\).
A finite reference value \(F_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and scale \(s>0\) are fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The anytime-performance record of a run is the right-continuous incumbent curve \(U(b)=\min\{F(x_k):b_k\le b\}\), with \(U(b)=+\infty\) before the first feasible incumbent. Its normalized loss is \(g(b)=\max\{0,(U(b)-F_{\mathrm{ref}})/s\}\). For an evaluation horizon \(B>0\), report the budget-indexed values \(g(b_k)\) and the integrated loss \(A_B=B^{-1}\int_0^B g(b)\,db\), using a declared finite penalty when no incumbent exists. Algorithm comparisons must use the same resource definition, horizon, reference value, scale, and missing-incumbent penalty.

notation.meaning: Best objective value found by budget b
Horizon-normalized area under the loss curve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-form evaluation using incumbent quality over a declared resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The anytime-performance record of a run is the right-continuous incumbent curve \(U(b)=\min\{F(x_k):b_k\le b\}\), with \(U(b)=+\infty\) before the first feasible incumbent. Its normalized loss is \(g(b)=\max\{0,(U(b)-F_{\mathrm{ref}})/s\}\). For an evaluation horizon \(B>0\), report the budget-indexed values \(g(b_k)\) and the integrated loss \(A_B=B^{-1}\int_0^B g(b)\,db\), using a declared finite penalty when no incumbent exists. Algorithm comparisons must use the same resource definition, horizon, reference value, scale, and missing-incumbent penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anytime evaluation records incumbent quality at common resource budgets and summarizes the entire trajectory by a normalized area-under-loss measure.
knowledge_statements.title: Anytime Performance Evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this particular normalized anytime-loss metric or its comparison protocol. The formula also assigns +infinity before the first incumbent while subsequently requiring an undeclared finite substitution for integration, so A_B is not well-defined as written. A source and an explicit finite-valued penalized curve are required.

children.title: Convergence Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Stabilization behavior, termination outcomes, oscillation, plus sensitivity to stopping criteria.

assumptions_latex: Each run produces a measurable error sequence \((e_t)_{t\ge0}\) with \(e_t\ge0\).
A tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), persistence length \(h\in\mathbb{N}\), and maximum budget \(T\) are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The persistent convergence time is \(\tau_{\varepsilon,h}=\inf\{t\ge0:e_{t+j}\le\varepsilon\text{ for every }j=0,\ldots,h-1\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). A run converges within budget precisely when \(\tau_{\varepsilon,h}\le T-h+1\). Across independent runs, convergence evaluation reports the empirical success probability \(n^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{\tau^{(r)}_{\varepsilon,h}\le T-h+1\}\) and the distribution of finite hitting times. The definition of \(e_t\), whether based on objective error, bound gap, residual, or assignment stability, must be declared and held fixed across compared methods.

notation.meaning: Declared convergence error at step t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-budget empirical convergence with an explicit tolerance and persistence requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The persistent convergence time is \(\tau_{\varepsilon,h}=\inf\{t\ge0:e_{t+j}\le\varepsilon\text{ for every }j=0,\ldots,h-1\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). A run converges within budget precisely when \(\tau_{\varepsilon,h}\le T-h+1\). Across independent runs, convergence evaluation reports the empirical success probability \(n^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{\tau^{(r)}_{\varepsilon,h}\le T-h+1\}\) and the distribution of finite hitting times. The definition of \(e_t\), whether based on objective error, bound gap, residual, or assignment stability, must be declared and held fixed across compared methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence evaluation measures whether a declared error remains below tolerance, how often this occurs within budget, and the resulting hitting-time distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence Evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this persistence-based convergence protocol. The sequence is implicitly discrete, but the infimum ranges over t without declaring t in the nonnegative integers, and T and n are not fully introduced in the assumptions. Authoritative support and explicit discrete domains are required.

children.title: Anytime-Convergence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relationships between intermediate quality, eventual stabilization, plus finite evaluation horizons.

assumptions_latex: A minimization algorithm emits candidate assignments \((x_t)_{t\ge0}\) and certified lower bounds \((L_t)_{t\ge0}\).
Feasible candidates have finite objective value \(F(x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The run is monotone anytime when its reported incumbent values \(U_t=\min_{0\le k\le t,\,x_k\text{ feasible}}F(x_k)\) satisfy \(U_{t+1}\le U_t\). It is finite exact-convergent when some finite \(t_0\) satisfies \(U_t=L_t=F^\star\) for every \(t\ge t_0\). It is asymptotically exact-convergent when \(U_t-L_t\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\), without requiring a finite equality time. A run may be anytime without either exact-convergence property; conversely, an algorithm whose current candidate deteriorates is evaluated as anytime only through its best-so-far incumbent sequence.

notation.meaning: Best feasible objective through iteration t
Certified lower bound at iteration t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification for minimization runs with feasible incumbents and optional certified lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The run is monotone anytime when its reported incumbent values \(U_t=\min_{0\le k\le t,\,x_k\text{ feasible}}F(x_k)\) satisfy \(U_{t+1}\le U_t\). It is finite exact-convergent when some finite \(t_0\) satisfies \(U_t=L_t=F^\star\) for every \(t\ge t_0\). It is asymptotically exact-convergent when \(U_t-L_t\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\), without requiring a finite equality time. A run may be anytime without either exact-convergence property; conversely, an algorithm whose current candidate deteriorates is evaluated as anytime only through its best-so-far incumbent sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regimes distinguish monotone best-so-far improvement, finite certified optimality, and asymptotic closure of the certified optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Anytime-Convergence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the proposed regime taxonomy. The assumptions call L_t a certified lower bound but do not explicitly relate it to the finite optimum F^star or ensure incumbents exist, both of which matter for the stated gap criteria. A DCOP-relevant source and sufficient bound assumptions are required.

assumptions_latex: The private DCOP data are represented by a random variable \(S\) with declared prior distribution.
An observer's complete visible transcript is a random variable \(T\), including declared public outputs.
The entropy \(H(S)\) is finite and positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transcript privacy loss is \(L(S;T)=I(S;T)=H(S)-H(S\mid T)\), and its normalized form is \(\ell(S;T)=I(S;T)/H(S)\in[0,1]\). For an observer class \(\mathcal{O}\), evaluation reports \(L(S;T_o)\) for every \(o\in\mathcal{O}\), or the worst case \(L_{\max}=\sup_{o\in\mathcal{O}}I(S;T_o)\). The evaluation is meaningful only after specifying the private variable, prior, observer capabilities, transcript boundary, and whether the final solution is intentionally disclosed; changing any of these defines a different privacy experiment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic leakage under an explicitly declared observer and prior model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The transcript privacy loss is \(L(S;T)=I(S;T)=H(S)-H(S\mid T)\), and its normalized form is \(\ell(S;T)=I(S;T)/H(S)\in[0,1]\). For an observer class \(\mathcal{O}\), evaluation reports \(L(S;T_o)\) for every \(o\in\mathcal{O}\), or the worst case \(L_{\max}=\sup_{o\in\mathcal{O}}I(S;T_o)\). The evaluation is meaningful only after specifying the private variable, prior, observer capabilities, transcript boundary, and whether the final solution is intentionally disclosed; changing any of these defines a different privacy experiment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Privacy loss is the information about declared private data revealed by an observer's transcript, measured under a fixed prior and disclosure boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Privacy-Loss Evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports selecting mutual information as the privacy-loss evaluation for this DCOP container. The formulas are standard under the stated entropy assumptions, but they define only one information-theoretic privacy experiment and cannot stand as a general privacy-loss evaluation without an authoritative scope-specific citation.

assumptions_latex: A run records messages \(m_k=(s_k,r_k,\tau_k,\sigma_k,b_k,p_k)\) for \(k=1,ldots,M\).
Agent clocks are synchronized or timestamps are mapped to a declared common time base.

children.title: Pseudo-Tree Visualization
children.top_down_role: Tree edges, pseudo-edges, depth, separator context, plus branch balance views.

assumptions_latex: The interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\) is connected.
A rooted spanning tree \(T=(V,E_T)\) with root \(r\) is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rooted tree \(T\) is a pseudo-tree of \(G\) exactly when \(E_T\subseteq E\) and every non-tree edge \(\{u,v\}\in E\setminus E_T\) joins an ancestor-descendant pair in \(T\). A pseudo-tree visualization renders tree edges and non-tree edges with distinct encodings, identifies the root, and preserves the parent map \(p:V\setminus\{r\}\to V\). Depth \(d(v)\) and induced width may be displayed as annotations, but their values must be computed from the shown tree and interaction edges. Any edge violating the ancestor-descendant condition invalidates the displayed structure as a pseudo-tree.

children.title: Variable Ordering Visualization
children.top_down_role: Elimination, traversal, priority, plus search-order views.

assumptions_latex: The finite variable set is \(V\) with \(|V|=n\).
A total ordering is represented by a bijection \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A variable-ordering visualization must encode the bijection \(\pi\) so that \(\pi(u)<\pi(v)\) is visually recoverable for every distinct \(u,v\in V\). Given interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\), the induced elimination process removes variables in increasing order and connects all later neighbors before each removal. The visualization may display the resulting width \(w(\pi)=\max_{v\in V}|N^+_\pi(v)|\), where \(N^+_\pi(v)\) denotes the later neighbors of \(v\) at its elimination. Any displayed width or fill edge must be derived from the same declared ordering direction.

assumptions_latex: An interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\), rooted structure \(T\), and ordering \(\pi\) share the same variable identifiers.
Each annotation \(a(v)\) or \(a(e)\) is computed from a declared run or instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A structure-ordering overlay is a common-coordinate rendering \(\phi:V\to\mathbb{R}^2\) on which interaction edges \(E\), structural edges of \(T\), ranks \(\pi(v)\), and optional annotations \(a\) are superimposed. The overlay is consistent when every rendered object resolves to the same vertex set \(V\), every structural edge has endpoints in \(V\), and \(\pi\) is a bijection on \(V\). children.title: Algorithm Configuration Spaces
children.top_down_role: Parameter domains, implementation options, stopping controls, plus runtime environment settings.

assumptions_latex: An algorithm has parameters indexed by \(J=\{1,\ldots,q\}\).
Each parameter \(j\) has a declared domain \(D_j\), possibly finite, integer, real, or categorical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The raw configuration domain is \(D=\prod_{j\in J}D_j\). An algorithm configuration space is the feasible subset \(\Theta=\{\theta\in D:C_k(\theta)=1\text{ for every }k\in K\}\), where predicates \(C_k\) encode compatibility, conditional activation, and resource restrictions. Two configurations are distinct exactly when their active parameter-value maps differ. For reproducible evaluation, the specification of \(\Theta\) must include domains, defaults, activation predicates, feasibility predicates, numerical precision, and the transformation from a sampled point \(\theta\) to the executable algorithm settings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed and conditionally constrained parameter spaces for executable DCOP algorithms.

children.title: Algorithm Comparison Protocols
children.top_down_role: Instance matching, resource budgets, repetitions, baselines, plus reported comparison dimensions.

assumptions_latex: Algorithms \(a\in\mathcal{A}\) are evaluated on instances \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) under seeds \(s\in\mathcal{S}\).
A scalar loss \(Y_{a,i,s}\) and common stopping budget are fixed before execution.
The instance-seed pairs are sampled independently from a declared evaluation distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A paired comparison evaluates every \(a\in\mathcal{A}\) on the same admissible pairs \((i,s)\). For algorithms \(a,b\), define paired differences \(D_{i,s}=Y_{a,i,s}-Y_{b,i,s}\) and estimate \(\Delta_{a,b}=N^{-1}\sum_{(i,s)}D_{i,s}\), reporting uncertainty over the sampling unit. Configuration selection must use data disjoint from the final test pairs, or its cost and selection rule must be included in the comparison. Identical time, communication, or iteration limits are comparable only when the chosen resource has the same operational meaning for all algorithms; otherwise the protocol must report multiple declared resources.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired, held-out comparison under predeclared metrics and operationally comparable budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A paired comparison evaluates every \(a\in\mathcal{A}\) on the same admissible pairs \((i,s)\). For algorithms \(a,b\), define paired differences \(D_{i,s}=Y_{a,i,s}-Y_{b,i,s}\) and estimate \(\Delta_{a,b}=N^{-1}\sum_{(i,s)}D_{i,s}\), reporting uncertainty over the sampling unit. Configuration selection must use data disjoint from the final test pairs, or its cost and selection rule must be included in the comparison. Identical time, communication, or iteration limits are comparable only when the chosen resource has the same operational meaning for all algorithms; otherwise the protocol must report multiple declared resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algorithms are compared on paired instance-seed samples, with held-out tuning, predeclared loss and budgets, and uncertainty over the actual sampling unit.
knowledge_statements.title: Algorithm Comparison Protocols

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the paired protocol, held-out configuration rule, or operational-resource comparability principle. The notation N and the precise sampling unit are not introduced explicitly, while independence of instance-seed pairs may be stronger than common paired or blocked experimental designs permit. A suitable experimental-methodology source is required.

children.title: Configuration Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance variation across parameter choices, seeds, platforms, plus workload regimes.

assumptions_latex: The feasible configuration space is \(\Theta\), with configuration \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_q)\).
Performance loss \(Y(\theta,z)\) is integrable over evaluation condition \(z\sim P\).
A reference configuration \(\theta^0\in\Theta\) is fixed before sensitivity analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Let \(R(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim P}[Y(\theta,z)]\). The one-factor sensitivity of coordinate \(j\) at \(\theta^0\) is the response function \(S_j(v)=R(\theta^0_{-j},v)-R(\theta^0)\) over all \(v\) for which \((\theta^0_{-j},v)\in\Theta\). A scalar range summary is \(A_j=sup_v S_j(v)-inf_v S_j(v)\). Evaluation must report the reference configuration, varied domain, distribution \(P\), replication scheme, and uncertainty in estimated responses. This local one-factor measure does not identify interactions among simultaneously varied parameters.

notation.meaning: Expected performance loss at a configuration
One-factor response relative to the reference

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local one-factor sensitivity of expected performance around a predeclared reference configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim P}[Y(\theta,z)]\). The one-factor sensitivity of coordinate \(j\) at \(\theta^0\) is the response function \(S_j(v)=R(\theta^0_{-j},v)-R(\theta^0)\) over all \(v\) for which \((\theta^0_{-j},v)\in\Theta\). A scalar range summary is \(A_j=sup_v S_j(v)-inf_v S_j(v)\). Evaluation must report the reference configuration, varied domain, distribution \(P\), replication scheme, and uncertainty in estimated responses. This local one-factor measure does not identify interactions among simultaneously varied parameters.
