The statement also writes sup and inf without the required LaTeX operator commands, making A_j malformed. A directly supporting source and corrected operator notation are required.

children.title: Comparison Fairness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting valid comparisons across guarantees, information access, preprocessing, or resource budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparison Fairness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational fairness condition for empirical comparison of distributed constraint-optimization algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algorithms \(A\) and \(B\), a comparison is fair only if both are evaluated on the same sampled instances \(I\), with identical objective conventions, information availability, communication semantics, failure assumptions, and stopping rule. Their resource limits \((T,M,C)\) must be equal, where time, memory, and communication are measured by the same accounting method. Configuration selection must use equal tuning budgets and data partitions disjoint from the reported test set. A claimed dominance boundary is therefore valid only over the explicitly fixed protocol \(P=(I,T,M,C,S,H)\); changing any component of \(P\) defines a different comparison and invalidates direct aggregation of the results.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fair comparison fixes instances, semantics, resource accounting, stopping rules, and equal tuning opportunities. Results obtained under different protocols cannot be aggregated as direct evidence of dominance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) solve the same DCOP objective and report comparable solution-quality values.
\(I\) is sampled independently of configuration selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fair comparability holds only when \(P_A=P_B\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed necessary fairness conditions or the strong invalidation claim. The protocol component S is also undefined, so the exact condition P_A=P_B cannot yet be assessed reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Experiment Reproducibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replay certificate for experiments whose outcomes depend on distributed execution and communication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distributed experiment has a reproducibility certificate when it publishes an artifact \(R=(I,A,\theta,E,ho,L,V)\) containing the instance data, algorithm implementation and version, complete parameter vector, execution environment, random seeds, ordered event or message logs, and verification tolerances. Given \(R\), an independent execution must reconstruct every deterministic decision exactly and must reproduce each declared stochastic statistic \(q_j\) within its registered tolerance \(\varepsilon_j\), namely \(|q_j'-q_j|\leq\varepsilon_j\). If asynchronous schedules are not replayed, the certificate must specify their sampling law and enough independent repetitions to evaluate the same statistical estimand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reproducibility certificate records instances, code, parameters, environment, seeds, traces, and tolerances, enabling exact deterministic replay or statistically equivalent asynchronous reruns.
assumptions_latex: The recorded artifacts uniquely identify all externally supplied inputs.
Each reported stochastic quantity has a declared estimator and tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful replay verifies \(|q_j'-q_j|\leq\varepsilon_j\) for every registered quantity \(j\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate and its exact-replay or tolerance requirements are bespoke and uncited. An authoritative reproducibility source is needed to establish which artifacts and statistical conditions are necessary.

children.title: Distributed Meeting Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Multi-participant time, attendance, location, plus preference coordination.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Meeting Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-slot DCOP representation of meeting placement under private calendars and participant preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be meetings, \(T_m\) the admissible start slots for meeting \(m\), and \(P_m\) its required participants. Introduce \(x_m\in T_m\). Each participant agent \(i\) contributes a local cost \(c_{im}(x_m)\), equal to \(+\infty\) when the slot is unavailable, and a pairwise cost \(h_{imn}(x_m,x_n)\), equal to \(+\infty\) when meetings \(m,n\) requiring \(i\) overlap. Distributed meeting scheduling is the DCOP \[\min_{(x_m)}\ \sum_{m\in M}\sum_{i\in P_m}c_{im}(x_m)+\sum_{i}\sum_{\{m,n\}\subseteq M_i}h_{imn}(x_m,x_n).\] Any finite-cost minimizer is a conflict-free schedule minimizing aggregate inconvenience.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each meeting chooses one admissible slot. Participant-local costs encode availability and preferences, while infinite overlap costs enforce conflict-free calendars.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) and every \(T_m\) are finite.
Each meeting has fixed duration and required participant set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite optimum assigns one slot to each meeting and contains no participant overlap.

notation.meaning: Start slot selected for meeting m

children.title: Distributed Event Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Event placement across venues, resources, calendars, plus organizational owners.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Event Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon DCOP model for events sharing participants, venues, and other capacity-limited resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each event \(e\in E\) choose a start time and resource bundle \(x_e\in D_e\). Agent \(a\) owns local preference cost \(c_a((x_e)_{e\in E_a})\). For each resource \(r\) and time \(t\), let \(u_{er}(x_e,t)\) be the units consumed and \(b_{rt}\) the capacity. Distributed event scheduling minimizes \[\sum_a c_a((x_e)_{e\in E_a})\] subject to \[\sum_{e\in E}u_{er}(x_e,t)\leq b_{rt}\quad\text{for every }r,t.\] Domain restrictions encode permissible times and durations. Thus feasibility simultaneously enforces all local calendar restrictions and shared-resource capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Events select times and resource bundles. Local costs express preferences, and time-indexed capacity constraints prevent overbooking of participants, venues, or equipment.
assumptions_latex: \(E\), the scheduling horizon, and every domain \(D_e\) are finite.
Resource consumption is determined by an event's selected domain value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible minimizer satisfies every local domain restriction and every shared capacity bound.

notation.meaning: Time and resource choice for event e
Resource-r usage by event e at time t
Available capacity of resource r at time t

children.title: Coupled Calendar Coordination
children.top_down_role: Settings where meetings or events compete through shared calendars, participants, or facilities.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Calendar Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion distinguishing genuinely coupled calendar optimization from independent per-calendar scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let calendar \(i\) control \(x_i\in D_i\), let \(D=\prod_i D_i\), and write \(F(x)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)+G(x)\), where \(G\) includes all cross-calendar costs and extended-valued feasibility constraints. The calendar optimization decomposes into independent per-calendar problems exactly when there exist unary functions \(h_i:D_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and a constant \(k\) such that \(G(x)=k+\sum_i h_i(x_i)\) for every \(x\in D\). The calendars are coupled when no such representation exists. Shared meetings, precedence relations, synchronized availability, and shared capacities generally produce such coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calendar optimization separates only when the complete cross-calendar interaction, including feasibility constraints, can be rewritten as a constant plus independent unary terms. Otherwise the calendars are coupled.
assumptions_latex: Each calendar domain \(D_i\) is nonempty and finite.
All cross-calendar costs and constraints are included in \(G\), with infeasibility represented by \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independent per-calendar optimization is valid exactly when \(G(x)=k+\sum_i h_i(x_i)\) on \(D=\prod_iD_i\).

notation.meaning: Decision vector controlled by calendar i
Aggregate cross-calendar cost and feasibility term
Product of the individual calendar domains

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Agent Task Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary DCOP representation of allocating indivisible tasks to capacity-constrained agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite set of agents, \(J\) a finite set of indivisible tasks, and \(A_j\subseteq A\) the eligible agents for task \(j\). For each \(a\in A_j\), define \(x_{aj}\in\{0,1\}\), with \(x_{aj}=1\) exactly when agent \(a\) performs task \(j\), and impose \(\sum_{a\in A_j}x_{aj}=1\). If assignment \((a,j)\) consumes capacity vector \(r_{aj}\) and agent \(a\) has capacity vector \(b_a\), impose \(\sum_{j:\,a\in A_j}r_{aj}x_{aj}\leq b_a\) componentwise. With costs \(c_{aj}\) and optional agent-local interaction costs \(g_a\), the allocation minimizes \[\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{a\in A_j}c_{aj}x_{aj}+\sum_{a\in A}g_a((x_{aj})_{j:\,a\in A_j})\] subject to these assignment and capacity constraints. Assignment factors couple eligible agents, while capacity and interaction factors are local to individual agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables assign every indivisible task to exactly one eligible agent. Agent-local capacity and interaction constraints determine feasibility, and assignment and local costs determine the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(A\), \(J\), and every eligibility set \(A_j\) are finite.
Every \(A_j\) is nonempty.
Every task is indivisible and requires exactly one eligible agent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible optimum assigns each task to exactly one eligible agent without exceeding any agent capacity.

notation.meaning: Binary assignment of task j to eligible agent a

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Resource Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable-utility DCOP model for allocating divisible or indivisible shared resources among agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agents \(a\in A\) request resources \(r\in R\). Agent \(a\) chooses \(x_a\in X_a\), where component \(x_{ar}\) is its allocation, and incurs local cost \(f_a(x_a)\). With total resource capacities \(b_r\), distributed resource allocation is \[\min_{x_a\in X_a}\ \sum_{a\in A}f_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{a\in A}x_{ar}\leq b_r\ \text{ for every }r\in R.\] Integral domains model indivisible units; continuous domains model divisible resources. The shared capacity factors couple otherwise private agent objectives, making the model a DCOP whenever variables and factors are controlled by distinct agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents choose local allocations to minimize aggregate cost, while shared capacity constraints ensure total use of each resource does not exceed supply.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(R\) are finite.
Each local feasible set \(X_a\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible solution obeys \(\sum_a x_{ar}\leq b_r\) for all resources \(r\).

notation.meaning: Amount of resource r allocated to agent a
Local allocation domain of agent a

children.title: Distributed Routing
children.top_down_role: Decentralized path selection under capacity, timing, congestion, or locality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-factorized DCOP representation of routing multiple agents or commodities through a capacitated network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed network and \(K\) a finite set of commodities. Binary variable \(x_{ke}\) indicates whether commodity \(k\) uses edge \(e\). For each \(k\), flow conservation requires \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_{ke}-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_{ke}=\begin{cases}1,&v=s_k,\\-1,&v=t_k,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Edge capacities impose \(\sum_k d_kx_{ke}\leq u_e\). Minimizing \(\sum_{k,e}c_{ke}x_{ke}\), possibly augmented by congestion factors local to edges, yields a distributed routing DCOP when route variables or edge factors are owned by distinct agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each commodity selects a source-to-destination flow. Conservation enforces valid routes, edge capacities prevent overload, and local travel or congestion costs determine the optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(K\) are finite.
Each commodity has source \(s_k\), destination \(t_k\), and positive demand \(d_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible integral solution routes each commodity from \(s_k\) to \(t_k\) without exceeding edge capacities.

notation.meaning: Use of directed edge e by commodity k
Outgoing and incoming edges of vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Fleet Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrated assignment-and-sequencing DCOP model for vehicles with static route-load capacities and task time windows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a finite set of vehicles and \(J\) a finite set of service tasks. Task \(j\) has demand \(q_j\), service time \(s_j\), and a service-time window; vehicle \(k\) has capacity \(Q_k\). Binary variable \(y_{kj}\) assigns task \(j\) to vehicle \(k\), with \(\sum_{k\in K}y_{kj}=1\). Binary variable \(z_{kij}\) equals one when vehicle \(k\) performs task \(j\) immediately after task or depot node \(i\). Standard depot-flow constraints link \(y\) and \(z\) into one depot-rooted route per used vehicle. For a static route-load model, capacity is enforced by \(\sum_{j\in J}q_jy_{kj}\leq Q_k\). If \(t_j\) is the service start time, \(\tau_{ij}\) is travel time, and \(M_{kij}\) is a valid big-M bound, sequencing requires \(t_j\geq t_i+s_i+\tau_{ij}-M_{kij}(1-z_{kij})\), together with the task time windows. Minimizing declared travel, delay, and assignment costs coordinates the fleet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fleet coordination assigns each task to one vehicle and sequences assigned tasks into depot-rooted routes that satisfy static route-load capacities, travel times, and task time windows.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) and \(J\) are finite.
Demands \(q_j\) are nonnegative and represent load retained for the route, so total assigned demand is the relevant capacity measure.
Travel times, service times, vehicle capacities, depots, and time windows are specified.
Each \(M_{kij}\) is valid for its sequencing implication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution assigns every task once and realizes depot-rooted routes satisfying the stated static-load capacity and time constraints.

notation.meaning: Assignment of task j to vehicle k
Immediate sequencing of node i before task j on vehicle k
Service start time of task j
Static route-load capacity of vehicle k

knowledge_statements.title: Route-Fleet Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency conditions linking vehicle assignment, route incidence, capacity, and temporal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be vehicles, \(J\) tasks, and \(G=(V,E)\) a directed routing network in which task \(j\) is represented by node \(v_j\). Let \(y_{kj}\in\{0,1\}\) assign task \(j\) to vehicle \(k\), and let \(x_{ke}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate use of edge \(e\) by vehicle \(k\). Assignment and routing are consistently coupled when, for every \(k\in K\) and \(j\in J\), \[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v_j)}x_{ke}=y_{kj}=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v_j)}x_{ke}.\] Depot and flow constraints must make each used vehicle's selected edges a valid depot-rooted route. Load variables propagated over selected edges must remain within vehicle capacity \(Q_k\), and propagated arrival times must respect travel times, service times, and time windows. If either assignment-to-visit or visit-to-assignment linking is omitted, the formulation can permit an assigned task to remain unserved or a route to visit a task whose demand and cost are not assigned to that vehicle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assignment and route-incidence variables must agree in both directions. Valid depot flow, load propagation, and time propagation then ensure that every assigned visit is capacity- and time-feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(K\), \(J\), \(V\), and \(E\) are finite.
Each task corresponds to a distinct designated network node \(v_j\).
Every vehicle route begins and ends at its prescribed depot.
The route representation visits each task node at most once per vehicle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coupled feasibility requires \(\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v_j)}x_{ke}=y_{kj}=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v_j)}x_{ke}\) for every \(k,j\), together with valid depot flow, capacity propagation, and time propagation.

notation.meaning: Assignment of task j to vehicle k
Use of directed edge e by vehicle k
Incoming and outgoing edges of node v

knowledge_statements.title: Sensor-Network Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DCOP representation of sensor activation balancing target coverage, sink connectivity, and energy consumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let sensors be the vertices \(S\) of a finite communication graph \(G=(S,E)\), let \(s\in S\) be a designated sink, and let \(Q\) be a finite set of sensing targets. Sensor \(i\) chooses a mode \(x_i\in D_i\). Let \(z_i(x_i)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the selected mode is active, let \(a_{iq}(x_i)\geq0\) be its coverage contribution to target \(q\), and let \(e_i(x_i)\) be its energy cost. Required coverage levels \(L_q\) impose \[\sum_{i\in S}a_{iq}(x_i)\geq L_q\quad\text{for every }q\in Q.\] Requiring \(z_s(x_s)=1\) and the subgraph induced by \(\{i\in S:z_i(x_i)=1\}\) to be connected ensures that every active sensor has a communication path to the sink. Sensor-network coordination minimizes \(\sum_{i\in S}e_i(x_i)\), optionally plus declared sensing-quality penalties, subject to coverage and connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sensors choose operating modes. Coverage constraints meet every target requirement, active sensors must connect to a designated sink, and the objective minimizes energy with any declared sensing-quality penalties.
assumptions_latex: \(S\), \(Q\), and every mode domain \(D_i\) are finite.
Coverage contributions, energy costs, and communication edges are specified for every relevant sensor mode.
The designated sink \(s\) is a sensor vertex and has at least one active mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible optimum covers each target at level \(L_q\) and connects every active sensor to the sink.

notation.meaning: Coverage contribution of sensor i to target q
Required coverage level for target q
Indicator that sensor i is active in its selected mode

knowledge_statements.title: Wireless-Network Configuration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite DCOP model for joint channel and power selection under interference-dependent link requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N\) be a finite set of transmitters. Transmitter \(i\in N\) chooses a channel \(c_i\in C_i\) and power \(p_i\in P_i\), where \(C_i\) and \(P_i\) are finite. For its intended receiver \(r(i)\), define \[\operatorname{SINR}_i(c,p)=\frac{g_{i,r(i)}p_i}{\sigma_{r(i)}^2+\sum_{j\in N\setminus\{i\}:\,c_j=c_i}g_{j,r(i)}p_j}.\] Link feasibility requires \(\operatorname{SINR}_i(c,p)\geq\gamma_i\). Given a nonnegative power weight \(\alpha_i\) and a specified link-penalty function \(\ell_i:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\), a wireless-network configuration minimizes \[\sum_{i\in N}\alpha_i p_i+\sum_{i\in N}\ell_i(\operatorname{SINR}_i(c,p))\] over the finite channel-power domains subject to all SINR thresholds. Each SINR factor is scoped over the transmitter and the co-channel transmitters with nonzero gain to its receiver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transmitters jointly choose channels and powers. SINR thresholds enforce usable links, while specified power weights and link-penalty functions trade energy against interference-dependent link quality.
assumptions_latex: \(N\), every \(C_i\), and every \(P_i\) are finite.
Channel gains \(g_{j,r(i)}\) are nonnegative and receiver noise powers \(\sigma_{r(i)}^2\) are positive.
Each transmitter has a specified receiver \(r(i)\), SINR threshold \(\gamma_i\), nonnegative power weight \(\alpha_i\), and link-penalty function \(\ell_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible configuration satisfies \(\operatorname{SINR}_i(c,p)\geq\gamma_i\) for every \(i\in N\).

notation.meaning: Channel and transmit-power choice of transmitter i
Channel gain from transmitter j to the receiver of link i
Minimum SINR required by link i

children.title: Service Placement
children.top_down_role: Distributed placement of service instances across hosts, sites, edge nodes, or cloud regions.

assumptions_latex: The service set \(S\) and host set \(H\) are finite.
Each host \(h\) has capacity vector \(C_h\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\), and each service \(s\) has demand \(r_s\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\).
The admissible-host sets \(H_s\subseteq H\) and pairwise communication costs \(c_{st}:H_s\times H_t\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal F}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_s(x_s)+\sum_{\{s,t\}\in E_D}c_{st}(x_s,x_t)\right).\]

notation.meaning: Feasible placements satisfying admissibility and capacity.

review_flags: application-specific DCOP source with an exact service-placement formulation is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines capacitated, dependency-aware service placement as a finite DCOP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A service placement is a vector \(x=(x_s)_{s\in S}\) with \(x_s\in H_s\). Its feasible set is \[\mathcal F=\left\{x:\sum_{s:x_s=h}r_s\le C_h\ \text{componentwise for every }h\in H\right\}.\] Given unary placement costs \(a_s:H_s\to\mathbb R\) and a service-dependency graph \(E_D\), an optimal placement minimizes unary and dependency costs over \(\mathcal F\): \[\min_{x\in\mathcal F}\left\{\sum_{s\in S}a_s(x_s)+\sum_{\{s,t\}\in E_D}c_{st}(x_s,x_t)\right\}.\] A value \(+\infty\) encodes a forbidden joint placement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Service placement assigns every service to an admissible host, respects multidimensional host capacities, and minimizes local placement plus inter-service communication costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Service Placement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Service Placement leaf, and the variables and feasibility conditions are substantially explicit. However, no source is cited for this particular capacitated, dependency-aware DCOP formulation, so its application-specific modeling choices cannot be independently verified.

children.title: Component Placement
children.top_down_role: Placement of interacting software components subject to resource, affinity, locality, or dependency constraints.

assumptions_latex: The component set \(K\) and processing-node set \(V\) are finite.
Each component \(k\) requires resources \(d_k\in\mathbb R_+^q\), while node \(v\) provides capacity \(b_v\in\mathbb R_+^q\).
A component interaction graph \(G_K=(K,E_K)\) and admissible-node sets \(V_k\subseteq V\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathcal Y}\left(\sum_{k\in K}u_k(y_k)+\sum_{\{k,\ell\}\in E_K}w_{k\ell}(y_k,y_\ell)\right).\]
review_flags: application-specific DCOP source with an exact component-placement formulation is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses one placement variable per deployable component and pairwise interaction costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A component placement is a vector \(y=(y_k)_{k\in K}\) satisfying \(y_k\in V_k\). Capacity feasibility means \[\mathcal Y=\left\{y:\sum_{k:y_k=v}d_k\le b_v\ \text{componentwise for every }v\in V\right\}.\] With local deployment costs \(u_k:V_k\to\mathbb R\) and interaction costs \(w_{k\ell}:V_k\times V_\ell\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the placement problem is \[\min_{y\in\mathcal Y}\left\{\sum_{k\in K}u_k(y_k)+\sum_{\{k,\ell\}\in E_K}w_{k\ell}(y_k,y_\ell)\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component placement maps each deployable component to an admissible processing node while enforcing node capacities and accounting for deployment and intercomponent costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Placement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Component Placement leaf and distinguishes components from processing nodes consistently. No citation supports the exact capacity and pairwise-interaction formulation, so the record requires an inspectable application-specific source.

children.title: Placement Dependency Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cross-layer placement regimes linking service-level objectives to component-level dependencies.

assumptions_latex: A finite placement problem has variables \(x_i\in D_i\) indexed by a finite set \(I\), and dependency scopes \(S_\alpha\subseteq I\).
Each dependency cost \(f_\alpha:\prod_{i\in S_\alpha}D_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is locally evaluable.
The primal interaction graph is a simple graph whose vertices are the variable indices in \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{i,j\}\in E_G\iff i\ne j\ \text{ and }\ \exists\alpha\ \text{such that }\{i,j\}\subseteq S_\alpha.\]

notation.meaning: Placement variables and their finite domains.
Primal interaction graph induced by dependency scopes.

review_flags: exact source for the placement-specific coupling interpretation is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes how placement dependencies generate the DCOP interaction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dependency-coupled placement objective is \[F(x)=\sum_{\alpha}f_\alpha(x_{S_\alpha}).\] Its primal interaction graph \(G=(I,E_G)\) satisfies \[\{i,j\}\in E_G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i\ne j\ \text{ and }\ \exists\alpha:\{i,j\}\subseteq S_\alpha.\] Consequently, adding a dependency with scope \(S_\alpha\) adds all edges between distinct indices in \(S_\alpha\) to \(G\). A hard placement dependency is represented by \(f_\alpha(x_{S_\alpha})=+\infty\) precisely on the prohibited joint assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every multi-component placement dependency creates interactions between all distinct variables in its scope; hard dependencies assign infinite cost to prohibited joint placements.
knowledge_statements.title: Placement Dependency Coupling

assumptions_latex: Agents \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\) control finite resource-allocation variables \(x_i\in D_i\).
Each local or shared cost has a scope whose variables are known to its participating agents.
Global feasibility is representable by finite-valued costs and \(+\infty\)-valued violations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\prod_iD_i}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C}f_\alpha(x_{S_\alpha}).\]

notation.meaning: Collection of resource costs and constraints.

review_flags: distributed resource-management source establishing this DCOP representation is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents finite distributed resource management through scoped costs and hard constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A distributed computing resource-management instance is represented by the DCOP \[\min_{x\in\prod_{i=1}^nD_i}\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C}f_\alpha(x_{S_\alpha}),\] where each \(x_i\) encodes an allocation, scheduling, or configuration decision controlled by \(A_i\). A local capacity, compatibility, or service-level constraint is encoded by a scoped factor \(f_\alpha\), with \(f_\alpha=+\infty\) on infeasible assignments. The representation is distributed when every factor can be evaluated using information held by agents controlling variables in its scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed resource management is a DCOP when allocation decisions have finite domains and all capacities, compatibilities, and service costs decompose into agent-local scopes.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Computing Resource Management

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A DCOP representation is an appropriate knowledge kind for this application-family topic. The objective is mathematically coherent, but no resource-management source supports either the decomposition or the stated criterion for when it is distributed; scope-local evaluability alone may not capture ownership and communication assumptions.

assumptions_latex: The controlled junctions form a finite set \(J\), and each junction has a finite signal-plan domain \(D_j\).
Predicted traffic demand is fixed over the optimization horizon.
Every modeled delay or queue interaction has a finite junction scope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\prod_{j\in J}D_j}\left(\sum_{j\in J}d_j(p_j)+\sum_{e\in E_R}q_e(p_{S_e})\right).\]
review_flags: traffic-control DCOP source with explicit modeling assumptions is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon signal-plan selection with locally scoped congestion interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A traffic-control DCOP assigns one variable \(p_j\in D_j\) to each controlled junction \(j\in J\). For local delay costs \(d_j:D_j\to\mathbb R\) and road-interaction costs \(q_e:\prod_{j\in S_e}D_j\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), its objective is \[\min_{p\in\prod_{j\in J}D_j}\left\{\sum_{j\in J}d_j(p_j)+\sum_{e\in E_R}q_e(p_{S_e})\right\}.\] Coordination is local exactly when each scope \(S_e\) contains only junctions whose signal choices jointly affect the modeled flow or queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traffic control becomes a DCOP by assigning signal plans to junctions and decomposing predicted delay and queue interactions over locally coupled roads.
knowledge_statements.title: Traffic Control

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-horizon signal-plan representation fits the Traffic Control topic. An application-specific source is required, especially for the claim that coordination is local exactly under the stated scope condition, which is stronger than the objective formulation itself establishes.

children.title: Smart-Grid Coordination
children.top_down_role: Distributed coordination of grid devices, local controllers, network constraints, plus operational objectives.

assumptions_latex: Grid agents \(i\in I\) choose finite-domain schedules \(x_i\in D_i\).
Local operating costs and network coupling factors are defined over finite scopes.
Infeasible electrical or operational states receive cost \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\prod_iD_i}\left(\sum_{i\in I}c_i(x_i)+\sum_{\ell\in L}g_\ell(x_{S_\ell})\right).\]

notation.meaning: Grid agents and their schedule variables.

review_flags: exact smart-grid DCOP source is missing; supplied energy-network locator is indirect
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain coordination model for grid schedules and network constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smart-grid coordination instance has the DCOP representation \[\min_{x\in\prod_{i\in I}D_i}\left\{\sum_{i\in I}c_i(x_i)+\sum_{\ell\in L}g_\ell(x_{S_\ell})\right\}.\] Here \(x_i\) is agent \(i\)'s schedule, \(c_i\) is its local operating cost, and \(g_\ell\) models a network, balance, or market interaction among agents in \(S_\ell\). Hard limits are encoded by \(+\infty\). This is a DCOP precisely when the decision domains and factor scopes are finite and each factor is assigned to participating agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smart-grid coordination is represented by finite local schedules, private operating costs, and scoped factors for network, balance, or market interactions.
knowledge_statements.title: Smart-Grid Coordination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Smart-Grid Coordination and keeps the model finite-domain. No cited source supports the selected network, balance, and market factorization or the asserted precise condition for obtaining a DCOP, so the application model remains source-dependent.

children.title: Economic Dispatch Coordination
children.top_down_role: Distributed generation scheduling, load balancing, cost allocation, plus dispatch feasibility.

assumptions_latex: Generators \(i\in I\) choose outputs from finite sets \(P_i\subset\mathbb R\).
Each generator has cost \(C_i:P_i\to\mathbb R\) and bounds already incorporated in \(P_i\).
Demand \(D\) and an imbalance penalty \(\rho:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R_+\cup\{+\infty\}\) are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p_i\in P_i}\left\{\sum_{i\in I}C_i(p_i)+\rho\left(\sum_{i\in I}p_i-D\right)\right\}.\]
review_flags: exact distributed economic-dispatch DCOP source is missing; supplied energy-network locator is indirect
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete economic dispatch with a global balance factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Discrete economic dispatch can be represented as \[\min_{p_i\in P_i}\left\{\sum_{i\in I}C_i(p_i)+\rho\left(\sum_{i\in I}p_i-D\right)\right\}.\] Exact power balance is obtained by defining \(\rho(z)=0\) when \(z=0\) and \(\rho(z)=+\infty\) otherwise. The generator variables are local, whereas the balance term couples all generators in its scope. A distributed factorization may replace this global factor by auxiliary flow or partial-sum variables together with local equality factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete economic dispatch minimizes generator costs while an imbalance factor enforces or penalizes deviation of total generation from demand.
knowledge_statements.title: Economic Dispatch Coordination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The discrete dispatch representation is coherent and appropriate for the leaf. Nevertheless, no citation supports the exact DCOP formulation or the claim that auxiliary flow or partial-sum variables yield a distributed local factorization while preserving the intended dispatch model.

children.title: Grid-Dispatch Coupling
children.top_down_role: Regimes linking network-operational limits to distributed dispatch decisions.

assumptions_latex: Generator variables \(p_i\) occur in local cost factors \(C_i(p_i)\).
A balance factor enforces \(\sum_{i\in I}p_i=D\).
The primal interaction graph connects variables sharing any factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{p_i,p_j\}\in E_G\quad\text{for every distinct }i,j\in I.\]
review_flags: exact source connecting dispatch balance constraints to DCOP graph coupling is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows how an unfactored balance constraint globally couples dispatch variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent exact balance by the factor \[b(p_I)=\begin{cases}0,&\sum_{i\in I}p_i=D,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Because the scope of \(b\) is \(I\), the primal interaction graph contains the clique \(K_{|I|}\): every distinct pair \(p_i,p_j\) shares the balance factor. Hence an unfactored dispatch model has global coupling even when all generation costs \(C_i(p_i)\) are local. Introducing auxiliary flow or partial-sum variables can alter this graph while preserving feasible generator assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single exact power-balance factor couples every generator pair, producing a clique unless auxiliary variables refactor the balance equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Grid-Dispatch Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique consequence of placing every generator variable in one balance factor fits the Grid-Dispatch Coupling leaf and the property content kind. A source is still required for the dispatch-specific interpretation and for the auxiliary-variable preservation claim.

assumptions_latex: Devices \(i\in I\) have finite schedule domains \(D_i\).
A horizon \(T\), exogenous base load \(b_t\), and device load profiles \(q_{it}(x_i)\) are given.
Comfort and device constraints are locally evaluable or expressed by scoped factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\prod_iD_i}\left\{\sum_i c_i(x_i)+\sum_{t\in T}\phi_t\left(b_t+\sum_iq_{it}(x_i)\right)\right\}.\]

notation.meaning: Load contributed by device \(i\) at time \(t\).

review_flags: smart-home device-coordination DCOP source with an exact formulation is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon device scheduling coupled through aggregate household load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smart-home coordination problem assigns each device \(i\) a schedule \(x_i\in D_i\) and minimizes \[\sum_{i\in I}c_i(x_i)+\sum_{t\in T}\phi_t\left(b_t+\sum_{i\in I}q_{it}(x_i)\right).\] The term \(c_i\) represents local discomfort or operating cost, while \(\phi_t\) prices or penalizes aggregate load. Prohibited schedules are removed from \(D_i\) or assigned cost \(+\infty\). The model is a finite DCOP after each aggregate term is represented as a finite-scope factor, possibly using auxiliary sum variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smart-home coordination selects finite device schedules to balance local comfort costs against time-indexed costs of aggregate household load.
knowledge_statements.title: Smart-Home Device Coordination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite schedule representation fits Smart-Home Device Coordination. No cited source establishes this exact aggregate-load objective or the auxiliary-sum factorization needed to turn globally scoped time terms into the claimed distributed formulation.

assumptions_latex: The damaged network is a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) with controllable lines or switches.
Each controller chooses a finite switching or energization decision.
Radiality, capacity, safety, and supply-demand requirements are represented by finite-scope factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\prod_iD_i}\left(U(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C}f_\alpha(x_{S_\alpha})\right).\]

notation.meaning: Total penalty for unserved prioritized load.

review_flags: power-restoration DCOP source specifying network and electrical assumptions is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite switching representation of post-fault distribution restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A power-supply restoration DCOP has finite local decisions \(x_i\in D_i\) describing switch states, line energization, or load pickup. Its objective is \[\min_{x\in\prod_iD_i}\left\{U(x)+\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C}f_\alpha(x_{S_\alpha})\right\},\] where \(U(x)\) penalizes unserved prioritized load. Each factor \(f_\alpha\) equals \(+\infty\) when its scoped assignment violates a modeled radiality, line-capacity, voltage, safety, or consistency requirement. The formulation is distributed when every factor is evaluable by controllers associated with its scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power restoration selects finite switching and load-pickup actions, minimizing unserved-load penalties while hard factors enforce modeled network and safety constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Supply Restoration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A representation is suitable for the Power-Supply Restoration topic, but the global term \(U(x)\) is not decomposed into finite scopes, and the record does not specify the electrical variables or approximation under which voltage and capacity requirements depend only on the listed finite decisions. A restoration-specific source is necessary to determine a reliable formulation.

assumptions_latex: A finite pairwise DCOP has primal graph \(G=(V,E)\), and every variable has a domain of the same cardinality \(d\ge2\).
Pairwise costs may be arbitrary, and exact variable elimination represents generated factors explicitly as tables.
The induced width \(w^*\) is the minimum, over all elimination orders, of the maximum number of higher-priority neighbors created by elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{worst-case storage}=\Omega(d^{w^*})\quad\text{and}\quad\text{worst-case arithmetic work}=\Omega(d^{w^*+1}).\]

notation.meaning: Minimum induced width over elimination orders.

review_flags: authoritative DCOP inference-complexity source with exact bounds is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for explicit table-based exact variable elimination on densely coupled DCOPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w^*\) be the minimum induced width of \(G\) over all elimination orders, and suppose every variable domain has cardinality \(d\ge2\). For explicit table-based exact variable elimination, there are pairwise cost functions on \(G\) for which an order of induced width \(w^*\) generates a factor with \(w^*\) arguments and processes a bucket containing those arguments together with the eliminated variable. Consequently, worst-case storage is \(\Omega(d^{w^*})\) and worst-case arithmetic work is \(\Omega(d^{w^*+1})\). For a complete graph on \(n\) variables, \(w^*=n-1\), so these resources are exponential in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For explicit table-based exact elimination with equally sized domains, dense interaction graphs can force exponentially large intermediate tables and exponential arithmetic work; a complete graph has induced width one less than its variable count.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Interaction Graphs

children.title: Large Separator Pathology
children.top_down_role: Instances whose decomposition boundaries expose large shared variable contexts.

assumptions_latex: A finite DCOP is decomposed by an elimination order or pseudo-tree.
A generated separator contains \(s\) variables, each with domain size at most \(d\).
The separator cost is represented explicitly without exploitable algebraic compression.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{message entries}=\Theta\left(\prod_{i\in S}|D_i|\right)\le d^s,\quad\text{with equality when }|D_i|=d.\]
review_flags: authoritative source for separator-message size in exact DCOP inference is missing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit separator tables become exponential in separator cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit cost message over separator \(S\) is a function \(m_S:\prod_{i\in S}D_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Without compression or special structure, representing an arbitrary such message requires \[\Theta\left(\prod_{i\in S}|D_i|\right)\] entries. If every separator variable has domain size \(d\), the requirement is \(\Theta(d^s)\), where \(s=|S|\). Therefore unbounded separator cardinality prevents polynomial memory in the number of variables, even when each individual domain has fixed size \(d\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary explicit message over a separator needs one entry per joint separator assignment, so large separators cause exponential memory even with fixed-size domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Large Separator Pathology

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit-table cardinality statement is mathematically consistent and the failure-boundary kind matches Large Separator Pathology. However, no authoritative source is supplied for its use as an exact DCOP separator-message complexity claim.

children.title: High Induced-Width Pathology
children.top_down_role: Instances whose elimination or ordering structure produces broad intermediate dependency contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: High Induced-Width Pathology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential boundary for exact elimination-based DCOP inference under a fixed ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite DCOP have maximum domain size \(d\ge 2\), and eliminate its variables according to an ordering \(\pi\). If the induced width of \(\pi\) is \(w\), some intermediate function may depend on \(w\) uneliminated neighbors and therefore contain as many as \(d^w\) values. Computing that function by enumerating the eliminated variable can require \(\Theta(d^{w+1})\) local evaluations. Consequently, when \(w=\Omega(n)\), tabular exact inference can require exponential memory and computation even if the original constraint graph is sparse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large induced width makes exact tabular inference exponential; linear width can defeat scalability even on an originally sparse constraint graph.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) variables have finite domains of size at most \(d\ge 2\).
Intermediate functions are represented extensionally without compression.
Inference follows the elimination ordering \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=O(d^w)\), \(T=O(d^{w+1})\), and \(w=\Omega(n)\) permits exponential resource use.

notation.meaning: induced width of the elimination ordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but no relevant citation or locator supports the elimination model or bounds. The statement discusses possible worst-case requirements, whereas the conclusion gives only upper bounds; a source is needed to establish the intended worst-case lower/tight bounds and conventions.

children.title: Separator-Width Coupling
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where separator growth accompanies or predicts induced-width growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Separator-Width Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between pseudo-tree separators and induced width in exact inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted pseudo-tree and a node \(i\), let \(S_i\) be the ancestors adjacent to \(i\) or to a descendant of \(i\). Eliminating variables in a reverse pseudo-tree order produces an intermediate function from the subtree of \(i\) whose remaining scope is contained in \(S_i\). Thus its tabular size is at most \(\prod_{j\in S_i}|D_j|\). For the compatible elimination graph, the largest such separator cardinality is bounded by the ordering's induced width \(w\); large separators therefore witness correspondingly large inference width.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subtree communicates through its ancestor separator, whose size is controlled by the induced width of the compatible elimination ordering.
assumptions_latex: The constraint graph is finite and equipped with a rooted pseudo-tree.
Variables are eliminated in a reverse order compatible with that pseudo-tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{scope}(m_i)\subseteq S_i\), \(|m_i|\le\prod_{j\in S_i}|D_j|\), and \(\max_i|S_i|\le w\).

notation.meaning: ancestor separator of node i's subtree
induced width of the compatible ordering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits, but the ancestor-separator definition and its relation to induced width depend on pseudo-tree and ordering conventions. No inspectable DCOP source is supplied to validate the claimed inequality.

children.title: Inference Resource Consequences
children.top_down_role: Memory, message-size, preprocessing, plus local-computation pressure associated with these structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Inference Resource Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case tabular resources for exact pseudo-tree inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider exact bottom-up inference on a pseudo-tree with maximum separator size \(w\) and maximum domain size \(d\). A utility message indexed by a separator contains at most \(d^w\) values. Constructing it by minimizing over one local variable requires at most \(O(d^{w+1})\) arithmetic or comparison operations per node under bounded local constraint incidence. Across \(n\) nodes, the resulting worst-case bounds are \(O(nd^w)\) transmitted or stored values and \(O(nd^{w+1})\) local operations; compression or exploitable factor structure can reduce these bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact tabular pseudo-tree inference is exponential in separator width for message size, memory, communication volume, and local computation.
assumptions_latex: All domains have cardinality at most \(d\).
Messages are explicit tables and local constraint incidence is bounded.
The largest message separator has cardinality \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{values}}=O(nd^w)\) and \(T=O(nd^{w+1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits. The per-node and aggregate computation, storage, and transmission bounds depend on the precise inference algorithm, message retention policy, and bounded-incidence assumption, none of which has cited support.

children.title: Deep Pseudo-Tree Pathology
children.top_down_role: Decompositions with long dependency chains or limited parallel depth.

knowledge_statements.title: Deep Pseudo-Tree Pathology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential-round boundary imposed by pseudo-tree height.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a pseudo-tree have height \(h\), measured in edges on its longest root-to-leaf path. In any bottom-up protocol where a node sends its aggregate only after receiving every child aggregate, information originating at a deepest leaf requires at least \(h\) dependent communication rounds to reach the root. A path-shaped pseudo-tree on \(n\) nodes has \(h=n-1\), so its aggregation span is \(\Omega(n)\), independently of message size and the number of available processors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deep pseudo-tree creates a long dependency chain; a path requires linearly many aggregation rounds despite unlimited processors.
assumptions_latex: Each tree edge transmits at most one aggregation stage per communication round.
A parent aggregate depends on all child aggregates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\ge h\); for a path, \(R\ge n-1=\Omega(n)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the dependency-chain claim is plausible under the stated synchronous model, but no source with a specific locator supports that model or its application to DCOP pseudo-tree inference.

children.title: Poorly Balanced Pseudo-Tree Pathology
children.top_down_role: Decompositions with skewed branches, uneven workloads, or concentrated subproblem mass.

knowledge_statements.title: Poorly Balanced Pseudo-Tree Pathology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Load and span pathology caused by uneven pseudo-tree branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted pseudo-tree, let \(h_k\) be the height of the subtree rooted at child \(k\) of the root. A synchronized bottom-up computation cannot finish before the slowest branch, so its round complexity is at least \(1+\max_k h_k\). If one branch contains \(n-O(1)\) nodes while all other branches have bounded height, then \(\max_k h_k=\Theta(n)\). The short branches become idle while the long branch executes, and adding processors cannot reduce this critical-path bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbalanced pseudo-tree leaves short branches idle while one long branch determines linear completion time.
assumptions_latex: Parent processing waits for every child result.
Each dependency edge consumes at least one processing or communication stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\ge 1+\max_k h_k\), which is \(\Theta(n)\) for a single linear-size branch.

notation.meaning: height of the subtree rooted at root child k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but a branch containing n-O(1) nodes need not have height Theta(n); it could be broad and shallow. A source and corrected structural hypothesis, such as a linear-height branch, are required.

children.title: Depth-Balance Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where excessive depth combines with workload imbalance.

knowledge_statements.title: Depth-Balance Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint effect of critical-path depth and branch work imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign nonnegative work \(W_v\) to each pseudo-tree node and let \(P\) processors execute nodes only after their children complete. If \(W=\sum_v W_v\) and \(L\) is the maximum work sum along a root-to-leaf path, every schedule has makespan \(T_P\ge\max\{W/P,L\}\). Increasing branch balance can improve utilization and reduce \(W/P\)-limited idle time, but it cannot overcome a large critical path \(L\); reducing depth without balancing branch work can likewise leave the workload term dominant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runtime is bounded below by both average work per processor and the heaviest root-to-leaf dependency path; good structure must address both.
assumptions_latex: Node computations are nonpreemptive and obey child-before-parent dependencies.
At most \(P\) nodes execute simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_P\ge\max\{W/P,L\}\).

notation.meaning: number of processors or agents able to compute concurrently

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is reasonable, and the work/critical-path lower bound is standard for the stated precedence model. No authoritative locator supports the model or the additional claims about balance, utilization, and DCOP applicability.

children.title: Parallelism Loss
children.top_down_role: Coordination delay, idle capacity, critical-path growth, plus uneven agent utilization.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallelism Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel speedup ceiling induced by pseudo-tree dependencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\) be total unit-time work and \(h\) the number of nodes on a longest leaf-to-root dependency chain. On \(P\) processors, any valid bottom-up schedule has time \(T_P\ge\max\{W/P,h\}\), hence speedup \(S_P=T_1/T_P\le\min\{P,W/h\}\). For a chain pseudo-tree, \(W=h=n\), so \(S_P\le1\): no amount of additional processing capacity yields asymptotic parallel speedup. Broad independent subtrees can increase available parallelism but do not remove the critical chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pseudo-tree depth caps parallel speedup; a chain has no exploitable bottom-up parallelism even with arbitrarily many processors.
assumptions_latex: Every node has one unit of work.
A node executes only after all its children complete.
Communication overhead is excluded from \(T_P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_P\le\min\{P,W/h\}\); for a chain, \(S_P\le1\).

notation.meaning: parallel completion time on P processors
number of nodes on the critical dependency chain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits. The speedup ceiling follows under the unit-work, zero-communication scheduling model, but no cited source establishes that model or its use for pseudo-tree DCOP computation.

children.title: Large Domain Pathology
children.top_down_role: Instances with high-cardinality variable domains that enlarge local search or representation burdens.

knowledge_statements.title: Large Domain Pathology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-cardinality boundary for explicit exact inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every DCOP variable have at most \(d\) values, and suppose an intermediate factor has scope cardinality \(s\ge1\). Its unrestricted extensional representation may require \(d^s\) entries, while eliminating one additional variable by enumeration may inspect \(d^{s+1}\) assignments. Thus bounded graph width does not imply bounded absolute resource use when \(d\) grows: even fixed \(s\) gives polynomial growth of degree \(s\), and jointly increasing \(d\) and \(s\) produces exponential-scale tables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large domains can make exact tables and elimination expensive even when structural width remains fixed.
assumptions_latex: Factors are represented by unrestricted explicit tables.
All involved variables have domains of cardinality at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=O(d^s)\) and enumerative elimination costs \(O(d^{s+1})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but domains of size at most d yield upper bounds, not tables necessarily requiring d^s entries. The required worst-case or uniform-domain assumption and the meaning of exponential scale need authoritative support.

children.title: High-Arity Constraint Pathology
children.top_down_role: Instances containing constraints spanning many variables, agents, or ownership regions.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Arity Constraint Pathology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional representation boundary caused by constraint arity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unrestricted constraint \(f\) on variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\), with \(x_i\in D_i\), has one value for every tuple in \(D_1\times\cdots\times D_r\). Its extensional table therefore contains exactly \(\prod_{i=1}^r|D_i|\) entries. When \(|D_i|=d\ge2\), this is \(d^r\), exponential in arity \(r\). Consequently, high-arity constraints can make merely storing, communicating, or exhaustively evaluating the original DCOP input infeasible before any induced-width effects arise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted arity-r constraint needs a value for every domain tuple, producing exponential representation size when domains have at least two values.
assumptions_latex: The constraint is arbitrary and represented extensionally.
Every participating domain is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{table}(f)|=\prod_{i=1}^r|D_i|\), equal to \(d^r\) for uniform domains.

notation.meaning: domain of the i-th participating variable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the table-cardinality formula is precise under a complete extensional representation. No relevant source and locator is supplied for that representation model or its DCOP interpretation.

children.title: Domain-Arity Compounding
children.top_down_role: Regimes where domain size magnifies the burden created by broad constraint scopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Arity Compounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative interaction of domain size and factor arity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a factor with scope \(S\), the exact number of entries in its unrestricted extensional representation is \(N(S)=\prod_{i\in S}|D_i|\). Hence increasing one domain from \(d_i\) to \(d_i'\) multiplies storage by \(d_i'/d_i\), while adding a variable \(j\) multiplies it by \(|D_j|\). Under uniform domain size \(d\) and arity \(r\), \(N=d^r\); simultaneous increases in \(d\) and \(r\) therefore compound multiplicatively rather than additively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain size and arity multiply: enlarging a domain or adding a scoped variable scales every combination of the other dimensions.
assumptions_latex: The factor is represented as a complete explicit table.
All scoped domains are finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(S)=\prod_{i\in S}|D_i|\), and for uniform domains \(N=d^r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits and the multiplicative cardinality formula is mathematically coherent for complete explicit tables. It nevertheless lacks the required relevant citation and specific locator.

children.title: Representation Scale Consequences
children.top_down_role: Storage, evaluation, communication, plus local processing pressure from enlarged constraint representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Scale Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage and communication scale of explicit DCOP factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For explicit factors \(f_a\) with scopes \(S_a\), the input contains \(N=\sum_a\prod_{i\in S_a}|D_i|\) numeric entries. Storing the instance requires \(\Theta(Nb)\) bits when each entry uses \(b\) bits. Any protocol that transmits an arbitrary factor table losslessly across an ownership boundary must communicate at least its encoded information, up to coding assumptions; direct transmission uses \(b\prod_{i\in S_a}|D_i|\) bits. Intensional, sparse, or structured representations may avoid this extensional scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit factor storage and direct communication scale with the product of participating domain sizes, summed across constraints.
assumptions_latex: Every factor is stored as a complete table.
Each table value uses a fixed-width \(b\)-bit encoding.
Transmission is lossless.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{store}}=\Theta\!\left(b\sum_a\prod_{i\in S_a}|D_i|\right)\).

notation.meaning: bits used per encoded table value
total number of explicit factor entries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits for storage. The communication claim needs a precise worst-case, incompressibility, or fixed direct-encoding qualification because lossless protocols can compress particular tables. No source supports the encoding assumptions or lower bound.

children.title: Bandwidth Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Operational regimes constrained by link capacity, message volume, serialization cost, or contention.

knowledge_statements.title: Bandwidth Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication-time and throughput limits under finite link bandwidth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a communication link has payload bandwidth \(B>0\) bits per second and a coordination message has encoded length \(S\) bits. Even with zero propagation and processing delay, transmitting that message requires at least \(S/B\) seconds. If messages of length at least \(S\) traverse the same link sequentially, its sustained throughput is at most \(B/S\) messages per second. More generally, any network cut of aggregate capacity \(C\) carrying \(Q\) coordination bits imposes elapsed communication time at least \(Q/C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite bandwidth imposes message time equal to bits divided by capacity and limits coordination throughput across individual links and network cuts.
assumptions_latex: Bandwidth and cut capacities count usable payload bits per second.
The specified messages or bits must cross the relevant link or cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\ge S/B\), throughput is at most \(B/S\), and across a cut \(T\ge Q/C\).

notation.meaning: usable link bandwidth in bits per second
aggregate capacity of a network cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits and the serialization and cut-capacity bounds are plausible under the stated payload-capacity model. No relevant networking or DCOP source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Latency Bottlenecks
children.top_down_role: Operational regimes constrained by propagation delay, queueing delay, synchronization, or long communication paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Latency Bottlenecks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound induced by sequential message dependencies in a DCOP protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider one coordination episode whose message-dependency graph contains a directed path of length \(D\). If transmission \(k\) on that path has end-to-end latency \(\ell_k\), then the episode completion time \(T\) satisfies \[T\geq \sum_{k=1}^{D}\ell_k.\] Consequently, if \(\ell_k\geq \ell_{\min}>0\) for every dependency, then \(T\geq D\ell_{\min}\). Thus increasing bandwidth alone cannot reduce completion time below the sequential-latency bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chain of D dependent transmissions takes at least their total latency, regardless of bandwidth; with minimum latency l, completion requires at least D times l.
assumptions_latex: \(D\geq 1\) transmissions are causally sequential.
Each dependent transmission completes before its successor can begin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\geq \sum_{k=1}^{D}\ell_k\geq D\ell_{\min}\).

notation.meaning: length of a longest relevant message-dependency path

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports distributed-protocol latency lower bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential-latency bound is mathematically plausible and fits the failure-boundary container, but no citation or inspectable locator supports its communication model or DCOP interpretation.

children.title: Bandwidth-Latency Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where limited capacity amplifies delay or high delay changes effective throughput.

knowledge_statements.title: Bandwidth-Latency Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint throughput ceiling for bounded bandwidth and bounded in-flight coordination messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a communication channel have payload bandwidth \(B>0\), round-trip latency \(\ell>0\), and an in-flight window of at most \(W\) messages. If every coordination message has size at least \(s>0\), then any sustained delivery rate \(r\) obeys \[r\leq \min\!\left\{\frac{B}{s},\frac{W}{\ell}\right\}.\] Hence bandwidth limits serialization throughput, while latency limits reuse of the finite in-flight window; improving only one resource leaves the other ceiling unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Message throughput is bounded both by bandwidth divided by message size and by the in-flight window divided by round-trip latency.
assumptions_latex: The channel supplies payload bandwidth \(B\) and round-trip latency \(\ell\).
At most \(W\) messages may be in flight, each carrying at least \(s\) payload units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\leq \min\{B/s,W/\ell\}\).

notation.meaning: payload units transmissible per unit time
maximum number of simultaneously in-flight messages

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the bandwidth-delay window bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bandwidth ceiling is plausible, but the W/ell term depends on an acknowledgment-based window-reuse model that is not fully specified or supported by a cited locator.

children.title: Coordination Throughput Consequences
children.top_down_role: Effects on iteration rate, response time, scalability, plus timely solution delivery.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordination Throughput Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication-imposed upper bound on completed DCOP coordination episodes per unit time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each completed coordination episode requires at least \(q\) causally sequential message delays and transmits at least \(M\) payload units over a bottleneck link. For one-way latency \(\ell>0\) and payload bandwidth \(B>0\), its duration satisfies \[T\geq \max\!\left\{q\ell,\frac{M}{B}\right\}.\] Therefore the steady-state completion throughput \(\rho\) of non-overlapping episodes satisfies \[\rho\leq \min\!\left\{\frac{1}{q\ell},\frac{B}{M}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential delays and total communicated payload independently bound episode duration, so coordination throughput cannot exceed the smaller reciprocal bound.
assumptions_latex: Episodes do not overlap on the measured bottleneck resource.
Each episode requires at least \(q\) sequential delays and \(M\) payload units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho\leq \min\{1/(q\ell),B/M\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum sequential communication depth per episode
completed coordination episodes per unit time

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this DCOP communication-throughput model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound is coherent under the stated non-overlap assumptions and complexity_bound fits the terminal container, but no source supports this DCOP throughput model.

children.title: Message Loss
children.top_down_role: Missing transmissions, omission bursts, asymmetric loss, plus undelivered coordination state.

knowledge_statements.title: Message Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-based definition of message loss using unique transmission identifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the finite set of message identifiers sent during an execution and \(R\) the set of identifiers delivered before the execution deadline. Message loss occurs exactly when \[S\setminus R\neq\varnothing.\] The loss count is \(L=|S\setminus R|\), and the empirical loss fraction is \(L/|S|\) when \(|S|>0\). A delayed message is counted as lost relative to the chosen deadline, so that deadline is part of the execution specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sent message is lost when its unique identifier is absent from all deliveries made before the specified execution deadline.
assumptions_latex: Every transmission has a unique identifier.
A delivery deadline is fixed for the execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\setminus R\neq\varnothing\) characterizes message loss.

notation.meaning: set of identifiers delivered by the deadline

review_flags: No supplied locator directly defines communication-trace message loss.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent but adopts a deadline-relative convention under which delay becomes loss. That convention requires an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Message Reordering
children.top_down_role: Out-of-sequence delivery, stale arrivals, causal inversions, plus ordering ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Message Reordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trace-based violation of send-order preservation for messages on one logical channel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For messages with distinct identifiers on one logical channel, let \(s(m)\) and \(d(m)\) denote send and delivery times. Message reordering occurs when there exist delivered messages \(m\) and \(n\) such that \[s(m)<s(n)\quad\text{and}\quad d(n)<d(m).\] Equivalently, the delivery sequence is not an order-preserving subsequence of the send sequence after lost messages are removed. This definition separates reordering from loss and duplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reordering occurs when two delivered messages reverse their send-time order on the same logical channel.
assumptions_latex: Messages have distinct identifiers and comparable send and delivery times.
The compared messages use the same logical channel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists m,n:\ s(m)<s(n)\ \land\ d(n)<d(m)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly defines message reordering.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pairwise order-reversal predicate is plausible, but the claimed subsequence equivalence requires a precise treatment of duplicate deliveries. No source establishes the intended convention.

children.title: Message Duplication
children.top_down_role: Repeated delivery, replayed state, duplicate work, plus repeated control signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Message Duplication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity-based definition of duplicate delivery under stable message identifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each message identifier \(m\), let \(s_m\) be its transmission multiplicity and \(r_m\) its delivery multiplicity before the execution deadline. Message duplication occurs exactly when \[\exists m\quad r_m>s_m.\] In the usual unique-send convention \(s_m=1\), identifier \(m\) is duplicated precisely when \(r_m\geq 2\). The excess-duplicate count is \(D=\sum_m\max\{0,r_m-s_m\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplication occurs when a message identifier is delivered more times than it was transmitted; excess delivery multiplicities count the duplicates.
assumptions_latex: Identifiers remain stable across transmission and delivery.
Transmission and delivery multiplicities are measured over one execution interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists m:\ r_m>s_m\) characterizes duplication.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly defines duplicate message delivery.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicity predicate is coherent, but its treatment of retransmissions and stable identifiers is convention-dependent and unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Combined Delivery Faults
children.top_down_role: Operational regimes containing multiple delivery anomalies with interacting consistency effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Delivery Faults
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified trace predicate for loss, reordering, and duplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(m_1,\ldots,m_p)\) be the ordered send trace and \(R=(n_1,\ldots,n_q)\) the delivery trace on one logical channel. A combined delivery fault occurs when at least two of the following predicates hold: \(L\), some sent identifier has smaller delivery multiplicity; \(D\), some identifier has larger delivery multiplicity; and \(O\), two delivered identifiers occur in the reverse of their send order. Formally, \[\mathbf{1}_L+\mathbf{1}_D+\mathbf{1}_O\geq 2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined delivery fault is an execution exhibiting at least two among message loss, duplication, and order reversal.
assumptions_latex: Messages carry stable identifiers.
Send and delivery traces refer to one channel and one fixed observation interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbf{1}_L+\mathbf{1}_D+\mathbf{1}_O\geq 2\).
review_flags: The exact taxonomy convention for combined faults lacks supporting evidence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Defining a combined fault as at least two fault predicates is a nonstandard taxonomy choice that cannot be validated without a supporting source and precise constituent predicates.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Graph Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indistinguishability boundary for exact coordination across disconnected communication components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the communication graph be partitioned into nonempty components \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) with no intercomponent messages after time \(t_0\). Suppose two DCOP instances \(I\) and \(I'\) induce identical post-\(t_0\) information in every component, but every global optimum of \(I\) assigns some component \(C_j\) differently from every global optimum of \(I'\). Then any deterministic protocol operating after \(t_0\) produces the same output in \(C_j\) on both instances and therefore cannot be globally optimal on both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disconnected components cannot distinguish globally different instances with identical local information, so no deterministic protocol can guarantee an exact optimum for both.
assumptions_latex: No information crosses between distinct components after \(t_0\).
Instances \(I\) and \(I'\) are locally indistinguishable within every component.
Their global optima require different outputs in some component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No deterministic post-partition protocol is globally optimal on both \(I\) and \(I'\).

notation.meaning: a connected component of the partitioned communication graph
time after which intercomponent communication ceases

review_flags: The supplied graph-theory locators do not support the DCOP indistinguishability conclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indistinguishability boundary fits the container, but the local-state, output, and post-partition protocol model needs formal source support. The listed graph-theory material does not establish the DCOP conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Environmental Change Faster Than Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Staleness boundary when objective versions change before coordination can finish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_t\) be the DCOP objective active at time \(t\), and suppose a protocol needs at least \(\tau>0\) time from observing a version to installing its coordinated assignment. If each objective version remains active for less than \(\tau\), then an assignment computed solely from observations of that version cannot be installed while the same version remains active. Without a predictive relation between successive objectives, exact optimality for the current objective cannot be guaranteed from such stale observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every objective version changes sooner than coordination completes, snapshot-based assignments are stale at installation and cannot guarantee current optimality without prediction.
assumptions_latex: Coordination delay is at least \(\tau>0\).
Every objective version persists for a duration strictly below \(\tau\).
No predictive restriction links successive objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Snapshot-based coordination cannot guarantee an optimizer of the objective active at installation time.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports dynamic-DCOP staleness boundaries.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The staleness boundary is plausible, but the adversarial evolution and absence-of-prediction model needed for the impossibility conclusion are not backed by an inspectable dynamic-DCOP source.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Valuation Asymmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic boundary caused by private valuations omitted from protocol observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let agent \(i\) privately know valuation \(u_i(x)\), while a protocol observes only transcript \(H\). Suppose there exist valuation profiles \(u\) and \(u'\) producing the same transcript \(H\), but their welfare maximizers are disjoint: \[\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in X}\sum_i u_i(x)\;\cap\;\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in X}\sum_i u'_i(x)=\varnothing.\] Any deterministic transcript-based rule selects the same assignment under both profiles and therefore fails to maximize true welfare for at least one profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If distinct private valuation profiles look identical to the protocol but require different optima, one transcript-based decision must be wrong.
assumptions_latex: The feasible assignment set \(X\) is common to both profiles.
Profiles \(u\) and \(u'\) generate the same observable transcript.
Their welfare-maximizer sets are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No deterministic rule depending only on \(H\) maximizes true welfare for both profiles.
review_flags: No supplied locator supports this private-information indistinguishability boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transcript-indistinguishability argument is coherent and fits a failure boundary, but no source supports the private-valuation observation model or its applicability to DCOPs.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Aggregation Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic failure when the modeled aggregator and application objective select different assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the feasible assignment set, let the DCOP minimize the additive model \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}f_i(x)\), and let the application evaluate assignments by \(G(x)\), possibly using a nonadditive aggregator. An objective-aggregation mismatch affecting correctness occurs when \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\not\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}G(x).\] In that case, solving the DCOP exactly does not guarantee an application-optimal assignment.
